FOREWORD

前言

This foreword is written by Guy Spier , a Zurich -based investor and friend. He is the author of “ The Education of a Value Investor ” and the manager of the Aquamarine Fund .

这篇前言由常驻苏黎世的投资人兼好友盖伊·斯皮尔撰写。他是《价值投资者的教育》一书的作者，也是海蓝宝石基金的经理。

While this foreword focuses on investing, this book will help you achieve long-term success however you define it, be it financial, professional, personal, or spiritual. In fact, the four are deeply interconnected. For example, as Guy himself noted, it is hard to make good investing and professional decisions if your life and relationships outside of work are unstable.

虽然这篇前言侧重于投资，但本书将帮助你实现你所定义的长期成功，无论是财务、职业、个人还是精神方面的成功。事实上，这四者之间有着深刻的联系。例如，正如盖伊本人所指出的，如果你的工作之外的生活和人际关系不稳定，就很难做出良好的投资和职业决策。

Precisely because of his acknowledgment of how the naive optimization of any single area of our lives is counterproductive, and of his awareness of how survivorship bias makes us underestimate the importance of playing the long game, Guy seemed the natural choice for the foreword of this book. So , I felt honored when he wrote one.

正因为他认识到，对生活中任何单一领域的盲目优化都会适得其反，并且意识到幸存者偏差会让我们低估长远规划的重要性，盖伊自然而然地成为了本书序言的最佳人选。所以，当他真的为本书作序时，我感到非常荣幸。

Enjoy the foreword and, then, the book.

先欣赏前言，然后再阅读正文。

# ↩

Berkshire Hathaway might be the most successful company that ever existed. What made it so successful? Many talk about the Berkshire Hathaway system - but what exactly is that? Simply to call it “ Value Investing ” is nowhere near enough. Most would prefer to fall back on Charlie Munger's ideas: worldly wisdom, avoiding human misjudgments and applying the ancient stoics in daily life. Ultimately , that Seneca , Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus are the source of Berkshire’s success.

伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司或许是史上最成功的公司。它成功的秘诀是什么？许多人都在谈论伯克希尔·哈撒韦体系——但它究竟是什么？仅仅称之为“价值投资”远远不够。大多数人更倾向于查理·芒格的理念：汲取世俗智慧，避免人为误判，并将古代斯多葛学派的哲学应用于日常生活。归根结底，塞内卡、马可·奥勒留和爱比克泰德的思想才是伯克希尔成功的源泉。

That is all true - but it misses key elements. One is that Warren and Charlie have always played long games. It's a truism. But what does it mean in practice?

这些都没错——但却忽略了关键要素。其中之一是，沃伦和查理一向擅长长远布局。这虽是老生常谈，但实际操作中又意味着什么呢？

Despite my having been a student of Berkshire Hathaway , Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger as long as most, and despite knowing that a key to success is to play long-term games, I did not understand the ideas behind this in granular detail.

尽管我像大多数人一样，长期以来一直是伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司、沃伦·巴菲特和查理·芒格的追随者，也知道成功的关键在于进行长期投资，但我并不完全理解其中的理念。

Thankfully, help has come - from an unexpected source. Luca Dellanna is an Italian , from Turin , and is married to a Singaporean – in other words, far away from Berkshire Hathaway in Omaha .

幸好，意想不到的人伸出了援手。卢卡·德拉纳是意大利人，来自都灵，他的妻子是新加坡人——换句话说，他离位于奥马哈的伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司很远。

Nevertheless, his new book, Winning Long - Term Games , has revealed to me many of the pieces of the puzzle that up to now remained obscured. Any student of value investing, of Buffett , Munger and Berkshire Hathaway , will uncover in Dellanna's book gem upon gem of insight into how Warren did it at Berkshire and furthermore will develop many insights and strategies for how to play long-term games in their own lives.

然而，他的新书《赢得长期博弈》让我解开了许多此前一直不为人知的谜题。任何研究价值投资、巴菲特、芒格和伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司的人，都能在戴兰纳的书中发现许多关于沃伦在伯克希尔如何取得成功的真知灼见，并且还能从中获得许多关于如何在自己的生活中进行长期博弈的见解和策略。

In short: it’s a must read for all students of value investing, for all those who follow Warren and Charlie , and - most importantly - for all those who plan on being successful, and who take the goal of achieving that success with the deadly, focused and unwavering seriousness it deserves.

简而言之：对于所有价值投资的学生、所有追随沃伦和查理的人来说，以及——最重要的是——对于所有计划获得成功，并以应有的、极其专注和坚定不移的严肃态度对待实现成功目标的人来说，这都是一本必读之作。

Guy Spier

盖伊·斯皮尔

PART I
第一部分

WINNING LONG-TERM GAMES

赢得长期比赛

“Both short- and long-term players

“无论是短期参与者还是长期参与者。”

have long-term goals,

制定长期目标，

and they both play short-term games .

他们都玩的是短期游戏。

The difference is that short-term players

区别在于短期玩家

play short-term games to win them,

为了赢得短期胜利而玩弄短期游戏。

whereas long-term players play short-term games

而长期玩家则玩短期游戏。

to advance their long-term goals.”

以推进他们的长期目标。

# ↩
1

THE FIRST PRINCIPLE

第一原理

T he key to winning long-term games is to stop playing them as a succession of separate short-term games.

赢得长期比赛的关键在于停止将比赛视为一系列独立的短期比赛。

Yet, most people take the opposite approach.

然而，大多数人却采取相反的做法。

  1. The manager who views each interaction with her team as a separate game. Every time she talks to her subordinates, it’s to get things done rather than to develop their skills. As a result, she fails to build the long-term assets (a competent team) she needs in order to win her long-term game (a successful career).
    这位管理者将与团队的每一次互动都视为一场独立的游戏。她每次与下属交谈，都是为了完成任务，而不是为了培养他们的技能。结果，她无法建立起赢得长期目标（成功职业生涯）所需的长期资产（一支称职的团队）。
  2. The spouse who lies as a way to avoid responsibility. If lying has, say, a 1% chance of being discovered, it is a great short-term tactic (it succeeds 99% of the time) but a terrible long-term strategy (if you lie once a week, you have a 99.5% chance of getting caught over a decade).
    配偶为了逃避责任而撒谎。如果撒谎被发现的概率只有1%，那么短期内这是一种很好的策略（成功率高达99%），但长期来看却是一种糟糕的策略（如果你每周撒谎一次，十年后被发现的概率高达99.5%）。
  3. The solopreneur who treats each email to his mailing list as a separate game. He consumes his audience’s trust to generate more sales within a single email instead of building trust to create more sales over time.
    这位独立创业者把发给邮件列表的每一封邮件都当作一场独立的游戏。他为了在一封邮件中促成更多销售，不去建立信任，而是消耗受众的信任。

These three examples show that approaching long-term games as a succession of separate short-term games is a bad strategy despite working great over short time horizons.

这三个例子表明，尽管在短期内效果很好，但将长期博弈视为一系列独立的短期博弈是一种糟糕的策略。

The better strategy

更好的策略

…is to embrace the repeated nature of long-term games.

……就是要接受长期游戏的重复性。

This doesn’t mean proceeding slowly or delaying gratification; not at all. Instead , it means playing short-term games not to win them but to increase your chances of winning the long-term game.

这并非意味着放慢脚步或延迟满足；完全不是。相反，它的意思是参与短期游戏不是为了赢，而是为了增加赢得长期游戏的几率。

For example:

例如：

• Use short-term games to build long-term assets such as trust, know-how, habits, and relationships. Any success achieved without these won’t last long.

• 利用短期博弈来建立长期资产，例如信任、专业知识、习惯和人际关系。任何缺乏这些资产的成功都无法持久。

• Play iterated games. Interact with people not to get the most out of each interaction, but to improve the next one.

• 进行迭代式游戏。与人互动不是为了从每次互动中获得最大利益，而是为了改进下一次互动。

• Take risks, but never risks that might damage your long-term assets (capital, trust, health, etc.).

• 承担风险，但绝不能承担可能损害你的长期资产（资本、信托、健康等）的风险。

• Take on projects that might not work, but do it in such a way that even failure brings you closer to success by building skills, self-knowledge, and relationships.

• 承担一些可能不会成功的项目，但要以一种即使失败也能让你通过培养技能、自我认知和人际关系而更接近成功的方式来完成。

Notice the common thread. Winning long-term games isn't about going slow or avoiding short-term games.

注意其中的共同点。赢得长期比赛的关键不在于放慢速度或避免短期比赛。

It’s about playing short-term games as parts of long-term ones, not to win the former but to win the latter.

关键在于将短期博弈作为长期博弈的一部分，不是为了赢得短期博弈，而是为了赢得长期博弈。

# ↩

Chapter summary

章节概要

This chapter illustrates the first principle of winning long-term games: play short-term games not to win them, but to progress toward your long-term objective.

本章阐述了赢得长期比赛的第一原则：参与短期比赛不是为了赢得比赛，而是为了朝着你的长期目标前进。

When considering how to play a given short-term game, examine the impact of all options on your longer-term goals and choose the option with the most positive influence.

在考虑如何进行某个短期博弈时，要考察所有选项对长期目标的影响，并选择影响最大的选项。

Of course, sometimes you need to win short-term games to make progress toward your long-term goals, such as when an important deadline is looming. But even then, how you choose to win the short-term game will significantly impact your long-term goals, and this is something you should consider.

当然，有时候你需要赢得短期博弈才能朝着长期目标迈进，例如在重要截止日期临近时。但即便如此，你选择如何赢得短期博弈也会对你的长期目标产生重大影响，这一点你应该认真考虑。

Otherwise, you may find yourself winning short-term games but making no progress toward your long-term goals – a very frustrating situation.

否则，你可能会发现自己赢得了短期比赛，但在实现长期目标方面却毫无进展——这是一种非常令人沮丧的情况。

* * *

This was the first principle to win long-term games.

这是赢得长期比赛的第一原则。

The next chapter is about the second and last principle.

下一章将介绍第二个也是最后一个原则。

# ↩
2

THE SECOND PRINCIPLE

第二原则

Y ou can win long-term games without addressing common causes of failure, but the chances are that you won’t.

即使不解决常见的失败原因，你也有可能赢得长期比赛，但你很可能做不到。

Over short time frames, things are different: you can get away with ignoring common causes of failure, and you probably will. For example, if you have a single two-month project, you can safely ignore burnout. Work on it as hard as possible; you won’t burn out. But a whole career? Over long time frames, risks compound, and your chances of avoiding their consequences are slim.

在短期内，情况有所不同：你可以忽略一些常见的失败原因，而且你很可能真的会这么做。例如，如果你只有一个为期两个月的项目，你可以放心地忽略倦怠。尽你所能地努力工作；你不会倦怠。但如果是整个职业生涯呢？随着时间的推移，风险会不断累积，你避免其后果的可能性微乎其微。

As another example, over short time frames, you can ignore root problems. If your career isn’t taking off because you lack some fundamental skills, in the short term, you can overcompensate by working harder. But that’s not sustainable over extended time frames.

再举一个例子，在短期内，你可以忽略根本问题。如果你的事业发展不顺是因为你缺乏一些基本技能，短期内你可以通过更加努力来弥补。但这在长期来看是不可持续的。

As a third and final example, a common reason people get stuck in their careers after some initial progress is a lack of a solid professional network. While it is possible to succeed without one, not having one significantly reduces your chances. So , if professional achievement is important to you, you should do what it takes to maximize your chances of success.

第三个也是最后一个例子是，人们在事业初期取得一些进展后停滞不前的一个常见原因是缺乏稳固的专业人脉。虽然没有人脉也有可能成功，但缺乏人脉会大大降低成功的机会。因此，如果你重视职业成就，就应该尽一切努力最大限度地提高成功几率。

Can you spot the common thread across all three examples?

你能找出这三个例子之间的共同点吗？

In all of them, thinking about how you might fail is superfluous in the short term – in the sense that, in the short term, risks are unlikely to materialize, and thus, any risk management activity appears to be a waste of time.

在所有这些情况下，思考你可能会如何失败在短期内都是多余的——因为在短期内，风险不太可能发生，因此，任何风险管理活动似乎都是在浪费时间。

However, it is not superfluous over the long term, over which even unlikely risks have a significant chance of materializing.

然而，从长远来看，它并非多余，因为即使是不太可能发生的风险，在长期内也有很大的可能性变成现实。

Similarly, thinking about how you might fail is superfluous in the sense that you can succeed without addressing common causes of failure. Sometimes , people get lucky.

同样，思考你可能会如何失败是多余的，因为即使不考虑常见的失败原因，你也可能成功。有时候，人们只是运气好。

But it’s not superfluous if you’re unsatisfied with merely a chance at succeeding and want instead a good chance of success.

但如果你不满足于仅仅有成功的机会，而是想要有更大的成功机会，那么这样做就不是多余的。

To have a good chance of winning long-term games, you must be aware of common sources of failure and do something about them before it’s too late.

要想在长期游戏中取得好成绩，你必须意识到常见的失败原因，并在为时已晚之前采取措施加以解决。

One way to become aware of common sources of failure is a simple technique called pre-mortems. It consists of imagining yourself in a few years, in a scenario where you failed, and asking yourself, “ What could have caused me to fail, and what can I do about it now?”

了解常见失败原因的一种方法是使用一种叫做“事前验尸”的简单技巧。它包括想象几年后的自己，假设你当时失败了，然后问自己：“是什么原因导致我失败？我现在可以做些什么来避免这种情况？”

Another way to become aware of common sources of failure is to examine how others who had a similar goal to yours failed. The following few pages discuss this.

了解常见失败原因的另一种方法是研究那些与你目标相似的人是如何失败的。以下几页将对此进行探讨。

# ↩

22 common reasons you might fail

22个可能导致失败的常见原因

Below are 22 common reasons why you might not achieve your long-term goals. Other parts of this book explore most of these items in greater detail, but it’s useful to summarize them here.

以下列出了22个可能导致你无法实现长期目标的常见原因。本书其他章节会更详细地探讨其中大部分内容，但在此进行概括也很有帮助。

  1. You keep doing what brought you success at a previous stage of your life, even if it’s not what you need to get to the next stage. To move to the next stage, do what those at the next stage do, even though you’re not there yet.
    你继续做那些曾经让你获得成功的事情，即使它们并非你迈向下一阶段所需要的。想要进入下一阶段，就去做那些已经身处下一阶段的人正在做的事情，即使你尚未达到那个阶段。
  2. You do some of what is necessary to succeed, but not everything that’s necessary. For example, if you are a researcher and make a fantastic discovery but aren’t good at communicating it, you limit your chances of success, recognition, funding, and impact.
    你做了一些成功所必需的事情，但并非所有事情都做对了。例如，如果你是一名研究人员，取得了一项了不起的发现，但却不善于沟通，那么你获得成功、认可、资金和影响力的机会就会受到限制。
  3. You prioritize short-term gains over long-term assets. Instead of systematically building a reputation, a body of work, a community, expertise, or strong teams - assets that compound over time - you chase quick profits that leave nothing durable behind.
    你优先考虑短期收益而非长期资产。你没有系统地建立声誉、积累作品、建立社群、提升专业技能或组建强大的团队——这些资产会随着时间推移而增值——而是追求快速获利，却没有留下任何持久的东西。
  4. You don’t play iterated games. You enter each meeting (with partners, customers, etc.) as if it were a one-off transaction. This is fine if it is indeed a one-off transaction, but most interactions are iterated games (or should be). Approach them as such.
    你不会玩迭代博弈。你应该把每一次会面（与合作伙伴、客户等）都当作一次性交易来对待。如果确实是一次性交易，那当然没问题，但大多数互动都是迭代博弈（或者应该如此）。你应该以迭代博弈的视角来看待它们。
  5. You take excessive risks. Some level of risk-taking is beneficial and often necessary. However , in some fields, such as sports and investing, there is a concept called the Maximum Reproducible Return : an optimal growth rate you can only exceed by taking risks that increase potential outcomes but reduce average ones. ( More on this in a later chapter.)
    你承担了过多的风险。一定程度的风险承担是有益的，而且往往是必要的。然而，在某些领域，例如体育和投资，存在一个叫做“最大可复制回报”的概念：这是一个最优增长率，你只能通过承担那些会增加潜在收益但会降低平均收益的风险来超越它。（更多内容将在后续章节中讨论。）
  6. You do not take enough risks. As a result, you limit your growth rate to below the minimum level required to achieve your goals.
    你承担的风险不够。因此，你的增长速度低于实现目标所需的最低水平。
  7. You quit too early. Some projects are like seeds: they can only grow so fast and require enough watering before they blossom. It’s okay to quit sometimes, but it is problematic if you always quit before doing what it takes to give your seeds a reasonable chance to blossom.
    你放弃得太早了。有些项目就像种子：它们生长速度有限，需要充足的浇水才能开花结果。偶尔放弃是可以的，但如果你总是不尽力让种子有合理的机会开花结果就放弃，那就成问题了。
  8. You never quit. It is possible but unlikely that your first project, plan, or partner is the one that will work out great. More likely, you will have to try a few before one succeeds. This should be baked into your strategy.
    你永不放弃。你的第一个项目、计划或合作伙伴或许有可能一炮而红，但这种可能性不大。更可能的情况是，你需要尝试几次才能找到成功的。这一点应该纳入你的战略考量。
  9. You progress too slowly. By the time you notice, it’s too late. You need a system to know when you should go faster.
    你的进步太慢了。等你意识到这一点时，已经太晚了。你需要一个系统来判断何时应该加快速度。
  10. You try to be too smart. Of course, creativity and innovation will help you, and for some pursuits, they are necessary. However , while some innovation is good, reinventing the wheel comes with large risks and opportunity costs. Be considerate when choosing where to innovate and where instead to re-use what has worked for others.
    你太想耍小聪明了。当然，创造力和创新会对你有所帮助，在某些领域，它们更是必不可少。然而，虽然有些创新是好事，但重复发明轮子却会带来巨大的风险和机会成本。在选择创新方向和借鉴他人成功经验的方向时，务必慎重考虑。
  11. You work for a bad boss, a bad company, a bad partner, or someone who limits your potential.
    你为一个糟糕的老板、一家糟糕的公司、一个糟糕的合作伙伴，或者一个限制你潜能的人工作。
  12. You rely too much on yourself and do not seek the help or support of others, therefore limiting your potential.
    你太依赖自己，不寻求他人的帮助或支持，因此限制了你的潜力。
  13. You kill your Goose . To get the proverbial Golden Eggs , you need to grow a Goose first: a reputation, a network, a team, a body of work, etc. However , when we see others producing Golden Eggs faster than us, we are tempted to squeeze our Goose to keep up, killing it in the process.
    你杀了自己的鹅。要想获得传说中的金蛋，你首先需要养好一只鹅：声誉、人脉、团队、作品等等。然而，当我们看到别人比我们更快地产出金蛋时，我们就会忍不住榨干自己的鹅，试图跟上进度，结果却害死了它。
  14. You risk your Goose . This is a subtle variation of the previous point, in which you take bets with a large upside but also a risk of killing your Goose in case of failure, e.g., making a risky investment, risking your reputation, or burning out your collaborators. Even if the bet has a positive expected value, if you take enough of them, eventually, you will kill your Goose . Good long-term strategies never put the Goose at risk.
    你这是在拿你的“鹅”冒险。这是前一点的微妙变体，指的是你进行一些收益巨大但失败后会危及“鹅”的赌博，例如进行高风险投资、冒着损害声誉的风险，或者让合作者精疲力竭。即使赌博的预期收益为正，如果你赌博的次数过多，最终也会危及你的“鹅”。好的长期策略永远不会让“鹅”面临风险。
  15. You do not know what you want, nor do you have a strategy to discover it. If it takes you too long to find out what you want, you might lack the time to achieve it, or you might make it unlikely to happen.
    你既不知道自己想要什么，也没有找到答案的策略。如果你花了太长时间才弄明白自己想要什么，你可能就没有足够的时间去实现它，或者反而让它更难实现。
  16. 16. You want to succeed in a specific way. You refuse opportunities for happiness or success that look different from your expectations. There is nothing wrong with being specific, but you must acknowledge that the more specific you are, the more opportunities you will miss and the less likely you will eventually become successful.
    16. 你想要以某种特定的方式获得成功。你会拒绝那些与你的预期不符的幸福或成功机会。目标明确本身并没有错，但你必须意识到，你的目标越明确，你错失的机会就越多，最终成功的可能性也就越小。
  17. You have a non-reproducible definition of success. For example, aiming to become #1 in a field with a lot of competition is non-reproducible by definition because all it takes for you to fail is a single person more determined or luckier than you. You can succeed under these conditions, but you cannot guarantee success.
    你对成功的定义无法复制。例如，在竞争激烈的领域力争成为第一，从定义上来说就是无法复制的，因为只要有一个人比你更有决心或运气更好，你就可能失败。在这种情况下，你或许能成功，但你无法保证一定成功。
  18. You envy or imitate non-reproducible success. You adopt strategies that worked for someone but might not work for everyone, and you adopt them not with a “let’s try” attitude but by mindlessly following them.
    你羡慕或模仿那些无法复制的成功。你采用的策略可能对某些人有效，但未必对每个人都有效，而且你采用这些策略并非出于“不妨一试”的态度，而是盲目地照搬。
  19. You have incompatible objectives. You can become (nearly) anything, but you cannot become everything. List all your goals (professional, personal, etc.) and check whether you can reproducibly achieve them all together. If not, you might have to reconsider some.
    你的目标相互冲突。你可以成为（几乎）任何你想成为的人，但你不可能成为所有你想成为的人。列出你所有的目标（职业目标、个人目标等等），看看你是否能够同时实现所有这些目标。如果不能，你可能需要重新考虑其中一些目标。
  20. You compartmentalize success. You mindlessly try to maximize achievement in one area of your life without noticing its negative impact on other areas of your life until it’s too late.
    你把成功割裂开来。你盲目地试图在生活的某个领域取得最大成就，却没有注意到它对生活其他领域的负面影响，直到为时已晚。
  21. Your objectives are misaligned with your talents and dispositions. While you might win an uphill race, it will be much more difficult than winning a downhill one. Moreover , it will require so much time and energy that it will negatively impact the rest of your life. The alternative is to embrace your talents and predispositions.
    你的目标与你的才能和性格不符。虽然你或许能赢得一场逆境之战，但这远比赢得一场下坡之战要难得多。而且，这会耗费你大量的时间和精力，对你生活的其他方面产生负面影响。另一种选择是发挥你的才能和天性。
  22. You have mixed feelings about achieving your objectives. For example, you want to become wealthy but also have mixed feelings about wealthy people. This might become a major limiting factor.
    你对实现目标抱有复杂的情感。例如，你想变得富有，但对富人又抱有复杂的情感。这可能会成为一个重要的限制因素。

Of course, there are many reasons why people fail. Here , I have gathered twenty-two of the most common and actionable ones.

当然，人们失败的原因有很多。这里，我列举了二十二个最常见且最切实可行的失败原因。

In addition to these, take a few minutes to consider whether there are other common reasons for failure specific to your long-term goal(s).

除了以上原因之外，请花几分钟时间思考一下，对于你的长期目标，是否还有其他常见的失败原因。

For example, if your long-term goal is to become a successful lawyer, think carefully about why people who studied law might eventually fail to achieve this objective.

例如，如果你的长期目标是成为一名成功的律师，那么请仔细思考为什么学习法律的人最终可能无法实现这个目标。

Be careful about thinking, “ This problem won’t apply to me because I’m smarter than they are.” Smartness is often judged post-hoc, so you do not yet know how smart or wise you really are.

不要想“这个问题与我无关，因为我比他们聪明”。聪明与否往往是事后评判的，所以你现在还不知道自己到底有多聪明或多睿智。

If you do not think about how others failed,

如果你不去思考别人是如何失败的，

you might succeed in a way that won’t matter:

你或许会以某种无关紧要的方式获得成功：

either your success will be short-lived,

要么你的成功只是昙花一现，

or eclipsed by some larger problem you neglected.

或者被你忽略的某个更大的问题所掩盖。

Practical applications

实际应用

I regularly go through this list and ask if any of those points apply to my current strategy. That allows me to make the appropriate adjustments before it’s too late.

我经常查看这份清单，并问自己其中哪些要点适用于我当前的策略。这样我就可以在为时过晚之前做出相应的调整。

Then, to prevent any blind spots, I also ask myself, “ What are possible reasons why, in ten years, despite my current strategy, I might have failed to achieve my objectives?”

然后，为了避免出现任何盲点，我还会问自己：“十年后，尽管我采取了目前的策略，但可能有哪些原因导致我未能实现我的目标？”

This question often gives me great insights into possible points of failure, therefore increasing my chances of success.

这个问题常常能让我深入了解可能出现的失败点，从而提高我成功的几率。

3

PLATEAUING

平台期

O nly some of those whose trajectory trended upward a few years ago maintained that growing trajectory. Many plateaued – their growth stalled – or even fell back to where they started.

几年前发展势头良好的公司中，只有一部分保持了增长势头。许多公司的发展停滞不前，甚至回落到最初的水平。

Those whose trajectory continues to grow built their early success on strong foundations. Conversely , those whose trajectory plateaued built their early success on excessive risk-taking or taking shortcuts instead of building what’s required to sustain success over time.

那些发展势头持续上升的人，早期的成功都建立在坚实的基础之上。相反，那些发展停滞不前的人，早期的成功往往建立在过度冒险或走捷径之上，而不是建立起维持长期成功所需的基础。

Short-term vs long-term players

短期玩家与长期玩家

Short-term players care only about their rate of growth.

短线玩家只关心他们的增长速度。

Long-term players also care about their growth rate, obviously, but only the portion that is achieved on solid foundations and is likely to continue in the future.

长期投资者当然也关心增长率，但他们只关心建立在坚实基础上并有可能在未来继续增长的那部分。

Long-term players do not care about unsustainable success.

着眼长远的玩家并不在意短暂的成功。

Moving to the next stage

进入下一阶段

There is another common reason why people plateau. To understand what it is, let’s look at the corporate ladder.

人们职业发展停滞不前还有另一个常见原因。为了理解这一点，我们不妨看看企业晋升阶梯。

If you are an employee who’s already proficient in your current job, simply working harder won’t significantly increase your chances of promotion. Instead , acquiring and demonstrating the skills needed to handle your next job is what will make the difference.

如果你已经胜任目前的工作，仅仅更加努力工作并不会显著提高你的晋升机会。相反，掌握并展现胜任下一份工作所需的技能才是关键所在。

This principle applies in many other contexts. What has brought you success in your current stage of life is unlikely to be enough to propel you to the next stage. You advance to the next stage by demonstrating the skills and habits of people who are already at that level. ⁠ i

这条原则也适用于许多其他方面。你目前人生阶段的成功经验不太可能足以助你迈向下一个阶段。你需要展现出那些已经达到那个水平的人所具备的技能和习惯，才能进入下一个阶段。

Whenever you feel stuck, ask yourself whether you’re working on what brought you success instead of what will bring future success.

每当你感到停滞不前时，问问自己，你是否还在做那些曾经给你带来成功的事情，而不是那些将会带来未来成功的事情。

A good long-term strategy avoids plateauing by evaluating what to work on based not on current needs but on future ones.

一个好的长期战略会避免停滞不前，它会根据未来的需求而不是当前的需求来评估应该做什么。

This does not mean you should make rigid plans spanning decades; these might be counterproductive if assumptions change. Instead , it means that you should decide what to work on next based not on where you are currently but on where you want to go.

这并不意味着你应该制定跨越数十年的僵化计划；如果假设发生变化，这些计划可能会适得其反。相反，这意味着你应该根据你想要去往的地方，而不是你目前所处的位置来决定下一步的工作方向。

i Of course, there are plenty of people who got promoted to the next stage without having demonstrated the skills it requires. But the fact that it is possible to get promoted this way doesn’t mean it’s likely that you will get promoted this way. Remember the Second Principle, and do not forget about survivorship bias.

当然，很多人在晋升到下一阶段时并没有展现出所需的技能。但这种晋升方式的存在并不意味着你也一定会以这种方式晋升。记住第二原则，并且不要忘记幸存者偏差。

THE TERROR OF FALLING BEHIND

落后的恐惧

I f playing long-term games is so beneficial, why don’t more people play them?

如果玩长期游戏这么有益，为什么不是更多的人玩呢？

To answer this question, let’s consider investing. A key principle is that if you consistently achieve average market returns over extended periods, you will attain well-above-average results. ⁠ i

为了回答这个问题，我们不妨以投资为例。一个关键原则是，如果你能在较长一段时间内持续获得市场平均回报，你就能获得远高于平均水平的收益。

Yet, few investors adopt this simple long-term strategy. That’s because their resolve is tested daily by news of investors beating the market with risky short-term strategies.

然而，很少有投资者采用这种简单的长期投资策略。这是因为他们每天都会听到有投资者通过高风险的短期策略跑赢市场的新闻，这考验着他们的决心。

Of course, that strategy is likely to falter in the long term. Short -term success is more likely due to luck or short-term optimization than competence .⁠ ii

当然，这种策略从长远来看很可能行不通。短期成功更多是运气或短期优化的结果，而非能力使然。

Yet, the feeling of falling behind is strong.⁠ iii

然而，落后的感觉却很强烈。

And it is precisely this feeling of falling behind that makes many of us switch from good long-term strategies to poor short-term ones.

正是这种落后的感觉，导致我们中的许多人从良好的长期策略转向糟糕的短期策略。

But shouldn’t we imitate the successful?

难道我们不应该效仿成功者吗？

You shouldn’t imitate all successful people, only those who succeeded using good strategies – strategies that can reliably bring success to those using them.

你不应该模仿所有成功人士，而应该只模仿那些运用良好策略取得成功的人——这些策略能够可靠地为使用者带来成功。

I often use the example of casino croupiers. They are the only people at the gambling tables with a money-making strategy, yet every day, they see at least one player get richer than them. However , they must remind themselves that abandoning their job to become gamblers would be an error: they would make much less money. If you must choose whose strategy to imitate, copy the croupiers, not the lucky players.

我经常以赌场荷官为例。他们是赌桌上唯一拥有赚钱策略的人，然而每天，他们都会眼睁睁地看着至少一位玩家比他们赢钱。但是，他们必须时刻提醒自己，放弃工作去赌博是个错误：那样他们赚的钱会少得多。如果你必须选择模仿谁的策略，那就学习荷官的策略，而不是那些幸运玩家的策略。

Good strategies and bad strategies

好的策略和坏的策略

At the casino, it’s easy to spot who the croupier is. But in real life, it’s harder. How do you identify those with a plan worth imitating, and how do you differentiate them from those who just got lucky? The first step is to stop using short-term growth rates to estimate the quality of a strategy.

在赌场里，很容易就能认出荷官。但在现实生活中，这却很难。如何识别那些拥有值得效仿的策略的人，又如何将他们与那些只是运气好的人区分开来呢？第一步是停止用短期增长率来评估策略的质量。

While good strategies, on average, grow faster than bad ones, it’s also true that rapid growth can be due to unsustainable factors such as luck, excessive risk-taking, or behaviors with short-term benefits and long-term costs.

虽然好的策略平均而言比坏的策略增长得更快，但快速增长也可能是由于运气、过度冒险或短期收益和长期成本等不可持续的因素造成的。

In fact, among those growing fast, we will find many skilled people, but among those growing very fast, we will find plenty of skilled people who are making short-term choices. As a result, if we emulate those growing faster than us, we are more likely to imitate short-term optimization than competence.

事实上，在那些快速增长的公司中，我们会发现许多技能娴熟的人才；但在那些增长速度极快的公司中，我们会发现很多技能娴熟但只注重短期利益的公司。因此，如果我们效仿那些增长速度比我们快的公司，我们更有可能模仿的是短期优化而非真正的能力。

I’m not saying we should dismiss those growing faster than us. Of course, there is plenty to learn from many of them. But never imitate unquestioningly, and only replicate those behaviors that make sense over the long term .

我并不是说我们应该忽视那些发展速度比我们快的人。当然，我们可以从他们身上学到很多东西。但切勿盲目模仿，而应该只复制那些从长远来看行之有效的行为。

Skill and luck

技术与运气

Of all the successful people, only a few succeeded with reproducible strategies. Instead , most succeeded with non-reproducible strategies: strategies that, if you imitated them, your chance of success would be low. You shouldn’t imitate those. ( Unless as a series of short-term projects within a longer-term strategy; I will expand on this point later.)

在所有成功人士中，只有少数人凭借可复制的策略取得了成功。相反，大多数人凭借的是不可复制的策略：如果你模仿这些策略，成功的几率会很低。你不应该模仿这些策略。（除非是作为长期战略中的一系列短期项目；我稍后会详细阐述这一点。）

The tricky part is that people succeeding with non-reproducible strategies are often extremely intelligent and hard-working, which misleads us into believing that intelligence and hard work are sufficient to imitate their success. But that’s often not the case. Instead , luck or other difficult-to-reproduce conditions are frequently required, too.⁠ iv

棘手之处在于，那些凭借不可复制策略取得成功的人往往极其聪明且勤奋，这误导我们以为聪明才智和勤奋足以让我们模仿他们的成功。但事实并非总是如此。相反，运气或其他难以复制的条件也常常必不可少。

Don’t get me wrong. A key life skill is learning how to harness luck. However , we should differentiate between bets that might not work and strategies that might not work-you can afford the former, but not the latter.

别误会我的意思。学会驾驭运气的确是一项重要的人生技能。但是，我们应该区分可能失败的赌注和可能失败的策略——前者你可以承担，但后者你承担不起。

Imitate risk-takers, but only those who took risky bets within the context of a good strategy – one that, thanks to a good setup and a wise allocation of bets, none of which can fail ruinously, guarantees eventually achieving good outcomes.

要模仿那些敢于冒险的人，但只能模仿那些在良好策略框架下进行冒险投注的人——这种策略得益于良好的设置和明智的投注分配，任何投注都不会失败，从而保证最终取得良好的结果。

Only use strategies that lead to good outcomes with near certainty. ( It is possible! A later chapter titled “ Inevitability ” will teach you how.)

只采用那些几乎肯定能带来良好结果的策略。（这是完全可能的！后面的章节“必然性”会教你如何做到。）

# ↩

Case study

案例研究

According to a Morningstar study that analyzed 112 funds trying to beat a simple “60/40” investing strategy, only nine had better risk-adjusted returns than the 60/40 strategy.⁠ v

根据晨星公司的一项研究，该研究分析了112只试图超越简单的“60/40”投资策略的基金，结果显示，只有9只基金的风险调整后收益优于60/40策略。

The wise conclusion would be that looking for good returns is more likely to succeed than looking for great ones.

明智的结论是，追求良好回报比追求丰厚回报更容易成功。

Yet, most funds still try to beat the market, exhibiting the same overconfidence seen with which 93% of drivers believe they are better than average.⁠ vi

然而，大多数基金仍然试图跑赢市场，表现出与93%的司机认为自己驾驶技术高于平均水平一样的过度自信。

The point is not that beating the market is impossible. There are a few great investors who do so consistently. The point is that because we look at success through the lenses of hindsight and survivorship bias, we overestimate its reproducibility.

关键不在于战胜市场是不可能的。确实有一些优秀的投资者能够持续做到这一点。关键在于，因为我们总是用事后诸葛亮的眼光和幸存者偏差来看待成功，所以我们高估了成功的可复制性。

Because we overestimate the reproducibility of short-term strategies, we switch from strategies with great long-term returns to worse ones.

因为我们高估了短期策略的可复制性，所以我们从长期收益高的策略转向了长期收益低的策略。

Hindsight bias

后见之明偏见

The previous case study showed a common yet faulty reasoning: “ Everyone who succeeds is smart, everyone who fails is dumb, and I am smart; therefore, I will succeed.”

之前的案例研究表明了一种常见但错误的推理：“成功的人都是聪明的，失败的人都是愚蠢的，而我很聪明；因此，我一定会成功。”

The problem is that many people who now seem dumb once appeared smart before their failure. The use of hindsight to determine who is smart may lead you to underestimate the percentage of smart people who fail and, therefore, overestimate your chances of success.

问题在于，许多现在看起来愚蠢的人，在失败之前都曾显得聪明。用事后诸葛亮的眼光来判断谁聪明，可能会让你低估聪明人失败的比例，从而高估自己成功的几率。

The same faulty reasoning applies to our evaluations of strategies. Of course, everyone who succeeded had a great strategy – if we use hindsight to determine how great a strategy is. That might lead us to overestimate how likely we are to succeed with a great strategy.

同样的错误推理也适用于我们对策略的评估。当然，如果我们用事后诸葛亮的眼光来判断策略的好坏，那么所有成功者都拥有一个优秀的策略。这可能会导致我们高估自己运用优秀策略取得成功的可能性。

It’s not that great strategies aren’t powerful. They obviously are! But it’s hard to know what a great strategy looks like without relying on hindsight.

并不是说好的策略不强大。它们当然强大！但是，如果不借助事后诸葛亮，就很难知道好的策略到底是什么样子。

So, while having a great strategy is very helpful, the problem is that it is hard to know whether your strategy is great before you try it.

所以，虽然制定一个好的策略非常有帮助，但问题是，在尝试之前很难知道你的策略是否好。

Therefore, checking whether it worked for others is a good idea only if you can pinpoint exactly which parts of their strategy and actions were signal and which noise – an incredibly hard task.

因此，只有当你能够准确地指出他们的策略和行动中哪些部分是信号，哪些部分是噪音时，检查它对其他人是否有效才是个好主意——这是一项极其困难的任务。

That said, the next chapter will help you precisely with this, giving you a few criteria for evaluating how good a strategy is without relying on hindsight.

也就是说，下一章将专门帮助你做到这一点，为你提供一些评估策略优劣的标准，而无需依赖事后诸葛亮。

i Part of it is because of investors who accumulate losses so high that they must quit, and part of it is because an investment gone bad slows compounding (“Losses absorb future gains,” I wrote in my book Ergodicity ).

部分原因是投资者累积的损失过大，以至于不得不退出；部分原因是糟糕的投资会减缓复利增长（我在我的著作《遍历性》中写道：“损失会吸收未来的收益”）。

ii I justify this statement more extensively later on. For the moment, consider how to survive over the long term, one must avoid excessive risks, but in the short term, not only can they get away with risks, but taking high risks actually increases outcomes. As a result, over the short term, among the highest outcomes, people who took large risks will be over-represented, whereas, over the long term, many of them will face the consequences of their risk-taking and exit the sample.

二、我稍后会更详细地论证这一观点。目前，考虑如何长期生存，必须避免过度冒险；但在短期内，不仅可以侥幸逃脱风险，而且高风险实际上还能提高收益。因此，在短期内，那些承担高风险的人会在收益最高的人群中占据过高比例；而从长远来看，他们中的许多人将面临冒险行为的后果，并最终退出样本。

iii Falling behind can also have material consequences, such as investors fleeing to another fund.

iii 落后也可能造成实质性后果，例如投资者转向其他基金。

iv A further consideration is that some strategies offer reproducible outcomes but are still hard to reproduce because of opacity: people emulating the strategy imitate its irrelevant parts and/or miss some key point.

iv 进一步考虑的是，有些策略虽然能提供可重复的结果，但由于其不透明性，仍然难以复制：模仿该策略的人会模仿其无关的部分，和/或错过一些关键点。

v Source: “Tactical Funds Miss Their Chance,” Morningstar, February 2, 2012.

v 来源：“战术基金错失良机”，晨星公司，2012 年 2 月 2 日。

vi Source: “Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers,” O. Svenson, 1981. Hindsight bias and optimism bias are not the only reasons we overestimate how good a driver we are. Another reason has to do with how we interpret near misses – errors that could have led to an incident but didn’t. Take the following example: you’re driving too fast on a country road, and an animal crosses in front of you; you emergency brake and stop inches from it. What lesson will you learn? That you were driving too fast and thus are a bad driver, or that you have good reflexes and thus you are a good driver? The right lesson to learn is the latter, but many of us learn the former instead.

资料来源：“我们是否都比其他司机更谨慎、更熟练？” O. Svenson，1981年。后见之明偏差和乐观偏差并非我们高估自己驾驶水平的唯一原因。另一个原因与我们如何解读险些发生的事故——那些本可能导致事故但最终并未发生的失误——有关。举个例子：你在乡间小路上超速行驶，一只动物突然横穿马路；你紧急刹车，在距离动物几英寸的地方停了下来。你会从中吸取什么教训？是意识到自己开得太快，所以是个糟糕的司机，还是意识到自己反应迅速，所以是个好司机？正确的教训应该是后者，但我们中的许多人却吸取了前者的教训。

5

WHAT MAKES A GOOD STRATEGY?

好的策略需要具备哪些要素？

L ooking at society, we see plenty of people who have achieved quick or easy success. That becomes our standard for what a good strategy is, and we consider suboptimal any strategy that takes longer or requires more effort.

放眼社会，我们看到许多人轻而易举地获得了成功。这便成了我们衡量好策略的标准，而任何耗时更长或需要更多努力的策略，我们都认为是次优之选。

However, for every individual who achieved quick or easy success, there are many more who used the same tactic and failed. ⁠ i

然而，每一个获得快速或轻松成功的人背后，都有更多人使用同样的策略却以失败告终。

At the aggregate level, we do not care about a strategy’s chances of success. For example, we do not care about everyone who has tried to become a pop star but failed. We only care about those who succeeded.

从总体层面来看，我们并不关心一项策略成功的概率。例如，我们并不关心所有尝试成为流行歌星但失败的人，我们只关心那些成功的人。

But at the individual level, we do care very much about a strategy’s chances of success. In fact, because we only have one life, a strategy’s probability of success is its most important attribute, and speed and efficiency should be secondary to it.

但就个人而言，我们确实非常关心一项策略的成功概率。事实上，因为我们只有一次生命，所以一项策略的成功概率才是其最重要的属性，速度和效率则应退居其次。

# ↩

Tactic risk vs strategy risk

战术风险与战略风险

Before continuing, let me highlight a common misunderstanding.

在继续之前，我想先指出一个常见的误解。

Good strategies aim for certainty of success, but that doesn’t mean they avoid gambles that might not work. In fact, many good strategies rely on taking enough gambles to ensure at least one succeeds.

好的策略旨在确保成功，但这并不意味着它们会避免可能失败的尝试。事实上，许多好的策略都依赖于进行足够多的尝试，以确保至少有一次成功。

The key is that good strategies do take gambles, but only when they make sense in the long term. They never take gambles whose failure might endanger future chances of success.

关键在于，好的策略确实会涉及冒险，但前提是这些冒险在长期来看是合理的。好的策略绝不会进行那些失败可能会危及未来成功机会的冒险。

For example, long-term players might work on projects that could fail, but only in such a way that even failure wouldn’t endanger their reputation (e.g., by never overpromising and always communicating transparently).

例如，长期参与者可能会参与一些可能会失败的项目，但前提是即使失败也不会危及他们的声誉（例如，从不过度承诺，并始终保持透明的沟通）。

Tactics might be risky, but their risk must not transfer to the strategy.

战术可能存在风险，但这种风险绝不能转移到战略上。

Tactics might fail, but strategies must eventually guarantee success.

战术可能会失败，但战略最终必须保证成功。

* * *

So, we have seen that good strategies almost guarantee success. But how can we identify the strategies that possess this quality?

所以，我们已经看到，好的策略几乎可以保证成功。但是，我们如何才能找到具备这种特质的策略呢？

In the next chapter, we will explore three key properties of effective long-term strategies that contribute to achieving near-certain success.

在下一章中，我们将探讨有助于取得近乎确定成功的有效长期战略的三个关键特性。

i The main exception is people entering novel fields where the lack of competition allows for fast, easy, and reproducible success, but only for a limited time before the field gets too crowded.

主要的例外是那些进入新兴领域的人，由于缺乏竞争，他们可以快速、轻松且可复制地取得成功，但这种成功只是暂时的，之后该领域就会变得过于拥挤。

# ↩
6

THE 3 PROPERTIES OF GOOD LONG-TERM STRATEGIES

良好长期战略的三个特征

G ood long-term strategies have three properties.

好的长期战略具有三个特点。

1) They are sustainable. They do not require risks or sacrifices that you cannot take for long without severe consequences, or that would clash with your other long-term goals.

1）它们是可持续的。它们不需要你承担无法长期承受而不造成严重后果的风险或牺牲，也不会与你的其他长期目标相冲突。

2) They are constructive. They play iterated games and build, instead of consuming, the long-term assets that bring long-term success (such as trust, know-how, relationships, capital, etc).

2）他们是建设性的。他们进行反复博弈，并建立（而不是消耗）带来长期成功的长期资产（如信任、专业知识、人脉、资本等）。

3) They move towards inevitability. They proactively surface and address problems; they learn and adapt. They do not merely provide a chance of success but do what’s required to almost guarantee it.

3）他们迎难而上。他们积极主动地发现并解决问题；他们不断学习和适应。他们不仅提供成功的机会，而且采取一切必要措施几乎确保成功。

As you can see, long-term strategies not only have a long-term time horizon but also embrace it and leverage it to achieve better and more certain outcomes than what a short-term strategy can reliably achieve.

如您所见，长期战略不仅具有长期的时间跨度，而且还充分利用长期的时间跨度，以实现比短期战略能够可靠实现的更好、更确定的结果。

I cannot stress how important it is to leverage the longer time horizon to adopt strategies that are precluded to short-term players.

我必须强调，利用较长的时间跨度来采取短期投资者无法采用的策略是多么重要。

Over the next pages, let’s examine the three properties listed above.

接下来，我们将仔细研究上面列出的三个特性。

Good long-term strategies are Sustainable

良好的长期战略是可持续的。

Working overtime is a great tactic to maximize this week’s productivity. Not only will you get more done, but a week of evenings spent working is unlikely to cause burnout or a divorce.

加班是提高本周工作效率的绝佳策略。这样不仅能完成更多工作，而且一周晚上加班也不太可能导致精疲力竭或离婚。

However, consistently working overtime every other week for several years in a row makes burnout and divorce much more likely.

然而，连续几年每隔一周就加班，会大大增加倦怠和离婚的可能性。

Similarly, sending a sales email to your mailing list is a great tactic to increase sales. But if all you send to your mailing list are sales emails, people won’t read your emails anymore.

同样，向邮件列表发送销售邮件是提高销售额的好方法。但如果你发送的邮件全是销售邮件，人们就不会再阅读你的邮件了。

Some tactics are useful but shouldn’t become strategies: they are best suited for short-term gains, not long-term plans. At most, they should be used sparingly and thoughtfully as elements of a broader, long-term strategy.

有些战术虽然有用，但不应演变成战略：它们最适合短期获利，而非长期规划。至多，它们应谨慎且慎重地作为更广泛的长期战略的组成部分加以运用。

This means that:

这意味着：

  • Long-term strategies can contain risky projects, but those projects should only be risky in the sense that they might not work, and never in the sense that their failure might endanger the strategy.
    长期战略可以包含风险项目，但这些项目的风险仅仅在于它们可能失败，而绝不能在于它们的失败可能会危及战略本身。
  • Long-term strategies can use tactics that consume long-term assets (such as health and trust), but they must use these tactics sparingly and alternate them with long enough periods of building the assets they consume.
    长期战略可以使用消耗长期资产（如健康和信任）的策略，但必须谨慎使用这些策略，并与足够长的积累所消耗资产的时期交替进行。

* * *

You can use short-term strategies for short periods or long-term strategies for long periods, but never use short-term strategies for long-term periods.

你可以对短期策略使用短期策略，也可以对长期策略使用长期策略，但绝不能对长期策略使用短期策略。

# ↩

Good long-term strategies are Constructive

良好的长期战略是建设性的

If you have three shots to throw a ball into a distant hole, it doesn’t make sense to use all three shots trying for a hole-in-one. Instead , use the first shot to get closer to the hole, so that the other two shots are more likely to go in.

如果你有三次击球机会将球打入远处的球洞，那么三次都尝试一杆进洞是没有意义的。相反，你应该用第一杆尽可能靠近球洞，这样后两杆进洞的几率就会更大。

Similarly, too many people fail to achieve their life goals because they spend years working on projects that are “hole-in-one shots.”

同样，太多人未能实现人生目标，因为他们花费数年时间从事“一击即中”的项目。

Not only do “hole-in-one” projects have low chances of success, but when they miss, they do not make the following projects more likely to succeed.

“一杆进洞”项目不仅成功几率很低，而且失败后也不会增加后续项目成功的可能性。

If you have a long-term horizon to achieve a goal, it doesn’t make sense to use tactics that are optimal for holes-in-one. You want to use strategies optimal for a hole-in-three. Strategies that progressively get you closer to your goal.

如果你的目标是长期实现的，那么采用那些只适合一杆进洞的策略是没有意义的。你应该采用那些只适合三杆进洞的策略，那些能让你逐步接近目标的策略。

Ask yourself: what assets (skills, habits, relationships, resources, etc.) would make your future projects more likely to succeed?

问问自己：哪些资产（技能、习惯、人际关系、资源等）能使你未来的项目更有可能成功？

Long-term strategies take the time to build these long-term assets, even when it doesn’t seem like a good moment to do so.

长期战略需要时间来积累这些长期资产，即使现在看起来并不是积累这些资产的好时机。

* * *

“The key to success is to spend more time on important-yet-not-urgent activities than most of your peers.”

“成功的关键在于，比大多数同龄人花更多的时间在重要但不紧急的事情上。”

# ↩

Good long-term strategies are Inevitable

良好的长期战略是不可避免的。

Many long-term strategies are variations of the following: undertake a few projects that might fail, but do so in such a way that one project failing doesn’t compromise future projects, and in such a way that even in failure, you still build know-how, trust, and relationships. If you do this, eventually, you will succeed.

许多长期战略都是以下几种形式的变体：开展一些可能失败的项目，但要确保一个项目的失败不会影响未来的项目，即使失败也能积累经验、建立信任和人脉。如果这样做，最终你会成功。

As you can see, good long-term strategies often include projects that might fail, but only within the context of a strategy that cannot fail.

正如你所看到的，好的长期战略通常包含一些可能会失败的项目，但这些项目只有在不会失败的战略背景下才会失败。

Do not take the “cannot fail” too literally. Whether a 100% success rate is possible is irrelevant. What matters is not to be satisfied with less than that and continuously ask yourself, “ What might cause me to fail, and what can I do about it?”

不要把“不可能失败”理解得太字面化。100%的成功率是否可能并不重要。重要的是不要满足于低于这个数字的成功率，而是要不断地问自己：“什么可能导致我失败？我该如何应对？”

Asking that question might reveal that you are taking too many risks, or perhaps not enough.

问出这个问题可能会揭示你承担了太多风险，或者风险不够。

It might reveal that you are going too fast, skipping steps, or perhaps that you are being too slow or complacent.

它可能揭示出你行动过快，跳过了某些步骤，或者你行动过慢或过于自满。

It might reveal that there is some help you are refusing to ask for.

这或许会揭示出，你一直拒绝寻求某些帮助。

It might reveal that there is some lesson you don’t want to learn.

它或许会揭示出你不想吸取的一些教训。

It might reveal that you’re using the wrong strategy.

这或许会揭示出你使用了错误的策略。

From that one question, you might learn a lot.

从这一个问题中，你或许能学到很多东西。

* * *

The point is, never treat your strategy as you would treat a tactic. You can tolerate tactics that might not work, but you cannot tolerate strategies that might fail.

关键在于，永远不要把战略当作战术来对待。你可以容忍战术可能无效，但你无法容忍战略可能失败。

After all, you only get one life. Make your strategy inevitable.

毕竟，人生只有一次。制定一个万无一失的策略吧。

# ↩

Bad long-term strategies

糟糕的长期策略

We have seen the three properties of good long-term strategies: they are sustainable, constructive, and make success inevitable.

我们已经了解了好的长期战略的三个特点：它们是可持续的、建设性的，并且能够确保成功。

The next chapter will help you use these three properties to produce a good long-term strategy. For the moment, let\'s look at a few red flags that indicate a bad long-term strategy:

下一章将帮助你运用这三个特性制定良好的长期战略。现在，让我们先来看一些表明长期战略糟糕的危险信号：

  • It is not sustainable: it might bring you some early growth, but it cannot sustain it over time.
    这种做法不可持续：它可能在初期带来一些增长，但无法长期维持。
  • It is not constructive: it doesn’t build the long-term assets required for long-term success.
    它不具建设性：它无法积累长期成功所需的长期资产。
  • It is not inevitable: it might lead to success, but it also might not.
    这并非必然：它可能带来成功，但也可能不会。
  • It is not actionable: there are no clear next steps you can take today.
    目前尚无可操作步骤：今天没有明确的下一步措施可以采取。
  • It relies on the future not changing: it doesn’t incorporate learning and adaptation.
    它依赖于未来不变的假设：它没有纳入学习和适应的因素。
  • It focuses on a single area of your life and neglects the rest. It might bring you a pyrrhic victory , in which you achieve your objective, but it might still not matter because you have compromised another important area of your life.
    它只关注你生活的某个方面，而忽略了其他方面。它或许能给你带来一场得不偿失的胜利，让你达成目标，但这最终可能毫无意义，因为你已经牺牲了生活中其他重要的方面。

There are more red flags of a bad long-term strategy, but the above are the most important, and adding more to the list would only dilute it and make it worse.

长期战略糟糕的迹象还有很多，但以上几点最为重要，再增加其他因素只会削弱战略的有效性，使情况变得更糟。

# ↩
7

DESIGNING A GOOD LONG-TERM STRATEGY

设计一个好的长期战略

G oing through life without a strategy is like navigating a forest without a compass. Sure , you might find your way out eventually, but probably not to the destination you were hoping for.

人生没有策略，就像在森林里没有指南针。当然，你最终或许能找到出路，但很可能达不到你期望的目的地。

That said, while I believe in long-term strategies, I don't believe in rigid long-term plans . They tend to look good in theory but often have blind spots and prove fragile in an ever-changing environment.

话虽如此，虽然我相信长期战略，但我并不相信僵化的长期计划。它们在理论上看起来不错，但往往存在盲点，并且在瞬息万变的环境中显得不堪一击。

For me, it’s less about designing a strategy top-down and more about iterating on your current strategy by repeatedly asking yourself the following questions:

对我而言，与其说是自上而下地设计战略，不如说是通过反复问自己以下问题来迭代当前的战略：

  • Can I sustain my strategy long enough to guarantee success? If not, what changes should I make?
    我的策略能否长期有效以确保成功？如果不能，我应该做出哪些改变？
  • Does my strategy build enough long-term assets to guarantee success? If not, what changes should I make?
    我的策略能否积累足够的长期资产来保证成功？如果不能，我应该做出哪些改变？
  • Does my strategy merely give me a chance to succeed, or does it guarantee it? If not, what else should I do?
    我的策略仅仅是给了我成功的机会，还是能保证成功？如果不是，我还能做什么？

An iterative process

迭代过程

Of course, it is hard to answer these questions with precision and certainty.

当然，这些问题很难给出精确而肯定的答案。

But that’s not the point. The point is that by asking yourself these questions once a week or once a month for long enough and answering them with honesty and humility, you dramatically increase your chances of success.

但这并非重点。重点在于，如果你每周或每月都问自己这些问题，并且坚持足够长的时间，以诚实和谦逊的态度回答它们，你成功的几率就会大大增加。

Do not reinvent too many wheels

不要重复发明太多轮子

A common mistake at this stage is to “reinvent the wheel too much” or “try to figure it out yourself too much.” Don’t get me wrong, creativity and personal initiative are great! But you only have so many years to achieve your goals. So , while some level of making mistakes and learning from them is good, you cannot afford to make too many mistakes or proceed too slowly.

在这个阶段，一个常见的错误是“过度重复发明轮子”或“过度依赖自己摸索”。别误会，创造力和主动性固然重要！但你实现目标的时间有限。因此，虽然适度犯错并从中吸取教训是好事，但你不能犯太多错误，也不能进展太慢。

Find the right balance. Reinvent one wheel, but not all four. And use personal initiative, but only after analyzing how others have failed.

找到合适的平衡点。可以重新发明一个轮子，但不必四个都重新发明。要发挥个人主动性，但前提是要先分析他人失败的原因。

Always look at your trajectory and ask yourself whether it’s pointing towards where you want to be within an acceptable time frame – and if not, make the appropriate adjustments.

时刻审视你的发展轨迹，问问自己它是否在可接受的时间范围内指向你想要达到的目标——如果不是，就做出相应的调整。

Note: I expanded the contents of this page in the Appendix chapter titled “ Don’t be too smart.”

注：我在题为“不要太聪明”的附录章节中扩展了本页的内容。

# ↩
8

OPTIMIZING YOUR LIFE

优化你的生活

A t this point in the book, I should reiterate a key point from the first chapter, which began with the quote, “ The key to winning long-term games is to stop playing them as a succession of separate short-term games.”

在本书的这个部分，我应该重申第一章中的一个关键点，该章以这样一段引言开头：“赢得长期博弈的关键在于停止将它们视为一系列独立的短期博弈。”

A similar principle from business operations, one of my fields of expertise, is as follows: “ If you optimize each component of the system individually, you won’t have an optimal system.”

我的专业领域之一——商业运营中也有一个类似的原则，那就是：“如果单独优化系统的每个组件，就无法得到一个最优的系统。”

Of course, the problem is not optimization itself but the type of optimization. To have an optimal system, optimize the components for their effect on the system, not just their direct output.

当然，问题不在于优化本身，而在于优化的类型。要获得最优系统，应该优化各个组件对系统的整体影响，而不仅仅是它们的直接输出。

So, optimize your short-term goals and how you achieve them for how they progress your long-term objectives. This often means optimizing each short-term goal only up to a certain point. After all, there is such a thing as over-optimization, which happens when you optimize falsely assuming a static system or mistakenly neglecting externalities invisible in the short term but significant in the long term.

因此，要优化你的短期目标及其实现方式，使其与你的长期目标的推进方式相契合。这通常意味着每个短期目标的优化都应控制在一定范围内。毕竟，过度优化是存在的，它发生在你错误地假设系统是静态的，或者错误地忽略了短期内不可见但长期内至关重要的外部因素时。

Optimize your distribution of outcomes

优化结果分布

There are a few possible ways to optimize for your long-term objective.

有几种方法可以优化你的长期目标。

  1. Maximize the best-case scenario – for example, you are not satisfied with becoming wealthy, but you also want to amass as much wealth as possible.
    最大化最佳情况——例如，你不满足于变得富有，而是想积累尽可能多的财富。
  2. Achieve your objective as fast or as efficiently as possible – for example, you are not satisfied with becoming wealthy, but you also want to do so with as little work as possible and as fast as possible.
    尽可能快速或高效地实现你的目标——例如，你不满足于变得富有，但你也希望尽可能少地付出努力，尽可能快地实现这个目标。
  3. Maximize your chances of achieving your goal – for example, you are not satisfied with having a chance at achieving your objectives, but you want to be as certain as possible that you will achieve and sustain them over time.
    最大限度地提高实现目标的机会——例如，你不满足于仅仅有机会实现目标，而是希望尽可能确保能够实现目标并长期保持目标。

The three optimizations above are at odds with each other. You can pick one, but you cannot pick all three.

以上三种优化方案相互矛盾。你可以选择其中一种，但不能同时选择三种。

My suggestion, and my choice in life, is to optimize for the third option. I prefer to ensure that given ten possible futures, I’m happy in all of them, rather than maybe being very happy in one, moderately happy in seven, and unhappy in two.

我的建议，也是我的人生选择，是尽可能选择第三种方案。我宁愿确保在十种可能的未来中，每一种都让我感到快乐，而不是可能在一种未来中非常快乐，在七种未来中比较快乐，在两种未来中不快乐。

I optimize my distribution of outcomes.

我优化了结果分布。

That said, of course, you can make a different choice.

当然，你也可以做出不同的选择。

But do acknowledge that it is a choice. And do choose wisely and deliberately.

但请务必认识到，这是一种选择。并且请慎重、明智地做出选择。

THE PATH FORWARD

前进之路

S o far, we have seen the importance of not only having long-term objectives but, more importantly, of achieving them through long-term strategies.

到目前为止，我们已经看到了制定长期目标的重要性，更重要的是，要通过长期战略来实现这些目标。

At this point, you might be convinced of the benefits of long-term strategies but still hesitate to implement them instead of shorter-term strategies. After all, don't you want to succeed as quickly as possible?

此时，你或许已经认识到长期战略的好处，但仍然犹豫是否要实施长期战略，而不是选择短期战略。毕竟，你难道不想尽快取得成功吗？

Therefore, let’s move to the next chapter, which answers the question of whether long-term strategies are truly better than short-term ones.

因此，让我们进入下一章，这一章将回答长期战略是否真的比短期战略更好这个问题。

PART II
第二部分

ARE LONG-TERM STRATEGIES REALLY BETTER?

长期战略真的更好吗？

Some believe that long-term strategies are lazy or excessively conservative. Usually , that’s because they look at driven people and notice that most of them use aggressive short-term strategies.

有些人认为长期战略是懒惰或过于保守的表现。通常，这是因为他们观察那些积极进取的人，发现他们大多采用激进的短期战略。

However, driven people who consistently use long-term strategies achieve better results than those who use short-term ones, especially after taking into account survivorship bias. Hence , employing long-term strategies is not lazy or conservative, but rational and ambitious. ( I will discuss survivorship bias later.)

然而，那些始终坚持长期策略、目标明确的人，比那些只关注短期策略的人更容易取得更好的成绩，尤其是在考虑到幸存者偏差之后。因此，采用长期策略并非懒惰或保守，而是理性且富有雄心的表现。（我稍后会讨论幸存者偏差。）

Moreover, people using long-term strategies also achieve their objectives in a more fulfilling way and without side effects that might damage other areas of their lives.

此外，采用长期策略的人也能以更令人满意的方式实现目标，而且不会产生可能损害生活其他方面的副作用。

This chapter will demonstrate the hidden benefits of long-term strategies and prove that they are superior to short-term ones.

本章将展示长期战略的隐藏好处，并证明长期战略优于短期战略。

10

BETTER OPTIONS

更好的选择

I magine one of your life goals was to become a millionaire. And imagine you want to achieve it by tomorrow.

想象一下，你的人生目标之一是成为百万富翁。再想象一下，你希望明天就能实现这个目标。

What could you do to succeed? Invest your life savings in lottery tickets? Attempt a heist? A short time horizon constrains you to bad options.

为了成功，你能做些什么？把毕生积蓄都投到彩票上？去抢劫？时间太短，你只能选择糟糕的方案。

Now, imagine you gave yourself two years to become a millionaire.

现在，想象一下你给自己两年时间成为百万富翁。

What could you do? Take risky bets on the stock market? You would have better odds than in the previous scenario, but it would still be risky.

你可以怎么办？在股市上进行高风险赌博吗？虽然胜算会比之前的情况高，但仍然存在风险。

And what if you had thirty years to become a millionaire?

如果你有三十年的时间成为百万富翁呢？

You would have plenty of relatively safe options, such as a good career and periodically investing your savings without having to take excessively risky bets.

你将有很多相对安全的选择，例如一份好工作和定期投资你的积蓄，而无需进行风险过高的投资。

The longer your time horizon, the better and more reliable your options for achieving your goals. ⁠ i

时间跨度越长，实现目标的方案就越好、越可靠。

A better life

更美好的生活

A common misconception about playing the long game is that it means delaying gratification. I strongly disagree.

人们对长远布局常常存在一个误解，认为它意味着延迟满足。我强烈反对这种观点。

If you give yourself more time to achieve your goals, you can make your journey toward success more pleasurable. When playing the long game, you will have fewer transactional relationships, feel less pressure to take undue risks or overstep your boundaries, and have time to take very fulfilling long-term actions, such as learning and honing your craft.

如果你给自己更多的时间去实现目标，你的成功之路就会更加愉悦。着眼长远，你会减少交易型人际关系，减少承担不必要风险或越界的压力，并有时间去做一些真正有意义的长期行动，例如学习和精进技艺。

Note that this is not an invitation to slack off. Rather , it’s the realization that hard work with a long time horizon is more pleasurable and fulfilling than hard work with a short time horizon.

请注意，这并非鼓励大家偷懒。而是要认识到，着眼长远的努力比着眼短浅的努力更有乐趣和成就感。

Long-term strategies are constructive, sustainable, and inevitable: three qualities that will lead you to take actions that ultimately improve satisfaction, such as learning, building trust, having fun, and resting every now and then.

长期战略具有建设性、可持续性和必然性：这三个特质将引导你采取行动，最终提高满意度，例如学习、建立信任、享受乐趣以及时不时地休息。

Playing the long game has nothing to do with delaying gratification-only with delaying comparison. You must resist the temptation to compare yourself with others based on your short-term growth rate or temporary success.

着眼长远与延迟满足无关，而仅仅与延迟比较有关。你必须抵制住诱惑，不要因为短期的成长速度或暂时的成功而与他人攀比。

Ideally, avoid all comparisons, but if you must, compare yourself only against those who are also playing the long game. Those who are also unwilling to compromise their values, take excessive risks, or over-focus on a single area of their life to the detriment of others.

理想情况下，应避免一切比较；但如果必须比较，那就只与那些同样着眼长远的人比较。这些人也不愿为了追求目标而妥协自己的价值观，不愿承担过大的风险，也不愿为了专注于生活的某一方面而忽略其他方面。

Never compare yourself to someone with a shorter time horizon. Doing so will mislead you into making suboptimal choices.

永远不要和那些投资期限较短的人比较。这样做会误导你做出次优选择。

Compounding and Outlasting

复合与持久

“If your investment returns are in the 50th percentile every year, you will probably end up in the top 5-10% over a 20-year period.”

MORGAN HOUSEL

“如果你的投资回报率每年都处于前50%的水平，那么20年后你很可能会跻身前5%到10%。”——摩根·豪塞尔

Do not underestimate the power of compounding. Assets that produce more of the same asset over time (money, skill, audiences, etc.) grow faster the more you have. Instead of competing for the fastest growth rate now, compete to have the fastest reproducible growth rate over time .

不要低估复利的力量。随着时间推移能够产生更多同类资产（例如金钱、技能、受众等）的资源，其增长速度会随着你拥有的数量而加快。与其争夺当下最快的增长速度，不如争夺未来能够持续增长的最快速度。

Similarly, do not underestimate the power of outlasting your competition. When you begin your career in a new field, you will be one of thousands with no previous experience. But as time passes, you will become one of hundreds with some experience, and eventually one of a few with significant experience.

同样，不要低估坚持不懈的力量。当你进入一个新领域时，你只是成千上万个毫无经验的人之一。但随着时间的推移，你会成为数百个拥有一定经验的人之一，最终成为少数几个拥有丰富经验的人之一。

While it won’t necessarily get easier,⁠ ii the upside you get from staying in the game will grow.

虽然情况不一定会变得更容易，但你继续玩下去所获得的收益会越来越大。

The benefits of compounding and outlasting are so large and easy to reproduce that they are integral parts of Winning Long - Term Games .

复利和持久战的优势如此巨大且易于复制，以至于它们是赢得长期博弈不可或缺的组成部分。

* * *

The benefits of compounding are evident when it comes to money, but they also apply to relationships (e.g., the more people you know, the more events you will be invited to, and the more relationships you will develop) and skills (the more you can do, the more you will try and, therefore, the more you will learn).

复利的益处在金钱方面显而易见，但它也适用于人际关系（例如，你认识的人越多，你被邀请参加的活动就越多，你建立的关系就越多）和技能（你能做的事情越多，你就会尝试得越多，因此你学到的东西也就越多）。

Conversely, the benefits of outlasting are less known but no less important. Often , you might have ideas the world is not ready for (in the sense that there is not yet enough demand or infrastructure to support them); in this case, staying in the game will help you be there when the time is right, so you can finally profit.

反之，坚持到底的好处虽然鲜为人知，但同样重要。很多时候，你可能有一些想法，但世界尚未准备好接受它们（也就是说，市场需求或基础设施还不足以支撑这些想法）；在这种情况下，坚持下去能让你在时机成熟时占据有利位置，最终获利。

Similarly, many investors became rich, not so much thanks to their performance during bull markets, but thanks to their resilience during bear markets, which enabled them to be buyers at the bottom and thus acquire plenty of assets at great prices relative to their value.

同样，许多投资者致富，与其说是得益于他们在牛市中的表现，不如说是得益于他们在熊市中的韧性，这使他们能够在市场底部买入，从而以相对于其价值而言极低的价格获得大量资产。

There is plenty of value in outlasting your competition. However , this value is only visible if you adopt long-term evaluations.

比竞争对手坚持得更久固然很有价值，但只有采用长期评估方法，这种价值才能显现出来。

“Ninety percent of success can be boiled down to consistently doing the obvious thing for an uncommonly long period of time without convincing yourself that you're smarter than you are.”

SHANE PARRISH

“成功九成可以归结为：在一段异常长的时间里，始终如一地做显而易见的事情，并且不要自欺欺人地认为自己比实际更聪明。”——肖恩·帕里什
# ↩

A short-term focus reduces your potential

目光短浅会降低你的潜力

Another common reason people do not embrace the long-term nature of long-term games is that they think, " If I play each short game trying to become successful as quickly as possible, I might fail a few times, but sooner or later, I will succeed, and that will happen faster than if I played the long game."

人们不接受长期博弈的长期性质的另一个常见原因是，他们认为，“如果我玩每个短期游戏都试图尽快取得成功，我可能会失败几次，但迟早我会成功，而且这比我玩长期游戏要快得多。”

I strongly disagree. A significant drawback of playing short-term games as if they weren’t part of a long-term game is that they do not lead to progress in case of failure, and sometimes not even in case of success!

我强烈反对。把短期游戏当作长期游戏的一部分来玩，一个很大的弊端是，失败时不会带来任何进展，有时即使成功也不会！

There are plenty of people who accumulate small successes, yet fail to make any significant advancement. Think about the person who has many successful dates but fails to convert any of that into a long-term relationship, or the entrepreneur who closes many sales but fails to get any repeat customers. Their short-term focus causes them to win in a way that doesn’t foster progress.

很多人积累了不少小的成功，却始终无法取得任何实质性的进步。想想那些约会多次却始终无法发展成长期关系的人，或者那些成交量巨大却无法获得回头客的企业家。他们过于关注短期利益，导致他们取得的成功方式不利于长远发展。

Conversely, some long-term players accumulate failure after failure and nevertheless progress. Their long-term focus ensures that even in failure, they build skills, understanding, and relationships that eventually lead to success.

相反，一些长期参与者即使屡战屡败，最终也能取得进步。他们着眼长远，即使在失败中也能积累技能、知识和人脉，最终走向成功。

And some people accumulate short-term successes obtained through long-term focus, and these grow the fastest.

有些人通过长期专注而获得短期成功，而这些人的成功增长速度最快。

Playing without a long-term focus reduces your potential.

缺乏长远目标会降低你的潜力。

# ↩

The problem with chasing fast success

追求快速成功的弊端

Short-term players almost see winning long-term games as a failure, thinking, " You could have achieved that faster."

短视的玩家几乎把赢得长期比赛视为失败，他们会想：“你本可以更快地取得胜利。”

Therefore, short-term players often take actions that are unsustainable in the long run. They might sacrifice their health or personal lives, overspend, deplete their trust capital, or take small risks with potentially serious consequences.

因此，短期投资者往往会采取一些长期来看不可持续的行动。他们可能会牺牲健康或个人生活，过度消费，耗尽信托资本，或者承担一些虽小但可能造成严重后果的风险。

In contrast, long-term players only use strategies that are sustainable over time.

相比之下，长期投资者只会采用能够长期持续发展的策略。

Like everyone else, long-term players try to win as quickly as possible, but unlike others, they avoid strategies that jeopardize their long-term success.

和其他人一样，长期玩家也试图尽快获胜，但与其他人不同的是，他们会避免危及自身长期成功的策略。

They understand that while short-term wins are possible , only long-term strategies can (almost) guarantee success.

他们明白，虽然短期内有可能取得胜利，但只有长期战略才能（几乎）保证成功。

i Many social rituals, such as marriages and long-term employment, are about lengthening the time horizon to open better options and encourage long-term evaluations.

许多社会习俗，如婚姻和长期就业，都是为了延长时间跨度，从而创造更好的选择，并鼓励进行长期评估。

ii You will have fewer competitors, but they will be fiercer. Early on, you competed mostly against mediocre players; as the game goes on, the mediocre players drop, and you compete more and more against stronger players. This concept will be elaborated in the chapter titled “Races to the Bottom.”

二、你的竞争对手会减少，但竞争会更加激烈。游戏初期，你主要与水平一般的玩家竞争；随着游戏进行，水平一般的玩家会逐渐减少，而你将越来越多地与实力更强的玩家对抗。这一概念将在题为“逐底竞争”的章节中详细阐述。

# ↩
11

SURVIVORSHIP BIAS

幸存者偏差

S ome strategies appear better than they are because of a phenomenon called survivorship bias, in which we overestimate how good a strategy is because we only look at those who used it and became successful, but not at those who used it and failed.

由于一种称为幸存者偏差的现象，一些策略看起来比实际情况要好，在这种情况下，我们高估了某种策略的好坏，因为我们只关注那些使用该策略并取得成功的人，而忽略了那些使用该策略但失败的人。

Survivorship bias is particularly treacherous because of a phenomenon I call hindsight gerrymandering, which works as follows.

幸存者偏差尤其危险，因为我称之为事后操纵选区划分的现象，其运作方式如下。

Imagine you go to the casino with ten friends, and you all play a few rounds of roulette. Each of you uses a different strategy: one only bets on red, another keeps betting on the 36, a third one always bets on the last winning number, and so on. After twenty minutes, you notice that all of you have lost money, except for one friend who always bet on the last winning number – he doubled his money.

想象一下，你和十个朋友一起去赌场，玩了几轮轮盘赌。你们每个人都采用不同的策略：一个只押红色，一个一直押36，第三个总是押上一个中奖号码，等等。二十分钟后，你们发现除了那个一直押上一个中奖号码的朋友之外，其他人都输了钱——他赢了双倍的钱。

What is your conclusion?

你的结论是什么？

Is it that playing Roulette is likely to lose you money? Or is it that betting on the last winning number is a great strategy for playing Roulette ?

玩轮盘赌容易输钱吗？还是说，押注最后一个中奖号码是玩轮盘赌的好策略？

If you concluded the latter, you would be wrong. You committed hindsight gerrymandering : you used hindsight to draw boundaries between strategies that are actually all instances of the same flawed strategy: participating in a money-losing game.

如果你得出后一个结论，那就错了。你犯了事后诸葛亮式的划分错误：你利用事后诸葛亮的视角，将各种策略划分开来，而这些策略实际上都是同一种有缺陷的策略：参与一场赔钱的游戏。

In the previous example, the use of hindsight is obvious. That’s because everyone knows that Roulette is a game of pure luck, and because the odds are known and in favor of the casino.

在前一个例子中，事后诸葛亮的运用显而易见。这是因为人人都知道轮盘赌纯粹是靠运气，而且赔率是公开的，赌场占优势。

However, when it comes to other "games" where winners are determined by a mix of skill and luck, such as the stock market, it is much easier to commit hindsight gerrymandering without noticing and thus fall prey to survivorship bias.

然而，对于其他一些胜负取决于技巧和运气的“游戏”（例如股票市场），人们很容易在不知不觉中进行事后操纵，从而成为幸存者偏差的受害者。

For example, imagine that one year an investor becomes particularly successful. Other investors review his trades and notice that all of his most successful investments were in companies with foreign CEOs . Suddenly , there might be a tendency to believe that investing in companies with foreign CEOs is a great strategy! But unless this strategy was known before the fact, it might be the result of randomness. Maybe that successful investor didn't even notice he was investing in companies with foreign CEOs , or didn't think it was that important! And if other investors use hindsight to define strategies, they set themselves up for disappointment when, the following year, the strategy's good performance doesn't hold up.

例如，假设某年一位投资者特别成功。其他投资者查看他的交易记录后发现，他所有最成功的投资都投向了由外国CEO领导的公司。突然间，人们可能会倾向于认为投资由外国CEO领导的公司是一个绝佳的策略！但除非事先知道这一策略，否则这可能只是偶然的结果。或许这位成功的投资者根本没注意到自己投资了由外国CEO领导的公司，或者认为这并不重要！如果其他投资者用事后诸葛亮的眼光来定义策略，那么当第二年该策略的良好表现不再持续时，他们注定会失望。

In fact, using hindsight to draw a non-existent boundary between a good and a bad strategy is the most common reason that otherwise very smart investors temporarily forget survivorship bias and get lured into adopting money-losing strategies.

事实上，事后诸葛亮地在好策略和坏策略之间划出一条并不存在的界限，是导致原本非常聪明的投资者暂时忘记幸存者偏差并被诱入亏损策略的最常见原因。

But there’s another mechanism that makes survivorship bias hard to detect, and I will cover it on the next page.

但还有另一种机制使得幸存者偏差难以检测，我将在下一页介绍它。

# ↩

A numerical example

数值示例

Imagine two entrepreneurs, Alice and Bob . They each start a business with an initial capital of $100,000. Alice takes more risks, resulting in a high growth rate of 10%, but also a high failure rate of 5%. Bob , on the other hand, takes fewer risks, leading to a lower growth rate of 8% and a lower failure rate of 1%.

假设有两个创业者，爱丽丝和鲍勃。他们各自用10万美元的初始资金创办一家公司。爱丽丝承担的风险更大，因此增长率高达10%，但失败率也高达5%。而鲍勃则承担的风险更小，增长率较低，为8%，但失败率也更低，仅为1%。

Who do we expect to make the most money: Alice or Bob ?

我们认为爱丽丝和鲍勃谁赚的钱最多？

The answer is counterintuitive: Alice is more likely to be wealthier than Bob , yet we expect Bob to end up wealthier.

答案与直觉相悖：爱丽丝更有可能比鲍勃更富有，但我们却预期鲍勃最终会更富有。

Let me explain.

让我解释一下。

If we consider periods of a single year, Alice is expected to be wealthier than Bob 95% of the time. Yet , if you compare the expected wealth, Alice ’s is 95% times $100,000 times 110% = $104,500, whereas Bob’s is 99% times $100,000 times 108% = $106,920. Bob’s expected wealth is higher than Alice’s , despite Bob being less likely to be wealthier than Alice .

如果我们以一年为周期来考虑，爱丽丝95%的时间里都会比鲍勃更富有。然而，如果比较两人的预期财富，爱丽丝的预期财富是95% × 10万美元 × 110% = 104,500美元，而鲍勃的预期财富是99% × 10万美元 × 108% = 106,920美元。尽管鲍勃比爱丽丝更富有的可能性更小，但他的预期财富却高于爱丽丝。

Here is another way to see it. Given a hundred Alices and a hundred Bobs , the top 95 wealthiest entrepreneurs would all be Alices . Yet , in aggregate, Bobs would have more wealth.

换个角度来看。假设有100个爱丽丝和100个鲍勃，那么最富有的95位企业家都将是爱丽丝。然而，总体而言，鲍勃的财富反而会更多。

Survivorship bias makes us think that Alice’s strategy is better because all the winners are Alices , but her strategy is not better. Alice’s strategy has higher potential but is less reproducible; therefore, it ultimately performs worse when considering survivorship bias.

幸存者偏差让我们误以为爱丽丝的策略更好，因为所有获胜者都是爱丽丝，但实际上她的策略并非更优。爱丽丝的策略潜力更大，但可复制性更差；因此，考虑到幸存者偏差，她的策略最终表现更差。

# ↩

Running a simulation

运行模拟

I ran a Monte Carlo simulation,⁠ i computing the results of ten million Alices and ten million Bobs running their businesses for ten years (using the same parameters as the previous example).

我运行了一个蒙特卡罗模拟，计算了一千万个爱丽丝和一千万个鲍勃经营他们的企业十年的结果（使用与前面示例相同的参数）。

The results of the simulation are telling.

模拟结果很有启发性。

The top 10% of entrepreneurs by wealth are all Alices ! That gives the impression that Alice’s strategy is worth imitating more than Bob’s .

按财富排名前 10% 的企业家都是爱丽丝！这给人一种印象，似乎爱丽丝的策略比鲍勃的更值得效仿。

And yet, the average Alice has only $155,000, whereas the average Bob has $195,000. Bob ends up 26% wealthier despite not appearing in the top decile even once!

然而，普通爱丽丝只有 15.5 万美元，而普通鲍勃却有 19.5 万美元。鲍勃虽然一次也没有进入收入最高的 10% 行列，最终却比爱丽丝富有 26%！

What’s even more surprising is that, if we only consider the surviving Alices (i.e., those who didn’t fail), their average wealth is a whopping $259,000, whereas the wealth of the average surviving Bob is only $195,000. However , we shouldn’t look at only the surviving Alices – we should look at all of them.

更令人惊讶的是，如果我们只考虑那些幸存下来的爱丽丝（即那些没有失败的人），她们的平均财富高达25.9万美元，而幸存下来的鲍勃的平均财富只有19.5万美元。然而，我们不应该只关注幸存的爱丽丝——我们应该关注所有人。

This experiment shows how misleading survivorship bias is.

这个实验表明幸存者偏差有多么具有误导性。

The strategy producing the most winners is not always the best strategy for you.

能够带来最多胜利的策略，未必就是最适合你的策略。

i The code for this simulation and the others in this section of the book can be found at https://github.com/lucadellanna/Alice-and-Bob.

i 本模拟和本书本节中其他模拟的代码可在 https://github.com/lucadellanna/Alice-and-Bob 找到。

12

THE MAXIMUM REPRODUCIBLE RETURN

最大可复制回报

A s an investor, achieving average market returns is a pretty good strategy: it’s relatively cheap, doesn’t take much effort, and produces better returns than apparent. After all, we have already seen that if you achieve average returns for an above-average amount of time, you receive well-above-average returns.

作为投资者，追求平均市场回报是一个相当不错的策略：它成本相对较低，无需投入太多精力，而且实际收益可能高于表面值。毕竟，我们已经看到，如果以高于平均水平的时间持续获得平均回报，最终就能获得远高于平均水平的回报。

With some skill and hard work, you can even achieve returns that are slightly above the market. However , there is a limit to the returns you can achieve without taking excessive risks.

只要具备一定的技巧和努力，你甚至可以获得略高于市场平均水平的回报。然而，如果不承担过高的风险，你能获得的回报也是有限的。

If you were alone, you would stop once you achieve the Maximum Reproducible Returns – the highest growth rate you can get without excessively risking irreversible losses.

如果你独自一人，你会在达到最大可复制回报（即在不冒过大风险造成不可逆转损失的情况下所能达到的最高增长率）后停止。

However, you are not alone. Every day, there are investors earning more than you. You feel left behind.

然而，你并不孤单。每天都有投资者的收益比你高。你感到自己落后了。

They’re using non-reproducible strategies, but you don’t see that. They’re earning higher returns by taking higher risks than you, but you don’t see that. Or you see that, but the success of some of them makes you feel that those risks aren’t that high.

他们采用的是不可复制的策略，但你却浑然不觉。他们承担的风险比你高，却获得了更高的回报，但你也同样视而不见。或者，你或许看到了这一点，但他们中一些人的成功让你觉得这些风险并没有那么高。

Either way, you have a choice. Either you stick to your strategy and keep reaping the Maximum Reproducible Returns . Or you copy their strategy and, for a while, enjoy higher returns, until one day, inevitably, the risks you ignored materialize and generate losses big enough to offset all the extra profits and then some.

无论如何，你都面临选择。你可以坚持自己的策略，持续获得最大可复制收益；也可以效仿他们的策略，暂时享受更高的回报，但总有一天，你忽略的风险会不可避免地显现出来，造成足以抵消所有额外收益甚至更大的损失。

Much of being a great investor consists of putting in the hard work and effort required to achieve the Maximum Reproducible Return and then ignoring anyone who earns more than that, knowing that, eventually, they will crash.

成为一名优秀的投资者，很大程度上在于投入必要的努力和汗水，以实现最大可复制回报，然后忽略任何收益超过这个目标的人，因为你知道，他们最终都会崩盘。

Note that the above is not fully true. First of all, you never want to fully ignore your competitors. You always want to check whether they’re doing something right that’s worth learning from.

请注意，以上说法并不完全正确。首先，你永远不应该完全忽视你的竞争对手。你始终应该关注他们是否做对了什么，值得你学习。

Also, note that not everyone who uses a Non - Reproducible Strategy crashes. Some succeed. Some even triumph. But only some.

另外，请注意，并非所有使用不可复现策略的人都会失败。有些人会成功，有些人甚至会取得胜利。但只有一部分人会成功。

If the Maximum Reproducible Returns are, say, 10%, of course, there will be someone who reaps 12%. Of course, you could reap 12%. This doesn’t mean that if you pursued those returns, you would earn them.

如果最大可复制回报率是10%，那么当然会有人获得12%的回报率。当然，你也有可能获得12%的回报率。但这并不意味着如果你追求这样的回报率，你就能获得它。

What matters is not the Maximum Possible Outcome but the Distribution of Outcomes .

重要的不是最大可能的结果，而是结果的分布。

# ↩
13

THE DISTRIBUTION OF OUTCOMES

结果分布

W hen you see someone achieving tremendous success, especially very quickly, you are only seeing one of many parallel worlds.

当你看到有人取得巨大的成功，尤其是很快取得的成功时，你看到的只是众多平行世界中的一个。

The question is, given ten parallel worlds in which that person uses the same strategy, in how many of them would they achieve success?

问题是，假设存在十个平行世界，每个人使用相同的策略，那么在多少个平行世界中，这个人会取得成功？

If the answer is ten, congratulations! They are probably using a Reproducible Success Strategy , and you might want to learn from them.

如果答案是十，恭喜！他们可能正在使用可复制的成功策略，您不妨向他们学习。

If the answer is less than ten, then they are using a non- Reproducible Success Strategy . Imitate them at your own risk.

如果答案少于十个，那么他们使用的是一种不可复制的成功策略。模仿他们，后果自负。

Do not judge strategies based on their best-case scenario ⁠ i (which, because of survivorship bias, is probably what you observe). Instead , judge strategies based on their distribution of outcomes.

不要根据策略的最佳情况（由于幸存者偏差，这很可能就是你观察到的情况）来评判它们。相反，应该根据策略结果的分布情况来评判它们。

Good strategies have satisfactory long-term outcomes both in the case of good and bad luck. ( How they achieve this will be covered later, but here is a hint: they are designed so that they never put your long-term assets at risk, and so that even failures grow them.)

好的策略无论运气好坏都能带来令人满意的长期结果。（它们是如何做到这一点的，我们稍后会详细讲解，但这里先透露一点：它们的设计宗旨是绝不会让你的长期资产面临风险，而且即使失败也能让你的资产增值。）

An example of the importance of the distribution of outcomes

结果分布重要性的一个例子

Let’s use the lottery as an example of why estimating the distribution of outcomes of a strategy is more important than estimating its expected value. ( As a reminder, the expected value of a strategy is the average of its outcomes.)

让我们以彩票为例，说明为什么估计策略结果的分布比估计其期望值更重要。（提醒一下，策略的期望值是其结果的平均值。）

The reason most of us do not play the lottery is that the expected value of purchasing a ticket is negative. For example, if a ticket costs $1 and you have a one-in-a-billion chance of winning a hundred million, the expected value of buying the ticket is -$0.90.

大多数人不买彩票的原因是，买彩票的期望值为负。例如，如果一张彩票售价 1 美元，而你赢得一亿美元的概率是十亿分之一，那么买这张彩票的期望值就是 -0.90 美元。

But what if the expected value of playing the lottery were positive? For example, what if you had a one-in-a-billion chance of winning 10 billion?

但如果买彩票的期望值为正呢？例如，如果你有十亿分之一的概率赢得100亿美元呢？

The expected value of buying a ticket would be +9$. Yet , you should still not play the lottery.

购买彩票的预期收益为9美元。然而，你仍然不应该购买彩票。

The reason is that if you spent $1,000 to buy a thousand tickets, you would still only have a one-in-a-million chance of winning 10 billion and a 99.9999% chance of losing $1,000.

原因是，即使你花 1000 美元买了 1000 张彩票，你赢得 100 亿美元的概率也只有百万分之一，而损失 1000 美元的概率却高达 99.9999%。

And if you spent a million? You would have a 0.1% chance of becoming a billionaire and a 99.9% chance of losing a million. It's not a good bet unless you are already so wealthy that losing a million is inconsequential.

如果你投入一百万美元呢？你成为亿万富翁的概率只有0.1%，而损失一百万美元的概率高达99.9%。除非你已经富可敌国，损失一百万美元也无关紧要，否则这绝对不是一笔划算的买卖。

What matters is not the expected value of a bet but its distribution of outcomes.

重要的不是赌注的预期价值，而是结果的分布情况。

i The best-case scenario is an important factor in evaluating tactics, but is much less important when evaluating strategies.

最佳情况是评估战术的重要因素，但对于评估战略而言，它的重要性要小得多。

Again, you want to take high-upside bets! But only if their downside doesn’t prevent you from taking many of them, so that even if each bet is individually unlikely to succeed, a strategy of bets is likely to succeed.

再次强调，你要下注高收益的赌注！但前提是其风险不会阻止你进行多次下注，这样即使每次下注单独来看成功的可能性很小，但下注策略本身就有可能成功。
