14

TIME HORIZON BIAS

时间跨度偏差

I n the previous chapters, I introduced a concept of paramount importance: a strategy that is optimal for short time horizons might fail to produce good returns over long ones, and a strategy that is optimal for long time horizons might seem inefficient over short ones.

在前几章中，我介绍了一个至关重要的概念：短期内最优的策略可能无法在长期内产生良好的回报，而长期内最优的策略在短期内可能显得效率低下。

Without a strong belief in this concept, you might be tempted to imitate short-term strategies that come with a high but unsustainable growth rate. Doing so might set you back in the long run.

如果对这个理念没有坚定的信念，你可能会忍不住去模仿那些增长速度快但不可持续的短期策略。这样做从长远来看可能会让你吃亏。

So, let's look at a numerical example that will demonstrate this counterintuitive principle. Imagine two solopreneurs , Alice and Bob , who are growing their social media audience by writing engaging posts.

那么，让我们来看一个数值例子来说明这个违反直觉的原理。假设有两个独立创业者，爱丽丝和鲍勃，他们通过撰写引人入胜的帖子来扩大社交媒体受众群体。

They both start with zero followers. Alice is more aggressive and uses lies and exaggerations to grow faster. As a result, she gets an average of 100 followers per post but also has a 5% chance that her lie will be discovered, leading to a 20% loss of followers. Conversely , Bob never lies but only grows at a rate of 50 followers per post, half of Alice's .

他们俩一开始都是零粉丝。爱丽丝更激进，她会撒谎和夸大其词来快速涨粉。因此，她平均每篇帖子能涨100个粉，但同时也有5%的概率谎言会被揭穿，导致20%的粉丝流失。相比之下，鲍勃从不撒谎，但他每篇帖子只能涨50个粉，只有爱丽丝的一半。

They both post once a day. Who do we expect to have more followers? Think about the answer before continuing to the next page.

他们俩都每天发一条帖子。我们觉得谁的粉丝会更多？在继续下一页之前，请思考一下答案。

# ↩

The right answer is that it depends on the time frame considered.

正确答案是，这取决于所考虑的时间范围。

As the chart below illustrates, Alice’s strategy initially holds an advantage for about a month, after which Bob is expected to gain more followers.

如下表所示，Alice 的策略最初在大约一个月内具有优势，之后 Bob 预计会获得更多追随者。

Of course, this is just a thought experiment. In real life, we would expect things to work differently: for example, Alice might learn from her mistakes, followers do not grow linearly, and so on.

当然，这只是一个思想实验。在现实生活中，事情的发展会有所不同：例如，爱丽丝可能会从错误中吸取教训，粉丝数量并非线性增长，等等。

Yet, the core point remains – a strategy performing better over short time frames might be suboptimal for long time frames.

然而，核心要点依然是——在短期内表现较好的策略，在长期内可能并非最佳选择。

Hence, do not extrapolate long-term performance from short-term performance, but always ask yourself how the short-term performance is achieved: performance obtained through excessive risk-taking is unlikely to be sustainable over time.

因此，不要根据短期业绩推断长期业绩，而要始终问问自己短期业绩是如何实现的：通过过度冒险获得的业绩不太可能长期持续。

# ↩

Time horizon bias and survivorship bias

时间范围偏差和幸存者偏差

Let me link this chapter to the one on survivorship bias by noting that, in this thought experiment where Alice and Bob grow their social media following, Alice has only a 10% chance of getting more followers than Bob after 100 days. However , that would still mean that, given 100 Alices and 100 Bobs , the top 10 influencers by social media followers are all Alices ! – even though Bobs are expected to have more followers on average. Again , beware of survivorship bias.

让我把这一章和关于幸存者偏差的那一章联系起来。在这个思想实验中，假设爱丽丝和鲍勃都在发展他们的社交媒体粉丝，那么100天后，爱丽丝的粉丝数量超过鲍勃的概率只有10%。然而，即便如此，如果假设有100个爱丽丝和100个鲍勃，那么社交媒体粉丝数量排名前十的影响力人物竟然全是爱丽丝！——尽管鲍勃的平均粉丝数量通常应该更多。所以，再次提醒大家注意幸存者偏差。

That said, because the rewards of social media disproportionately accrue to the top influencers, some readers might still be thinking: “ I’d rather have a 10% chance of becoming a top influencer than a 100% chance of having a good-but-not-great following.”

也就是说，由于社交媒体的回报不成比例地流向了顶级影响者，一些读者可能仍然会想：“我宁愿有 10% 的机会成为顶级影响者，也不愿有 100% 的机会拥有一个不错但并不出色的粉丝群体。”

Yes, but also consider that 10% is the chance of being a top influencer after 100 days, whereas after 200 days, those chances go below 1%, and after a year, below 0.01%. ⁠ i You don’t want a mere 0.01% chance.

是的，但也要考虑到，100天后成为顶级网红的概率是10%，200天后这个概率会低于1%，一年后甚至低于0.01%。你肯定不想只有0.01%的概率。

Of course, this is an exaggerated thought experiment. But the point remains: when we observe someone becoming successful quickly, we are observing a suboptimal level of risk-taking compared to what would be optimal for a longer time horizon and after accounting for survivorship bias.

当然，这只是一个夸张的思维实验。但重点依然是：当我们观察到某人迅速获得成功时，我们看到的其实是他承担的风险水平低于从更长的时间跨度来看，并考虑到幸存者偏差后的最佳风险水平。

Those are levels of risk-taking that are optimal for “taking many people and selecting the best.” But you cannot do that with yourself: your n is 1. Hence , adjust optimal risk-taking accordingly.

这些风险承受水平对于“从众多人员中选拔最优秀者”来说是最优的。但你不能对自己这样做：你的样本量 n 为 1。因此，需要相应地调整最优风险承受水平。

Practical applications

实际应用

Always evaluate the quality of a strategy over the relevant time horizon, and never over a shorter one.

评估策略的质量时，一定要在相关的时间范围内进行，切勿在较短的时间内进行评估。

If you are an investor, do not compare the yearly returns of two strategies; instead, compare the expected long-term outcomes of using them over the next decade or so (or even longer).

如果你是一名投资者，不要比较两种策略的年度收益；而是比较在未来十年左右（甚至更长时间）使用它们的预期长期结果。

If you are an entrepreneur, notice that there are activities, such as training, maintenance, and building a solid organizational culture, that may look like waste in the short term but are necessary for a high chance of long-term success.⁠ ii

如果您是一位企业家，请注意，有些活动，例如培训、维护和建立稳固的组织文化，短期内可能看起来像是浪费时间，但对于长期的成功至关重要。

If you are a salesperson, the best tactic to close a sale today might not be the best tactic for gaining a lifetime customer: the former can benefit from destroying trust, while the latter depends on building it.

如果你是一名销售人员，那么今天促成交易的最佳策略可能并不是获得终身客户的最佳策略：前者可以通过破坏信任来获利，而后者则依赖于建立信任。

If you are an employee, spending minimal effort to do your job may seem like the best way to get through the day, but it also sets you up for a career of mediocrity. Instead , consider investing some effort in learning, improving, building relationships and trust, and so on.

如果你是一名员工，看似最省力地完成工作是混日子的最佳方式，但这也会让你的职业生涯走向平庸。相反，你应该考虑投入一些精力去学习、提升自己、建立人脉和信任等等。

Winning long-term games requires managing long-term risks, even if they seem small in the short term, and building long-term assets, even if they seem unprofitable in the short term.

要想赢得长期的比赛，就需要管理长期的风险，即使这些风险在短期内看起来很小；并且需要建立长期的资产，即使这些资产在短期内看起来无利可图。

Chapter summary

章节概要

Strategies that work well in the short term might fail to work over the long term. And strategies that are optimal for the long term might seem inefficient in the short term.

短期内行之有效的策略，长期来看可能无效。而长期来看最优的策略，短期内可能显得效率低下。

To win in the long term, compare strategies based on their long-term effectiveness and disregard their short-term impact.

要想取得长期的成功，应该根据策略的长期有效性来比较各种策略，而忽略其短期影响。

This doesn’t mean never doing things that make sense in the short term. It means doing things that make sense in the short term in a way that doesn’t endanger the long term. And it means doing things that don’t make sense in the short term but are required to succeed in the long term, such as managing long-term risks and building long-term assets, even when it doesn’t seem like the best moment to do so.

这并非意味着永远不做短期内有意义的事情。而是意味着做短期内有意义的事情时，要以不危及长期利益的方式进行。同时，这也意味着去做一些短期内无意义但对长期成功至关重要的事情，例如管理长期风险和积累长期资产，即使当时看起来并非最佳时机。

15

WHEN ARE LONG-TERM EFFORTS JUSTIFIED?

何时才应该进行长期努力？

W e have explored a few reasons why people opt for short-term games despite the greater benefits of playing long-term ones. But there is one more crucial reason, one so subtle that I missed it in the first edition of this book.

我们已经探讨了一些人们明明知道长期游戏收益更大，却仍然选择短期游戏的原因。但还有一个至关重要的原因，它非常微妙，以至于我在本书第一版中都忽略了。

Consider someone using a short-term mindset at work. They put minimal effort into improving their skills or connecting with colleagues. As a result, their job becomes increasingly dull, and their career flatlines. Eventually , they jump ship for another position.

设想一下，如果有人在工作中只关注短期利益，他们很少努力提升自身技能或与同事建立联系。结果，他们的工作变得越来越枯燥乏味，职业发展也停滞不前。最终，他们会跳槽到其他公司。

At first glance, their short-term approach seems rational. Why invest energy in mastering skills or building relationships at a dead-end job with no future? However , this neglects a critical factor: our attitude influences both the duration of our job and its potential.

乍一看，他们的短期策略似乎合情合理。为什么要把精力投入到一份没有前途的死胡同工作中去掌握技能或建立人脉呢？然而，这种做法忽略了一个关键因素：我们的态度会影响我们工作的持续时间和未来发展潜力。

To determine whether it’s worth playing long-term games, we shouldn’t consider our situation as it is, but as it could be (if we adopted a long-term attitude).

要确定是否值得进行长期博弈，我们不应该考虑我们目前的处境，而应该考虑如果我们采取长期态度，情况可能会如何。

Of course, this does not mean it’s always worth playing long-term games-just that to determine whether it is, we should consider not what is but what could be.

当然，这并不意味着玩长期游戏总是值得的——只是说，要确定是否值得，我们应该考虑的不是现在是什么，而是将来可能是什么。

16

STAGES OF LIFE

人生阶段

A particularly dangerous situation for your long-term happiness arises when you play long-term games, but only for your current stage of life.

当你只关注你当前人生阶段的长期利益时，就会出现一种对你长期幸福特别危险的情况。

This is the case when someone plays long-term games at work but not outside of it. This attitude might make sense in one’s twenties, and it would if one’s twenties lasted forever. However , people who forget to play long-term games outside of work inevitably are surprised by how empty they feel once they move to the later stages of life.

这种情况指的是，有些人只在工作中玩长期游戏，却不在工作之外玩。这种态度在二十多岁时或许情有可原，如果二十多岁永远持续下去，那当然也无可厚非。然而，那些忘记在工作之外玩长期游戏的人，一旦步入人生的后期阶段，必然会惊讶于自己内心的空虚。

It’s a mistake to over-optimize for one’s current stage of life as if it could last for the rest of one’s life. Life doesn’t work this way.

过度优化自己当前的生活阶段，仿佛这种状态会持续一生，这是个错误。生活并非如此运作。

During our lives, we will go through multiple stages. And while we shouldn’t optimize for future stages, we shouldn’t neglect them either.

人的一生会经历多个阶段。我们不应该只关注未来的阶段，但也不应该忽视当前的阶段。

Of course, it’s easier said than done. It does feel like our current stage of life will last forever. But talk to any elder, and it is going to be obvious it won’t. Our priorities and needs will shift. A full life requires acknowledging this.

当然，说起来容易做起来难。我们总觉得现在的生活阶段会永远持续下去。但只要和任何一位长者聊聊，他们都会告诉你，事实并非如此。我们的优先事项和需求都会发生变化。想要拥有充实的人生，就必须认识到这一点。

Balancing between areas and stages of our lives

平衡我们生活中的各个领域和阶段

In 2021, I was diagnosed with malignant eye cancer. Luckily , doctors caught it early, and the treatment was successful ( I’m completely healthy now!). However , this experience made me realize that I have no idea how long my life will be.

2021年，我被诊断出患有恶性眼癌。幸运的是，医生发现得早，治疗也很成功（我现在已经完全康复了！）。然而，这段经历让我意识到，我根本不知道自己还能活多久。

If I knew for certain that I would die at 80, I could plan accordingly, choosing which relationships to nurture, how intensely to work, and how much to save and invest. But since none of us knows our expiration date, optimizing for any single timeframe makes little sense. What if I only make it to 40? What if I live to 110?

如果我确切知道自己会活到80岁，我就可以据此规划，选择维系哪些人际关系，工作强度如何，以及储蓄和投资多少。但由于我们谁也不知道自己的寿命，因此针对任何单一时间段进行优化都意义不大。万一我只能活到40岁呢？万一我活到110岁呢？

So, how do I optimize for multiple time horizons?

那么，如何针对多个时间跨度进行优化呢？

It’s simple. Every week, I try to do at least one thing I will be happy I did if I die tomorrow and at least one thing I will be happy I did if I live until 100 years old.

很简单。我每周都会尽量做至少一件如果我明天就去世我会感到欣慰的事，以及至少一件如果我能活到100岁我会感到欣慰的事。

You have probably heard of the Pareto Principle —the idea that roughly 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. For instance, 80% of your relationship joy comes from 20% of your friends, and 80% of your career progress comes from 20% of your activities. ( These aren’t exact numbers, of course, but the broad principle holds more often than not.)

你可能听说过帕累托法则——大约80%的结果来自20%的努力。例如，你80%的人际关系幸福感来自20%的朋友，你80%的职业发展进步来自20%的活动。（当然，这些并非精确数字，但这条普遍规律在大多数情况下都适用。）

You can apply this idea by acknowledging that if you spend 20% of your time and resources on one time horizon and 20% on another, you can ensure you will have at least an 80% fulfilled life, no matter when you die.

你可以这样理解：如果你将 20% 的时间和资源投入到一个时间段，将 20% 的时间和资源投入到另一个时间段，那么无论你何时去世，你都可以确保自己至少拥有 80% 的充实人生。

Maximizing your life isn't about picking one life stage to optimize for but rather about investing a bit of effort in each, ensuring you will be prepared no matter how long a life you will be given.

最大化你的人生价值，不是选择人生中的某个阶段进行优化，而是在每个阶段都投入一些精力，确保无论你的生命有多长，你都能做好准备。

And – this is crucial – at no stage should you take actions that might preclude you from happiness in other stages.

而且——这一点至关重要——在任何阶段，你都不应该采取任何可能妨碍你在其他阶段获得幸福的行动。

Do not burn bridges with your future selves.

不要与未来的自己断绝关系。

PART III
第三部分

LEVERAGING THE LONG TERM

利用长期优势

Good long-term strategies do not merely have a long time horizon but also leverage it to take actions that are unavailable to shorter-term players.

好的长期战略不仅具有长远的时间跨度，而且还能利用这种跨度采取短期参与者无法采取的行动。

For example, both a short-term and a long-term player might aim to retire wealthy. The difference is that the short-term player aims to make quick bucks and, therefore, will only take actions with good short-term returns. Conversely , the long-term player is willing to forego short-term gains if doing so allows for better long-term gains.

例如，短期投资者和长期投资者都可能以退休时拥有丰厚财富为目标。区别在于，短期投资者追求快速获利，因此只会采取短期收益高的行动。相反，长期投资者则愿意放弃短期收益，以换取更大的长期回报。

But what exactly are such long-term actions, and how can you take them effectively?

但究竟什么是长期行动，以及如何才能有效地采取这些行动呢？

This is the object of the third part of this book: how to take long-term actions.

本书第三部分的主题是：如何采取长期行动。

# ↩
18

LONG-TERM EVALUATIONS

长期评估

B oth short-term and long-term players have long-term objectives. Because of that, they both believe they are long-term players.

短期投资者和长期投资者都有长期目标。正因如此，他们都认为自己是长期投资者。

However, what makes a long-term player is not the time horizon of their objectives but that of their evaluations. Only long-term players consider the long-term impact of their actions (or lack thereof). ⁠ i

然而，决定一个人是否具有长期眼光的，并非其目标的时间跨度，而是其评估的时间跨度。只有长期眼光的参与者才会考虑其行为（或不作为）的长期影响。

The previous chapters illustrated some ways in which long-term games require different evaluations than what is effective for short-term ones. The problem with short-term evaluations is not that they are wrong (they are not), but rather that short-term evaluations get you stuck in winning short-term games without making any progress toward your long-term objectives.

前几章阐述了长期博弈需要与短期博弈不同的评估方法。短期评估的问题不在于它们本身是错误的（它们并没有错），而在于它们会让你陷入赢得短期博弈的泥潭，而无法朝着长期目标取得任何进展。

This chapter explains how you can make longer-term evaluations.

本章将解释如何进行长期评估。

Long-term assets

长期资产

If you are a manager or entrepreneur, you always have something urgent to do: a deadline to meet, a target to achieve… it never feels like a good moment to train your team. Yet , your potential is capped by the talent of your team. If you never train them, they will never perform at the level required to support your ambitions.

如果你是管理者或创业者，你总是有紧急的事情要做：要赶的截止日期、要达成的目标……你总觉得没有时间去培训团队。然而，你的潜力受限于团队的才能。如果你从不培训他们，他们就永远无法达到支持你实现目标所需的水平。

Training never makes sense in the short term (there is always something more urgent to do), yet it is indispensable for long-term success.

短期内，培训往往没有意义（总有更紧急的事情要做），但从长远来看，培训是取得成功的必要条件。

This is a common paradox. Building long-term assets (such as skills, habits, relationships, etc.) never makes sense in the short term (there is always a faster way to meet short-term objectives), yet it is necessary for long-term success.

这是一个常见的悖论。建立长期资产（例如技能、习惯、人际关系等）在短期内毫无意义（总有更快的方法来实现短期目标），但它对于长期成功却是必要的。

Your long-term success is limited to what your long-term assets allow. Increase your long-term assets, and you automatically increase your long-term potential.

你的长期成功取决于你的长期资产。增加你的长期资产，你的长期潜力自然也会随之提升。

The hard part is that building long-term assets requires making long-term evaluations in the face of short-term pressures – that’s the price of long-term success.

难点在于，构建长期资产需要在面对短期压力时进行长期评估——这就是长期成功的代价。

Practical applications

实际应用

You might have a small chance of achieving success without building long-term assets, but you can't count on it. Therefore , you should focus on building the long-term assets required to achieve your ambitions.

即使不积累长期资产，你或许也有很小的成功机会，但不能指望一定成功。因此，你应该专注于积累实现目标所需的长期资产。

First, list the long-term assets that will help you achieve your long-term objectives. Consider skills, habits, relationships, trust, a track record, a portfolio, a healthy body, and other relevant factors.

首先，列出有助于你实现长期目标的长期资产。考虑技能、习惯、人际关系、信任、过往业绩、投资组合、健康的身体以及其他相关因素。

Then, recognize that you need to start building those assets now – even if it doesn’t feel like the right time, because it never will.

然后，你要意识到，即使现在感觉时机不对，你也需要开始积累这些资产——因为时机永远不会对。

Of course, this doesn’t mean you should put your life on hold to focus solely on the long term, as that is often impractical or counterproductive. Instead , dedicate at least a couple of hours a week to doing things that may not make sense in the short term but are essential for the long term.

当然，这并不意味着你应该为了只关注长远目标而搁置自己的生活，因为这样做往往不切实际，甚至适得其反。相反，你应该每周至少抽出几个小时去做一些短期内可能看起来无关紧要，但对长远发展至关重要的事情。

A good practice I recommend to my consulting clients is to schedule time each week or month to focus on the long term. For example, I know of a few companies that reserve the second Friday of each month to work exclusively on long-term problems, such as building competencies, automating procedures, and discussing long-term risks.

我建议咨询客户的一个好做法是，每周或每月安排时间专注于长期目标。例如，我知道有些公司会把每月第二个星期五专门用来处理长期问题，比如提升员工能力、实现流程自动化以及探讨长期风险。

Start doing what doesn’t make sense now but is necessary for the long term – your Future Self will thank you.

开始做那些现在看起来没有意义但从长远来看必不可少的事情——未来的你会感谢现在的自己。

Over-optimization

过度优化

If you ever find yourself in a ski race, it’s relatively easy to be the fastest skier down a single slope: just crouch into a bullet position, keep your skis as parallel as possible, and maintain that position as long as you can – even as everyone else prepares for the next turn. You will eventually crash because you over-optimized for the straight part of the slope and won’t be able to survive the turn. But until then, you will be the fastest. ( Obviously , do not follow this advice.)

如果你参加滑雪比赛，想在单坡上成为最快的滑雪者其实很容易：只需蹲下身体，摆出子弹般的姿势，尽可能保持双板平行，并尽可能长时间地保持这个姿势——即使其他人都在准备下一个弯道。你最终会摔倒，因为你过度优化了直道上的速度，无法应对弯道。但在那之前，你将是最快的。（显然，不要照搬这个方法。）

It's a stupid strategy. Yet , plenty of people adopt it in business and life.⁠ ii They treat over-optimization as a shortcut to success, even if it leaves them unprepared for future challenges. What's worse, early successes can cause them to fixate on current strategies, further hindering their ability to adapt.

这是一种愚蠢的策略。然而，很多人在商业和生活中却都采用这种策略。他们把过度优化当作通往成功的捷径，即使这让他们无法应对未来的挑战。更糟糕的是，早期的成功会让他们固守当前的策略，进一步阻碍他们适应变化的能力。

The problem is that overoptimization is an excellent strategy for short-term wins but a terrible one for long-term success.

问题在于，过度优化对于短期胜利来说是一种极好的策略，但对于长期成功来说却是一种糟糕的策略。

Winning long-term games requires resisting overoptimization, even when it seems like the best approach.

要想赢得长期的比赛，就需要抵制过度优化，即使这看起来是最好的方法。

Optimization vs over-optimization

优化与过度优化

A common question I get is, “ Luca , over -optimization is obviously bad (as implicit in the word over ), but isn’t optimization desirable?”

我经常被问到的一个问题是：“卢卡，过度优化显然是不好的（正如‘过度’这个词所暗示的那样），但是优化难道不是可取的吗？”

Yes, but you should seek long-term optimization, not short-term optimization. Or , more precisely: do optimize for the short term, but never to the extent that it endangers the long term.

是的，但你应该追求长期优化，而不是短期优化。或者更准确地说：可以优化短期效益，但绝不能以牺牲长期利益为代价。

That said, it is also possible to over-optimize for the long term. Consider the person who delays gratification so much that they burn out, the entrepreneur who focuses so much on the long term that they lose short-term competitiveness, or the employee who plans their career in so much detail that they miss changes in the labor market.

话虽如此，过度追求长期利益也是有可能的。想想那些因为过度延迟满足而导致精疲力竭的人，那些过于关注长期发展而丧失短期竞争力的企业家，或者那些将职业生涯规划得过于细致而错失劳动力市场变化的员工。

As I already mentioned, my personal solution is to spend part of my time caring about the short-term, part of it caring about the medium-term, and part of it improving my long-term future – all without ever endangering any of the three time horizons.

正如我之前提到的，我的个人解决方案是，将一部分时间用于关注短期目标，一部分时间用于关注中期目标，一部分时间用于改善我的长期未来——所有这些都不会危及这三个时间跨度中的任何一个。

This ensures that I build the assets required to achieve my long-term objectives while also preventing risks such as burnout and retaining the flexibility required to adapt to an ever-changing world. Moreover , it ensures that I will have no regrets, regardless of whether I , my business, or my loved ones cease to exist tomorrow, in a decade, or fifty years.

这确保我能积累实现长期目标所需的资源，同时避免倦怠等风险，并保持适应瞬息万变的世界所需的灵活性。此外，它还能确保我无论明天、十年后还是五十年后，我、我的事业或我的亲人是否不复存在，都不会留下遗憾。

Only by balancing the three time horizons, instead of focusing on one exclusively, can you minimize your regrets in the face of uncertainty.

只有平衡三个时间跨度，而不是只关注其中一个，才能在面对不确定性时最大限度地减少遗憾。

# ↩

Cumulative Risks

累积风险

We have already seen how lying exemplifies a risk that is unlikely to materialize in the short term but becomes a significant liability over the long term. If there is, say, a 1% chance of it being discovered, it succeeds 99% of the time. However , if you lie once a week, you have a 99.5% chance of being caught over a decade.

我们已经看到，说谎体现了一种短期内不太可能发生，但长期来看却会造成重大损失的风险。假设说谎被发现的概率只有1%，那么它99%的情况下都会被识破。然而，如果你每周说谎一次，那么十年下来，你被揭穿的概率高达99.5%。

Actions with improbable risks are excellent tactics but terrible strategies.

采取风险极小的行动是极好的战术，但却是糟糕的战略。

This principle is very counterintuitive. If something is a good tactic when done once, it should also be a great tactic to repeat over and over, right?

这个原则非常违反直觉。如果某种策略在第一次使用时效果很好，那么它应该也是反复使用的绝佳策略，对吧？

Wrong.

错误的。

Time horizons matter, and risks accumulate.

时间跨度很重要，风险会不断累积。

If you want to succeed in the long term, you cannot afford to use tactics that carry a risk of ruin, however small. ( Small risks that do not significantly set you back if they materialize are fine.)

如果你想获得长期的成功，就不能使用任何可能带来毁灭性后果的策略，哪怕风险很小。（如果风险很小，即使发生也不会给你造成重大损失，那还可以接受。）

Never use short-term evaluations when estimating risks, especially when those risks accumulate.

在评估风险时，切勿使用短期评估，尤其是在风险累积的情况下。

Chapter summary

章节概要

Winning long-term games often involves avoiding what’s optimal in the short term.

要想赢得长期的比赛，往往需要避免短期内看似最优的选择。

Doing so requires training yourself to make long-term evaluations.

这样做需要训练自己进行长期评估。

This consists not only of seeing the long-term effects of your actions but also realizing that winning long-term games requires you to take long-term actions, even when it doesn’t seem like a good time to do so. There will always be something more urgent to do, but that urgent thing is unlikely to create a positive inflection point in your life trajectory.

这不仅意味着要看到你行为的长期影响，还要意识到，要想赢得长期的胜利，就需要采取长期的行动，即使现在看起来并非最佳时机。总会有更紧急的事情要做，但这些紧急的事情不太可能成为你人生轨迹的积极转折点。

As I wrote in my book “100 Truths You Will Learn Too Late ,”

正如我在我的书《你会为时已晚的100个真相》中所写的那样，

“Because the very important does not have a deadline, we have the impression that we can delay it for a few days. It is a huge mistake.

“因为非常重要的事情没有截止日期，所以我们误以为可以推迟几天。这是一个巨大的错误。”

Delaying something once opens the door to delaying it forever. If you think about it, the very important never feels urgent.”

拖延一次就可能永远拖延下去。仔细想想，真正重要的事情往往不会让人觉得迫在眉睫。

Make the important urgent: no one will do it for you.

把重要的事情放在首位：没有人会替你做。

i Similarly, both short-term players and long-term players play long-term games – after all, we all expect to live until our seventies or eighties. But short-term players play long-term games as if they were short-term ones, whereas only long-term players play long-term games embracing their long-term nature.

同样，短期玩家和长期玩家都在玩长期游戏——毕竟，我们都期望能活到七八十岁。但短期玩家玩长期游戏的方式就像玩短期游戏一样，而只有长期玩家才会真正理解并接受长期游戏的本质。

ii Not literally and not fully. However, there are indeed many people who adopt similar strategies that cause some early success followed by a large crash – maybe not a crash large enough to become a permanent game over, but large enough to set them back to a worse position than if they had followed a long-term strategy since the beginning.

二、并非完全如此。然而，确实有很多人采取类似的策略，在初期取得一些成功后，会遭遇巨大的挫折——或许这种挫折不足以彻底结束游戏，但足以让他们回到比从一开始就采取长期策略更糟糕的境地。

19

PLAYING ITERATED GAMES

玩迭代游戏

A great way to get yourself to play the long game is to approach every interaction with your audience, customers, collaborators, partners, etc., as if it were part of an iterated game. ⁠ i

要想让自己着眼长远，一个好方法就是把与受众、客户、合作者、伙伴等的每一次互动都当作一场迭代游戏的一部分来对待。

Do not (just) play it for what you can get in the current interaction. Play to make future ones better.

不要仅仅为了在当前的互动中获得什么而玩游戏，而应该为了让未来的互动变得更好而玩游戏。

This includes building trust and collecting information:

这包括建立信任和收集信息：

  • Building trust is critical. It could be trust that you are a good person, trust that you understand your interlocutor, or trust that you are competent. Make sure you cultivate all three types of trust.
    建立信任至关重要。信任可以是相信你是个好人，相信你理解对方，也可以是相信你能力出众。务必努力培养这三种类型的信任。
  • Collecting information is also critical. It could be information about what the other person likes or is worried about, but also what you are doing wrong, what you could do better, or what the rules of the game are.
    收集信息也至关重要。这可能包括对方的喜好或担忧，也可能包括你做错的地方、你可以改进的地方，或者游戏规则是什么。

When you interact with people, play iterated games: do not just think about what you need, but also about building trust and collecting information.

与人交往时，要玩迭代游戏：不仅要考虑你需要什么，还要考虑建立信任和收集信息。

Some examples of playing iterated games

一些玩迭代游戏的例子

– When performing a task, focus not only on getting it done this time, but also on learning how to get it done better or faster the next time.

– 在执行任务时，不仅要专注于这次完成任务，还要学习如何在下次做得更好或更快。

– When negotiating a deal, do not focus on getting as much as possible out of it, but instead on getting a fair deal while ensuring that your counterpart keeps wanting to make deals with you.

– 在谈判交易时，不要只想着从中获取尽可能多的利益，而应该想着达成公平的交易，同时确保你的交易对手愿意继续与你进行交易。

– When practicing a skill, focus not only on improving your skill but also on improving how you practice, so that you can improve faster.

练习一项技能时，不仅要注重提高技能本身，还要注重提高练习方法，这样才能进步更快。

– When selling a product or service, market and deliver it in such a way that not only do you make a profit but also improve your reputation.

– 在销售产品或服务时，要以既能盈利又能提升声誉的方式来进行营销和交付。

– When delegating a task, do it not just to get something done, but also in such a way that your delegee’s skills and engagement increase.

– 委派任务时，不仅要完成任务，还要提高被委派者的技能和参与度。

– When giving negative feedback, do it in such a way that not only does the recipient correct their mistake but also feels empowered. ⁠ ii

– 给予负面反馈时，要让接受者不仅能改正错误，还能感到更有力量。

– When making a decision, do it not only for its immediate result but also for the future behaviors it makes more or less likely.

– 做决定时，不仅要考虑其直接结果，还要考虑它会使未来行为发生的可能性增加还是减少。

Chapter summary

章节概要

Do not (just) take action for its direct outcome, but rather to make your future actions easier or more effective.

不要（仅仅）为了直接结果而采取行动，而应该为了让你未来的行动更容易或更有效而采取行动。

i Readers familiar with the book “Infinite Games” might wonder if this is a similar concept. It is, but only partially: the purpose here is not to keep playing indefinitely but to make success inevitable.

读过《无限游戏》这本书的读者可能会想，这是否与它的概念类似。的确如此，但只是部分类似：这里的目的并非无限期地玩下去，而是让成功成为必然。

ii Some principles to help with this include making your feedback as specific as possible, making it actionable (i.e., the recipient shouldn’t have to figure out what you meant or what they have to do differently), and building a track record of being competent, reliable, and well-meaning well before you give the feedback.

ii 一些有助于做到这一点的原则包括：使你的反馈尽可能具体，使其具有可操作性（即，接受者不应该需要弄清楚你的意思或他们需要做哪些不同的事情），以及在提供反馈之前，建立起胜任、可靠和善意的良好记录。

20

LONG-TERM ITERATED GAMES

长期迭代游戏

“The longer view you take, the more apparent it becomes that people who are seemingly competing with each other are actually collaborators.”

VISAKAN VEERASAMY

“从长远来看，越发明显地会发现，那些看似相互竞争的人，实际上是合作伙伴。”——维萨坎·维拉萨米

I terated games become very counterintuitive once you zoom out and consider time scales of a decade or more. For example, over long enough time frames, your competitors are also your collaborators. You still compete for a share of the pie, but you also work together to grow the pie.

一旦将视角拉远，考虑十年甚至更长时间尺度，迭代博弈就会变得非常违反直觉。例如，在足够长的时间跨度内，你的竞争对手同时也是你的合作伙伴。你们仍然在争夺市场份额，但同时也在携手合作，共同扩大蛋糕。

As a personal anecdote, I began my career as an author believing that other authors were my competitors. That is true over short time frames, such as when considering " What book will that reader buy next, mine or theirs?" However , over longer time frames, it’s more about, " How can my competitors and I educate readers about the value of our niche, so that they buy both my book and theirs?”

就我个人而言，我刚开始写作时，认为其他作者都是我的竞争对手。在短期内，这种想法没错，比如我会考虑“读者接下来会买哪本书，我的还是他们的？”。然而，从长远来看，更重要的是“我和我的竞争对手如何才能让读者了解我们各自领域的重要性，从而让他们既买我的书也买他们的书？”

As another anecdote, I began my career as a consultant believing that a competitor’s failing a project was good for me, for their client might fire them and hire me instead. Later on, I understood that a competitor’s failed project also lowers the perceived value of all consulting services.

再举个例子，我刚入行做咨询顾问时，认为竞争对手项目失败对我有利，因为他们的客户可能会解雇他们，转而聘用我。后来我才明白，竞争对手项目失败也会降低所有咨询服务的价值。

Don’t get me wrong! We are still competitors fighting over a share of the pie. But we should fight in ways that grow the pie and not in ways that shrink it.

别误会我的意思！我们仍然是竞争对手，都在争夺市场份额。但我们应该用能把蛋糕做大的方式去竞争，而不是用会把蛋糕做小的方式去竞争。

Another area in which iterated games produce counterintuitive results is negotiations. I already mentioned how the short-term approach to negotiations is to get as much as possible out of a single deal, whereas the long-term approach is to achieve a win-win so that the counterpart is more likely to come to us with another win-win deal.

迭代博弈产生反直觉结果的另一个领域是谈判。我已经提到过，短期谈判策略是尽可能从单笔交易中获取最大利益，而长期策略则是达成双赢，这样对方更有可能提出另一笔双赢交易。

However, I didn’t mention that, over long enough time frames, you want to negotiate win-wins that not only bring results to your suppliers and customers but also grow their long-term assets (skills, relationships, etc.) so that they can produce more or buy more from you.

然而，我没有提到，从足够长的时间跨度来看，你希望达成双赢的协议，这不仅能为你的供应商和客户带来成果，还能增长他们的长期资产（技能、关系等），以便他们能够生产更多产品或从你这里购买更多产品。

Chapter summary

章节概要

Plenty of games are zero-sum over the short term and positive-sum over the long term.

许多游戏在短期内是零和博弈，但在长期内是正和博弈。

Therefore, playing long-term games as if they were zero-sum often hinders your long-term growth.

因此，把长期游戏当作零和博弈来玩，往往会阻碍你的长期发展。

Consider which parts of the game you play might shift at least partially to positive-sum over long enough time horizons, and play them accordingly.

考虑一下你所玩的游戏的哪些部分在足够长的时间范围内可能会至少部分地转变为正和博弈，并据此进行相应的游戏。

LONG-TERM ASSETS

长期资产

H ere are some examples of long-term assets:

以下是一些长期资产的例子：

– Trust (of your customers, partners, collaborators, audience, etc.)

– 信任（来自您的客户、合作伙伴、协作者、受众等的信任）

– Health (a healthy body, a healthy mind, non-toxic friends, etc.)

– 健康（健康的身体、健康的心理、无害的朋友等等）

– Know-how (knowing what needs to be done and how to do it right)

– 专业知识（知道需要做什么以及如何正确地做）

– Relationships (access to an audience, a particular group of people, etc.)

– 人际关系（接触受众、特定人群等）

– A body of work (that you can sell, that is evidence of your abilities, etc.)

– 一系列作品（可以出售，能够证明你的能力等等）

What about money?

钱方面呢？

Money and other financial assets are also forms of long-term assets. That said, particular attention must be given to the fact that money alone won’t be sufficient to achieve your objectives in a sustainable and non-fragile way. Surprisingly , this also includes financial objectives.

金钱和其他金融资产也是长期资产的一种形式。尽管如此，必须特别注意的是，仅靠金钱不足以以可持续且稳健的方式实现您的目标。令人惊讶的是，这同样适用于财务目标。

If you aim to achieve your financial objectives solely through the accumulation of money and without also accumulating know-how and relationships, your financial capital will be extremely fragile.

如果你只想通过积累金钱来实现你的财务目标，而不去积累知识和人脉，那么你的财务资本将非常脆弱。

What about time?

时间呢？

When we hear that “time is an asset,” we often think about the obvious fact that the more time we have, the more things we are able to do.

当我们听到“时间是一种财富”这句话时，我们通常会想到一个显而易见的事实：我们拥有的时间越多，我们能做的事情就越多。

However, time is also an asset in another important way. The more time we have, the more we can use long-term strategies, which are more effective and reliable than short-term ones.

然而，时间在另一个重要方面也是一种资产。我们拥有的时间越多，就越能运用长期策略，而长期策略比短期策略更有效、更可靠。

Hence, it is important to treat long-term horizons as an asset worth building.

因此，将长期目标视为值得积累的资产非常重要。

I stress the word “building.” You cannot just decide that your time horizon is going to be long. You must build the conditions that enable it at the level of your finances, your obligations to others, who you work with and their incentives, your health, and so on.

我强调“构建”这个词。你不能只是决定你的时间规划要长远。你必须在财务、对他人的责任、你的合作伙伴及其激励机制、你的健康状况等等层面，构建实现这一目标的条件。

Trust and the long term

信任与长远

Just as many risks are almost invisible in the short term but become very significant in the long term, so too are trust and reputation.

许多风险在短期内几乎看不见，但在长期内却变得非常重要，信任和声誉也是如此。

In the short term, the impact of trust may seem minimal. If you send a salesy email to your audience, you see only the revenue from possible sales, not the trust that you might be destroying in the process.

短期来看，信任的影响似乎微乎其微。如果你向受众发送推销邮件，你看到的只是潜在销售带来的收入，而忽略了在此过程中可能正在破坏的信任。

Of course, this doesn't mean you shouldn't send sales emails. It means you should do so in a way that doesn't reduce their trust in you, because that will harm your long-term prospects more than is apparent.

当然，这并不意味着你不应该发送销售邮件。而是说，你应该以不会降低客户对你的信任的方式来发送，因为降低信任度会对你的长期潜在客户造成比表面看起来更大的损害。

The question is not whether you can progress toward your objective without having built trust. Of course, you can. Instead , the question is whether you can achieve your objective without having built trust, and the answer is probably not.

问题不在于你是否能在没有建立信任的情况下朝着目标前进。当然可以。问题在于你是否能在没有建立信任的情况下实现目标，而答案很可能是否定的。

THE GOOSE AND THE EGGS

鹅和鸡蛋

Y ou have probably heard Aesop’s fable of the Goose and the Golden Egg .⁠ i

你可能听过伊索寓言中关于金蛋的鹅的故事。

It is about a farmer who discovers that his goose has started laying golden eggs. Every day, it lays one. At first, the farmer is grateful. Over time, though, he grows impatient and asks himself, “ Why does the goose give me only one egg a day? Why can’t it give me all the eggs it has now?” So , he slays the goose and, to his disappointment, discovers that it is empty inside – and now, he cannot get any more eggs.

故事讲述的是一位农夫发现他的鹅开始下金蛋了。它每天都下一颗。起初，农夫非常感激。但随着时间的推移，他渐渐失去了耐心，开始疑惑：“为什么鹅一天只给我一个蛋？为什么它不能把所有的蛋都给我呢？”于是，他宰了鹅，却失望地发现鹅肚子里空空如也——从此以后，他再也得不到任何蛋了。

This metaphor explains surprisingly well a common reason that talented and determined people fail to achieve success.

这个比喻出人意料地很好地解释了有才华且意志坚定的人未能取得成功的一个常见原因。

They kill their Goose .

他们杀人自尽。

They have some asset – a skill, a product, a reputation, a relationship – and in a bid to get more yield, they squeeze it to the point of damaging its capacity to produce yield.

他们拥有一些资产——技能、产品、声誉、人脉——为了获得更多收益，他们榨取这些资产的价值，以至于损害了其产生收益的能力。

Never kill your Goose , nor risk it.

永远不要杀掉你的鹅，也不要冒这个险。

Some ways in which people kill their Goose

人们杀死自己鹅的一些方式

  • An athlete training too hard or taking too many risks and injuring their body (their Goose ).
    运动员训练过度或冒险过度，导致身体受伤（他们的“鹅”）。
  • A solopreneur who writes too many emails to their audience (their Goose ) , selling products instead of providing valuable content, which teaches their audience to ignore their emails.
    一位个体经营者向他的受众（他的“鹅”）发送了太多电子邮件，推销产品而不是提供有价值的内容，这让他的受众学会了忽略他的电子邮件。
  • A husband or wife who takes their spouse (their Goose ) for granted, giving them less and less attention to pursue their career, eventually losing them and all the good moments they could have spent together in the future (the Golden Eggs ).
    丈夫或妻子如果把配偶（他们的鹅）视为理所当然，为了追求事业而越来越忽视他们，最终失去配偶以及未来本可以一起度过的所有美好时光（金蛋）。
  • A company that releases a faulty product on the market, breaking the trust of its customers (their Goose ).
    一家公司向市场上发布了有缺陷的产品，辜负了顾客（他们的“鹅”）的信任。
  • A manager who never invests in the development of their team (their Goose ) and instead squeezes every last bit of productivity out of them.
    一位经理从不投资于团队成员（他们的“鹅”）的发展，而是榨干他们最后一丝生产力。
  • An investor who invests too much of their money (their Goose ) in an excessively risky asset to chase marginally higher returns.
    投资者将过多的资金（他们的“鹅”）投入风险过高的资产，以追求略高的回报。

As you can see , the most common reason people kill their Goose or at least put their Goose at risk is because of the desire to get more or to get it faster.

正如你所看到的，人们杀死自己的鹅，或者至少让自己的鹅处于危险之中的最常见原因是，他们渴望获得更多或更快地获得它。

Ask yourself how you can go faster, but never go faster in a way that puts your Goose at risk.

问问自己怎样才能跑得更快，但千万不要以危及你的鹅的方式跑得更快。

There will always be someone getting successful faster than you

总会有人比你更快成功。

In the first part of this book, I explained how the casino croupier is the only one at the gambling tables with a money-making strategy, yet every day he sees a few lucky players get richer than he does. Still , he would be foolish to abandon his strategy to become a player. Even if he could get rich faster, the most likely outcome is that he would get poorer instead.

本书第一部分我解释了赌场荷官是赌桌上唯一拥有赚钱策略的人，然而他每天都眼睁睁地看着几个幸运的玩家比他更富有。尽管如此，他若放弃自己的策略转而成为玩家，那将是愚蠢的。即使他能更快地致富，最有可能的结果却是他反而会变得更穷。

There will always be someone who achieves success faster than you.

总会有人比你更快地获得成功。

That doesn’t necessarily mean that they have a better strategy than yours.

但这并不一定意味着他们的策略比你的更好。

Maybe they do, but probably they don’t. What matters is not the outcome that their strategy produced for them but the distribution of outcomes that their strategy is likely to yield.

或许他们会这样做，但很可能不会。重要的不是他们的策略最终给他们带来了什么结果，而是他们的策略可能产生的各种结果的分布情况。

Never envy someone with a strategy that produces a worse distribution of outcomes than yours, even if, for them, it did produce a better outcome.

即使对方的策略产生了比你更差的结果，也永远不要羡慕那些策略结果比你更差的人，即使对他们来说，这种策略确实产生了更好的结果。

And never confuse what you could achieve with a strategy with what you are likely to achieve.

永远不要把通过策略可能取得的成就与你可能取得的成就混淆起来。

In fact, never judge a strategy based on what happens if it works, but judge it based on what happens if it doesn’t.

事实上，永远不要根据策略成功后的结果来评判它，而应该根据策略失败后的结果来评判它。

HIGH- AND LOW-QUALITY SUCCESS

高质量和低质量的成功

S uccess can be high-quality or low-quality, depending on whether it is built on strong or weak foundations.

成功有好有坏，取决于它建立在坚实的基础之上还是脆弱的基础之上。

For example, a sale made by lying to a customer is a form of low-quality success. Conversely , a sale made by honestly answering a customer’s questions is a form of high-quality success.

例如，通过欺骗顾客达成的销售是一种低质量的成功。相反，通过诚实回答顾客的问题达成的销售是一种高质量的成功。

Because of its weak foundations, low-quality success is often temporary and rarely helps with long-term goals. If you rely on luck, it won’t last. If you rely on consuming trust, you will eventually run out of it. And if you rely on poor quality, people will notice.

由于根基薄弱，低质量的成功往往是短暂的，很少能帮助实现长期目标。如果你依赖运气，那不会长久；如果你依赖消耗信任，最终会耗尽信任；如果你依赖低质量，人们会察觉到。

If your tactic is to overcompensate for a bad product with marketing, you will find yourself with a less profitable structure than your competitors, which will ultimately hurt your growth.⁠ i

如果你的策略是过度依赖营销来弥补产品缺陷，你会发现自己的盈利能力不如竞争对手，最终会损害你的发展。

Moreover, low-quality success is rarely reproducible.

此外，低质量的成功很少能复制。

Doing more of what brought you low-quality success yields disappointing results. And imitating someone who achieved low-quality success is unlikely to bring you the same success.

继续做那些只给你带来低质量成功的事情，只会带来令人失望的结果。模仿那些取得低质量成功的人，也不太可能给你带来同样的成功。

Low-quality success is popular because it requires less time and effort, and it is more efficient and easier to scale, but only at first .

低质量的成功之所以受欢迎，是因为它需要的时间和精力更少，效率更高，更容易扩展，但这只是暂时的。

For example, consider two salespeople. The one who lies will likely have superior sales in the first year. However , sales will become increasingly difficult as they run out of clients to deceive and must invest heavily in advertising to acquire new clients. In contrast, the second salesperson will realize that customers they didn’t deceive might eventually return and make repeat purchases. Some might even refer friends and colleagues.

例如，假设有两个销售员。说谎的那个人第一年业绩可能更好。然而，随着他能欺骗的客户越来越少，销售就会变得越来越困难，他必须投入大量资金进行广告宣传才能获得新客户。相比之下，第二个销售员会意识到，那些他没有欺骗的客户最终可能会再次光顾并重复购买。有些人甚至可能会推荐朋友和同事。

High-quality success has a greater potential for long-term scaling and sustainability.

高质量的成功更有利于长期规模化和可持续发展。

THE PATH FORWARD

DERISK, DERISK, DERISK

德里克，德里克，德里克

There are people who succeed without managing their risks. However , if you do not manage your risks, not only are your chances of success low (remember survivorship bias?), but your potential will also be limited.

有些人不管理风险也能获得成功。然而，如果你不管理风险，不仅成功的概率会很低（还记得幸存者偏差吗？），而且你的发展潜力也会受到限制。

In fact, just like brakes are not for driving slowly but for enabling driving fast, risk management is not a burden but an enabler of fast growth. ⁠ i

事实上，正如刹车不是为了减速而是为了加速行驶一样，风险管理不是负担，而是快速增长的推动力。

So, over the next few pages, let’s see how you can apply some risk management to your pursuit of success without having to spend too much time and effort on it.

那么，在接下来的几页中，让我们看看如何在追求成功的过程中运用一些风险管理方法，而无需花费太多时间和精力。

i When done right and reasonably, obviously. Excesses are always bad.

如果方法得当且合理，那当然没问题。过犹不及。过犹不及总是不好的。

LEARNING FROM FAILURE

从失败中学习

S tudying the successful can be a risky path to success. You might imitate someone who implemented a risky strategy that seldom yields good outcomes or that requires sacrifices you aren't willing to make.

研究成功人士的经验可能是一条通往成功的风险之路。你可能会模仿那些实施高风险策略的人，而这种策略很少能带来好的结果，或者需要你做出你不愿意做出的牺牲。

A more reliable path is to study those who failed despite having decent skills and a strong work ethic. This approach is likely to yield valuable insights into the risks you might face in your journey toward success. Then , you can develop a strategy that manages those risks.

更可靠的方法是研究那些拥有不错技能和良好职业道德却最终失败的人。这种方法很可能让你深入了解在通往成功的道路上可能面临的风险。然后，你可以制定相应的策略来应对这些风险。

Make a list of how those smarter than you have failed, how those as smart as you have failed, and how those less smart than you have failed. Smartness is often reassessed after the fact, so you don't yet know how smart you truly are.

列出比你聪明的人失败的原因、和你一样聪明的人失败的原因以及不如你聪明的人失败的原因。聪明与否往往是事后重新评估的，所以你现在还不清楚自己到底有多聪明。

Then, ask yourself not whether you will commit these mistakes but what might lead you to make them.

然后，不要问自己是否会犯这些错误，而是问自己是什么原因会导致你犯这些错误。

And finally, instead of avoiding the mistake, avoid the conditions that lead to that mistake. For example, if "doing drugs" is a common reason for failure, don't ask yourself whether you might do drugs. Ask yourself what could lead you to do drugs and prevent that.

最后，与其避免犯错，不如避免导致错误发生的因素。例如，如果“吸毒”是失败的常见原因，不要问自己是否会吸毒，而是问问自己什么因素会导致你吸毒，并努力避免这种情况发生。

De-risk, not no-risk

降低风险，而非消除风险

Derisking does not mean taking zero risks.

降低风险并不意味着完全不承担任何风险。

In fact, a common reason many people fail to achieve their goals is that they do not take enough risks.

事实上，许多人未能实现目标的一个常见原因是他们承担的风险不够大。

The key is to derisk your long-term goals, not necessarily your short-term bets.

关键在于降低长期目标的风险，而不是降低短期投资的风险。

Let me explain.

让我解释一下。

To achieve most goals, you will have to take a few bets: ideas that might fail, projects that might not work out, contacting people who might refuse you, and so on. These bets are inherently risky. Reducing their risk to zero would be impossible or counterproductive, as it would carry excessive opportunity costs.

要实现大多数目标，你必须承担一些风险：比如可能失败的想法、可能无法完成的项目、可能被拒绝的人等等。这些风险本身就存在。将风险降至零既不可能，也可能适得其反，因为这会带来过高的机会成本。

However, you should still ensure that these bets cannot fail in a way that would impair your long-term future. If there’s a risk they do, you will have to derisk that.

但是，你仍然应该确保这些投资不会失败，以免损害你的长远未来。如果存在失败的风险，你就必须降低这种风险。

Moreover, while you can hardly reduce the risk of a bet to zero, there are usually at least a few actions you can take that, with little work or cost, can significantly increase your odds of success. You should take those de-risking actions.

此外，虽然你几乎不可能将投注风险降至零，但通常至少有一些措施可以让你以极少的精力和成本显著提高成功的几率。你应该采取这些降低风险的措施。

Now that we’ve covered the why of derisking, let’s move to the how. The first technique we will see is learning from the failures of others.

既然我们已经探讨了降低风险的原因，接下来就让我们看看如何降低风险。我们将要介绍的第一种技巧是从他人的失败中吸取教训。

LEARN FROM THE FAILURES OF OTHERS

从他人的失败中吸取教训

I n the second chapter of this book, I covered 22 common reasons why people fail. I suggest you use that list to complete the following exercise:

本书第二章列举了人们失败的22个常见原因。我建议你参考这份清单完成以下练习：

  1. Pick a long-term goal of yours.
    选择一个你的长期目标。
  2. Go through the 22 points on the list, and ask yourself which ones, if any, might cause you to fail at achieving that goal. Write these down.
    仔细阅读清单上的22条，问问自己，如果有的话，哪些条款可能会导致你无法实现目标。把这些条款写下来。
  3. Ask yourself in what other ways people with the same goal as you commonly fail. Write those down.
    问问自己，和你目标相同的人通常会在哪些方面失败？把这些都写下来。
  4. Examine all the points you wrote down, and for each, write what you will do to avoid those issues causing you to fail.
    检查你写下的所有要点，并针对每一项，写下你将采取哪些措施来避免导致你失败的问题。

One tip for you: while doing the previous exercise, avoid thinking you’re smarter than others and, therefore, cannot fail. Even if you are indeed smarter, that only means you are more likely to do what’s required to succeed, but not necessarily what’s required to avoid failure – ask any investor who was smart enough to pick the right stocks but not wise enough to avoid over-leverage.

给你一个建议：在做之前的练习时，不要觉得自己比别人聪明，因此就不会失败。即使你真的更聪明，那也只意味着你更有可能做到成功所需的步骤，但并不一定意味着你就能做到避免失败所需的步骤——问问那些聪明到能选对股票，却不够明智到避免过度杠杆的投资者就知道了。

Base rates, hindsight, and near misses

基准率、事后诸葛亮和险些酿成大祸

We often overestimate how smart we are simply because we haven’t done anything stupid recently, or the consequences of our actions haven’t yet materialized. For example, 93% of American drivers believe they are better than average – an obvious statistical impossibility. ⁠ i

我们常常高估自己的聪明才智，仅仅是因为我们最近没有做过什么蠢事，或者我们的行为后果还没有显现。例如，93%的美国司机认为自己的驾驶技术高于平均水平——这显然在统计学上是不可能的。

The culprit is our tendency to rely on hindsight to determine who is a bad driver. If someone drives too fast and crashes, they are a bad driver, but if you drive too fast and haven’t crashed yet, you might think you are a good driver.

罪魁祸首是我们倾向于事后诸葛亮，以此来判断谁是糟糕的驾驶员。如果有人超速行驶并发生事故，他们就是糟糕的驾驶员；但如果你超速行驶却还没出事故，你可能会认为自己是个好驾驶员。

Of course, that doesn’t make sense. Driving too fast is precisely what makes you a bad driver, regardless of whether you have crashed or got lucky enough and haven’t crashed yet.

当然，这说不通。无论你是否发生过事故，或者只是运气好还没发生过事故，超速行驶恰恰会让你成为一个糟糕的驾驶员。

Yes, yes, perhaps you’re truly a good driver, and maybe you can drive fast and safely. But the chances are that it’s precisely your confidence in being a good driver that might make you a bad one, as it might lead to complacency or excessive risk-taking.

没错，没错，或许你确实是个好司机，也许你能开得又快又安全。但很可能正是你对自己驾驶技术的自信，反而会让你变成一个糟糕的司机，因为它可能导致自满或过度冒险。

The antidote is to look at base rates (if a risk is common, the chances are that it’s common for you, too) and near misses (risky situations that could have resulted in an incident but didn’t).

解决办法是查看基本发生率（如果某种风险很常见，那么它对你来说也很常见）和险些发生的事故（可能导致事故但最终没有发生的危险情况）。

For example, if you frequently have to emergency brake to avoid an incident, you are a bad driver – even if you never caused one, because eventually, you will.

例如，如果你经常需要紧急刹车来避免事故，那么你就是一个糟糕的驾驶员——即使你从未造成过事故，因为最终你肯定会造成事故。

i Source: “Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers,” O. Svenson, 1981.

i 来源：“我们是否都比其他司机更安全、更有技巧？” O. Svenson，1981 年。

27

LEARN FROM YOUR FAILURES

从失败中吸取教训

A common reason people fail to achieve success is that they do not learn from their failures, or do not learn enough from their failures, or learn from their failures but refuse to change their way of doing things based on what they have learned.

人们失败的一个常见原因是他们没有从失败中吸取教训，或者没有从失败中吸取足够的教训，或者从失败中吸取了教训，但拒绝根据所学到的东西改变他们的做事方式。

The core issue is that many of us do not just want to succeed; we want to succeed in a particular way . And that is often the seed of failure.

问题的核心在于，我们很多人想要的不仅仅是成功，而是以某种特定的方式成功。而这往往是失败的根源。

Of course, I’m not saying that you should abandon all your preferences, far from it. However , you should realize that preferences come with a hefty opportunity cost. Therefore , be deliberate about your priorities.

当然，我并不是说你应该放弃所有喜好，恰恰相反。但是，你应该意识到，喜好往往伴随着巨大的机会成本。因此，要慎重考虑你的优先事项。

Of course, you might succeed in a particular way. But how likely is it? If the answer is significantly lower than 100%, what are you willing to be flexible on to improve your chances?

当然，你或许能以某种方式成功。但这种可能性有多大？如果答案远低于100%，为了提高成功率，你愿意在哪些方面做出妥协？

Avoid fixating so much on one particular way of succeeding that you ignore experiences showing that a change in direction could increase your chances of success.

不要过于执着于某种特定的成功方式，以至于忽略了那些表明改变方向可以增加成功机会的经验。

Learning from your failures

从失败中学习

The only thing worse than not learning from your failures is learning the wrong lessons from them.

比不从失败中吸取教训更糟糕的是从失败中吸取错误的教训。

When there are multiple things we could do differently to improve our outcomes, we often focus on the one we would mind doing the least instead of the most important one.

当有很多方法可以改善结果时，我们往往会把注意力放在最不情愿做的事情上，而不是最重要的事情上。

A good antidote is to acknowledge that our path toward success is paved with lessons we do not want to learn, and the way forward consists of asking ourselves what unpleasant lessons we have been avoiding.

一个好的解决办法是承认，我们通往成功的道路是由我们不想学习的教训铺成的，而前进的方向在于问问自己，我们一直在逃避哪些不愉快的教训。

Another possibility is to ask ourselves, " If I had done X and Y , I might have avoided failure. But would X and Y have been sufficient to prevent failure fully, or should I have also done something else?" Often , that something else is the true lesson to be learned.

另一种方法是问问自己：“如果我做了X和Y，或许就能避免失败。但X和Y足以完全避免失败吗？或者我是否还应该做些别的事情？”通常，那件“别的事情”才是真正需要吸取的教训。

That said, learning from your failures after they happen is painful. It's better to learn from your failures before they happen. This is possible with the use of pre-mortems and fishbone diagrams , which are the topic of the next chapter.

话虽如此，事后从失败中吸取教训是痛苦的。最好是在失败发生之前就从中吸取教训。这可以通过事前分析和鱼骨图来实现，而这些正是下一章的主题。

# ↩
28

LEARN FROM FUTURE FAILURES

从未来的失败中吸取教训

Y ou do not have to wait for failure to learn from it.

你不必等到失败才从中吸取教训。

Ask yourself, " Let's imagine I follow my plan and still fail. What might have gone wrong, and what can I do about it now?"

问问自己：“假设我按照计划行事，但仍然失败了。可能哪里出了问题，我现在可以做些什么来弥补？”

This simple question, called a pre-mortem , is a great way to learn from failure without having to suffer the consequences.

这个简单的问题，被称为“事前验尸”，是避免承担失败后果、从失败中吸取教训的好方法。

Of course, this technique has blind spots, but applying it will still provide you with at least a few good lessons.

当然，这种方法也有盲点，但运用它仍然至少能给你带来一些有益的经验。

To reduce blind spots, you can use an advanced variation of this technique called the fishbone diagram. I've included it in the appendix because describing it takes a few pages, and I didn’t want to disrupt the flow of the book. For the moment, let’s focus on pre-mortems.

为了减少盲点，你可以使用一种名为鱼骨图的高级技巧。我把它放在附录里，因为描述它需要好几页篇幅，我不想打断本书的流畅性。现在，我们先来关注一下事前分析。

If you successfully think about all the ways in which you might fail, as well as how others with similar objectives have failed, you will bulletproof your strategy and dramatically increase your chance of success.

如果你能认真思考所有可能失败的方式，以及其他有类似目标的人是如何失败的，你就能确保你的策略万无一失，并大大提高成功的几率。

The next pages contain a few examples.

接下来的几页包含一些示例。

Example #1: a happy retirement

例一：幸福的退休生活

First of all, let me clarify that I do not optimize my life for retirement. I am still only 35, and as far as I know, I might die tomorrow, at 50, at 75, or at 100 years old. It wouldn’t make sense to optimize for a single time horizon. As I already mentioned, I try to live my life so that I will die happy, regardless of when that happens.

首先，我想澄清一下，我并没有为了退休而优化我的人生。我才35岁，而且据我所知，我可能明天就去世，也可能50岁、75岁甚至100岁。仅仅为了某个特定的时间目标而优化人生毫无意义。正如我之前提到的，我努力让自己无论何时离世都能幸福快乐地度过余生。

That said, I often ask myself, “ What could cause me to be unhappy if I make it to an older age, and what can I do about it now?”

话虽如此，我经常问自己：“如果我活到老年，什么会让我不快乐？我现在能做些什么来避免这种情况呢？”

Some answers that come to mind are:

我想到的一些答案是：

  • I might have health problems. A healthy lifestyle will prevent that.
    我可能存在健康问题。健康的生活方式可以预防这些问题。
  • I might feel lonely. Building a solid marriage, nurturing a group of good friends, and having a good relationship with my children will help.
    我可能会感到孤独。建立稳固的婚姻、培养一群好朋友、与孩子保持良好的关系都会有所帮助。
  • I might be poor. Getting a good income and investing a significant part of it will help.
    我可能比较穷。如果能获得一份不错的收入，并将其中相当一部分进行投资，情况就会有所改善。

For the record, I do not think that the chances of my ending up lonely are very high. Still , I must take them seriously. It’s precisely taking them seriously that will keep those chances low.

说实话，我觉得我孤独终老的概率并不高。不过，我还是得认真对待。只有认真对待，才能把这种概率降到最低。

After all, many elders feel lonely, including people who didn’t think they would. So , do not only prevent the risks you think might happen to you, but also look at what has happened to others.

毕竟，很多老年人都会感到孤独，其中也包括一些原本认为自己不会孤独的人。所以，不仅要防范你认为可能发生在你身上的风险，也要关注其他人经历过类似的事情。

Once you come up with a list of possible reasons for failure, work on addressing each to ensure it won’t happen to you.

一旦你列出了可能导致失败的原因，就逐一解决，以确保它不会发生在你身上。

# ↩

Example #2: delegation

示例 2：委托

As part of my work as a management advisor, I often teach the leaders I consult to pre-mortem the tasks they delegate.

作为管理顾问，我的工作之一就是教导我咨询的领导者们在委派任务之前进行事前分析。

I often ask them,

我经常问他们：

"Imagine you are about to delegate this task to your subordinate. Let's say you delegate the task to them, and they fail. What might have caused this failure? What are common reasons why people fail when similar tasks are delegated to them?"

“假设你正准备将这项任务委派给你的下属。假设你委派了任务，但他们失败了。是什么原因导致了这次失败？人们在被委派类似任务时失败的常见原因有哪些？”

These two questions greatly help my clients delegate more effectively. Not only does this make the successful completion of the delegated task more likely, but it also helps prevent poor delegation from causing failure – something that can greatly damage the trust between a subordinate and their manager.

这两个问题极大地帮助我的客户更有效地进行任务委派。这不仅能提高任务成功完成的概率，还能防止因委派不当而导致的失败——而失败会严重损害下属与上级之间的信任。

A one-minute exercise to de-risk your life

只需一分钟，就能降低你的生命风险

  1. Imagine you wake up in a hospital. What could have been the most likely reason? Is there anything you can do today to prevent that?
    想象一下，你醒来发现自己在医院里。最可能的原因是什么？今天你能做些什么来预防这种情况发生？
  2. Imagine your partner breaks up with you. What could have been the most likely reason? Is there anything you can do today to prevent that?
    想象一下，你的伴侣和你分手了。最可能的原因是什么？你今天可以做些什么来避免这种情况发生？
  3. Imagine you lose your job. What could have been the most likely reason? Is there anything you can do today to prevent that?
    想象一下你失业了。最可能的原因是什么？你今天可以做些什么来避免这种情况发生？
  4. Imagine you get sued. What could have been the most likely reason? Is there anything you can do today to prevent that?
    想象一下你被起诉了。最可能的原因是什么？你今天可以做些什么来避免这种情况发生？
  5. Imagine you go on a business trip and receive a missed call from your family in the middle of the night. What could have been the most likely reason? Is there anything you can do today to prevent that?
    想象一下，你出差在外，半夜接到家人打来的未接来电。最可能的原因是什么？你今天可以做些什么来避免这种情况发生？

A one-minute exercise to improve your life

一分钟练习，改善你的生活

The previous exercise was about avoiding negative risks.

之前的练习是关于避免负面风险。

This exercise is about taking positive risks: risks with limited downside and high upside.

这项练习旨在鼓励承担积极的风险：即下行风险有限、收益潜力巨大的风险。

  1. Imagine your relationship with your partner becomes exceptional (even if it’s already very good) . What could have been the most likely reason among those in your control? Is there anything you can do today to make that happen?
    想象一下，你和伴侣的关系变得格外亲密（即使你们的关系已经很好了）。在你能控制的因素中，最可能的原因是什么？你今天能做些什么来促成这件事？
  2. Imagine that in five years, you doubled your income. What could have been the most likely reason among those in your control? Is there anything you can do today to make that happen?
    想象一下，五年后你的收入翻了一番。在你可控的因素中，最可能的原因是什么？你今天能做些什么来促成此事？
  3. Imagine that your project doesn’t merely succeed but beats every expectation. What could have been the most likely reason among those in your control? Is there anything you can do today to make that happen?
    想象一下，你的项目不仅成功了，而且超出了所有预期。在你可控的因素中，最可能的原因是什么？你今天能做些什么来促成此事？

Remember that de-risking isn't just about preventing the risk of your project ending badly. De -risking is also about preventing the risk of your project ending up good, but not fantastic.

记住，降低风险不仅仅是防止项目以糟糕的方式结束，也是为了防止项目最终结果良好但不够出色。

EMOTIONAL BLINDSPOTS

情感盲点

I expect most readers to think that the content of the last few chapters was valuable, yet somewhat banal. After all, they have probably already applied much of it to their own lives.

我估计大多数读者会觉得最后几章的内容很有价值，但又有些平淡无奇。毕竟，他们可能已经把其中很多内容运用到自己的生活中了。

And yet.

然而。

I bet that every reader has at least one area of their life in which they are not yet derisking or learning from failure. It’s precisely in those areas that the contents of the previous chapters are most valuable.

我敢肯定，每个读者在生活中至少有一个领域还没有开始规避风险或从失败中吸取教训。而前几章的内容恰恰在这些领域最有价值。

When it comes to smart and motivated people, as I expect most of my readers to be, blind spots are more likely to be emotional than informational. You know what to do, or at least you would know what to do if prompted, but you are not doing it, or are avoiding thinking about it in the first place, hiding it under an " I’ve gotten away with it all my life" mentality.

对于像我大多数读者一样聪明且积极进取的人来说，他们的盲点往往是情感上的而非信息上的。你知道该怎么做，或者至少如果有人提醒你，你就会知道该怎么做，但你却不去做，或者一开始就刻意回避这个问题，用一种“我以前一直都这么做，都没出过什么岔子”的心态来掩盖它。

Don’t. Avoidance is a great short-term strategy but a poor long-term one. You can only get away with it for so long.

别这么做。逃避是短期内有效的策略，但从长远来看却行不通。你不可能永远靠逃避蒙混过关。

Face and derisk what you’ve been avoiding. That’s where the biggest improvements lie.

直面并消除你一直逃避的风险。最大的进步就在于此。

DO NOT ADDRESS EVERY RISK, BUT DO CONSIDER EVERY RISK

不要面面俱到地考虑所有风险，但要考虑到所有风险。

T he exercises in the previous pages probably produced a long list of possible reasons why you might not achieve your long-term goals.

前面几页的练习可能列出了一长串你可能无法实现长期目标的原因。

You do not need to address every risk, but you do need to consider every risk.

你不需要解决所有风险，但你需要考虑所有风险。

# ↩

In particular, here are six dos and don’ts:

具体来说，以下是六条应该做和不应该做的事情：

  • Do accept a risk of failing at a short-term game, but only if that failure does not endanger your long-term strategy. For example, it is okay for a project to fail, but not in a way that endangers your reputation.
    短期策略中，你可以承担失败的风险，但前提是这种失败不会危及你的长期战略。例如，项目失败是可以接受的，但不能以损害你声誉的方式失败。
  • • Do not underestimate base rates. If a risk frequently causes failure for others, it is very likely to be a major risk for you as well, even if you feel immune to it.
    • 不要低估基本风险发生率。如果某种风险经常导致他人失败，那么即使你觉得自己不会受到影响，它也很可能对你构成重大风险。
  • Do consider the cumulative nature of risks with a low chance of happening next year but a high chance of occurring over the next decade.
    要考虑到风险的累积性，这些风险明年发生的概率很低，但在未来十年内发生的概率很高。
  • Do not address every risk perfectly: some are too expensive to nullify.
    不要完美地应对所有风险：有些风险消除起来代价太高。
  • Do, for every risk, ask yourself: Is there at least an imperfect action I can take to reduce its chances of occurring? Apply the 80/20 rule.
    针对每一种风险，都要问问自己：我是否可以采取哪怕是最不完美的措施来降低它发生的概率？运用80/20法则。
  • Do not, under any circumstances, accept a risk that might lower your chances of succeeding eventually below 99%. ( See the chapter after the next one, “ Inevitability .”)
    在任何情况下，都不要承担可能将你最终成功概率降低到99%以下的风险。（参见下一章“必然性”。）

WHEN TO STICK WITH A PROJECT AND WHEN TO ABANDON IT

何时应该坚持一个项目，何时应该放弃它

H ere are two common mistakes people make:

以下是人们常犯的两个错误：

  1. Abandoning a project too early.
    过早放弃项目。
  2. Sticking with a project for too long.
    长时间坚持做某个项目。

Given a single project, it is hard to know whether you are committing one of these mistakes. However , you can look at patterns in your behavior across projects, such as:

仅凭一个项目很难判断你是否犯了上述错误之一。但是，你可以观察你在各个项目中的行为模式，例如：

  • You always drop projects early, never giving them a proper chance, and never iterating at least once on them.
    你总是过早放弃项目，从不给它们一个合适的机会，也从不至少进行一次迭代。
  • You never drop projects voluntarily, always spending time and effort on them even after it would have been time to move on.
    你从不主动放弃项目，即使到了该继续推进的时候，你仍然会投入时间和精力。
  • You keep procrastinating on key to-do items in your project, which indefinitely delays meaningful progress.
    你不断拖延项目中的关键待办事项，导致项目无法取得实质性进展。

These three red flags point to a limiting belief, psychological obstacle, or emotional association that will prevent you from succeeding until you address it. Depending on which applies to you, you should consider adjusting your approach in the opposite direction more than it seems instinctive.

这三个危险信号指向某种限制性信念、心理障碍或情感联想，它们会阻碍你成功，除非你解决它们。根据你自身的情况，你应该考虑调整方法，即使这并非你的本能反应，也要尽量反其道而行之。

INEVITABILITY

必然性

You only get one life.

人生只有一次。

Why spend it pursuing paths that might not work out?

为什么要把时间浪费在可能行不通的道路上呢？

S hort-term strategies can work. If enough people try them, there will be many winners. So , such strategies look impressive and worth imitating.

短期策略有时确实有效。如果足够多的人尝试，就会有很多赢家。因此，这类策略看起来令人印象深刻，值得效仿。

But you only have one life. You shouldn’t be satisfied with a strategy that might work. You want to adapt your strategy so that your success is inevitable.

但人生只有一次。你不应该满足于可能奏效的策略。你应该不断调整策略，让成功成为必然。

Is this possible, though?

但这有可能吗？

Not for all types of success, obviously. For example, no strategy can guarantee becoming the #1 in the world at something – because all it takes is a second person to implement the same strategy to make it a coin toss.

显然，并非所有类型的成功都适用。例如，没有任何策略能保证你成为某个领域的世界第一——因为只要第二个人也采用同样的策略，结果就完全取决于运气了。

But for most types of success, you can have a strategy that stacks the odds of success in your favor, making your success almost inevitable. Or , at the very least, you can adapt your current strategy by asking yourself, “ How can I make my success more inevitable?”

但对于大多数类型的成功，你可以制定策略来增加成功的几率，使成功几乎成为必然。或者，至少你可以通过问自己“我怎样才能让我的成功更加确定无疑？”来调整你当前的策略。

How to increase inevitability

如何增加必然性

Do not be satisfied with a chance of success. Instead , continuously ask yourself, “ How can I increase my chances of success until almost certainty?”

不要满足于成功的几率。相反，要不断地问自己：“我怎样才能提高成功的几率，直到几乎肯定成功？”

This usually means doing two things. The first one is to play short-term games not to win them but to advance towards your long-term objectives. For example, do projects not to make the most money out of them but to learn skills, test hypotheses, and build trust and an audience. If you do so, each project will grow the long-term assets that will eventually make your success almost inevitable.

这通常意味着要做两件事。第一件事是参与短期项目，目的不是为了赢，而是为了朝着长期目标迈进。例如，做项目的目的不是为了赚最多的钱，而是为了学习技能、验证假设、建立信任和积累受众。如果这样做，每个项目都会积累长期资产，最终使你的成功几乎是必然的。

The second thing to do to increase inevitability is to take more bets than apparently necessary, work on more projects than apparently necessary, meet more people than apparently necessary, and so on. The more you do this, the higher the chance that at least one of them will represent a major step forward towards success.

第二点，为了增加成功的必然性，你需要做的就是比表面上认为必要的更多地去冒险，比表面上认为必要的更多地参与项目，比表面上认为必要的更多地结识人脉，等等。你这样做越多，其中至少有一项举措会成为你迈向成功的重要一步的概率就越高。

The next chapter is about how to do that.

下一章将介绍如何做到这一点。

INCREASE YOUR LUCK

提升你的运气

M ost successful people are talented and/or hard-working. That said, they also got lucky.

大多数成功人士都才华横溢和/或勤奋努力。话虽如此，他们也有一定的运气成分。

This does not mean that they didn’t deserve their success. First of all, it is not that they did not work hard. Moreover , if they got lucky, it is often because they put themselves in situations where they could get lucky.

但这并不意味着他们的成功不配拥有。首先，这并非意味着他们不努力。其次，如果他们取得了成功，往往是因为他们把自己置于可能获得成功的机会之中。

The lesson is that relying only on talent and hard work might not be enough. You must also increase your luck – or, more precisely, its surface area. This roughly means two things:

这说明，仅仅依靠天赋和努力可能还不够。你还必须提升你的运气——或者更准确地说，是扩大你的运气覆盖范围。这大致意味着两件事：

  1. You should expose yourself to sources of upside: meeting people, showing your work, trying things that might not work, etc. Not doing this will severely limit your potential.
    你应该让自己接触各种有利因素：结识人脉、展示作品、尝试可能失败的事情等等。否则，你的潜力将受到严重限制。
  2. Doing the above may not suffice unless repeated often enough to ensure a high likelihood of achieving the desired success within the relevant timeframe. Failure to do so means one might do everything correctly and still fail.
    除非反复进行，以确保在相关时间范围内有较高的概率取得预期成功，否则仅靠上述方法可能不足以达到目的。否则，即使一切都做得正确，最终也可能失败。

The second point is of paramount importance yet often neglected.

第二点至关重要，但却常常被忽视。

Practical applications

实际应用

If you are an author, one book might be enough to achieve success, but perhaps it will take ten. You must acknowledge this possibility. So , work on your books quickly enough that you are able to write ten before it’s too late.

如果你是一位作家，一本书或许足以让你获得成功，但也可能需要十本。你必须意识到这种可能性。所以，要抓紧时间写作，争取在为时已晚之前写出十本书。

Of course, you cannot simply publish a bad book. You must work on it long enough to ensure it is good enough to have a decent chance at succeeding. ( More on this in the appendix chapter, “ Managing Bets .”) Still , if you work on it too slowly, publishing at most one or two books within your lifetime, you’re limiting your chances of success.

当然，你不能随便出版一本烂书。你必须花足够的时间打磨它，确保它足够好，才有相当大的成功机会。（更多内容请参见附录章节“如何管理投资”。）然而，如果你投入的时间太少，一生中最多只出版一两本书，那么你成功的几率就会受到限制。

As another example, if you are an entrepreneur, you might achieve success with your first product, but perhaps it will take ten. Adjust your processes and spending to increase both your launch cadence and financial runway so that you are able to take those ten bets. Also , play the long game. Do not over-promise what the first product does; in case of failure, you will break the trust that early investors and adopters placed in you. Instead , communicate transparently in such a way that even if you fail, you will have strengthened the relationships that will make the second launch more likely to succeed.

再举个例子，如果你是一位创业者，你或许能凭借第一款产品获得成功，但可能需要推出十款才能最终成功。调整你的流程和支出，提高产品发布频率和资金储备，这样你才能有能力进行这十次尝试。此外，要着眼长远。不要对第一款产品的功能做出过分的承诺；一旦失败，你将辜负早期投资者和用户的信任。相反，要保持透明的沟通，这样即使失败，你也能巩固关系，从而提高第二次产品发布成功的可能性。

Do not play short-term games hoping to succeed with your first attempt. Instead , play the long game (which, in this case, doesn’t mean taking forever to launch but rather taking many bets).

不要玩短期游戏，指望第一次尝试就能成功。相反，要着眼长远（在这种情况下，这并不意味着要拖延很久才开始，而是指要进行多次尝试）。

PART V
第五部分

HOLISTIC SUCCESS

全面成功

Just as you cannot optimize short-term games in a vacuum but must instead optimize them for their effect on the long game, you cannot optimize for a long-term goal in a vacuum but must optimize it for its effect on your life as a whole.

就像你不能孤立地优化短期游戏，而必须考虑其对长期游戏的影响一样，你也不能孤立地优化长期目标，而必须考虑其对你整个生活的影响。

Let’s say that one of your long-term goals is to become a CEO . You cannot fully optimize for that goal unless it is the only thing you want and will want out of your life. People who achieve their goals by working so hard that they destroy their health and marriage succeed in one sense, yet fail overall.

假设你的长期目标之一是成为首席执行官。除非这是你一生中唯一想要且唯一想要的东西，否则你无法最大限度地实现这个目标。那些为了实现目标而拼命工作，以至于损害健康和婚姻的人，从某种意义上说是成功的，但从整体上看却是失败的。

If you optimize your long-term goals in a vacuum, you might achieve them in a way that will not matter because it will have precluded your other eventual goals.

如果你孤立地优化你的长期目标，你可能会以一种毫无意义的方式实现这些目标，因为这会妨碍你实现其他最终目标。

So, how do you optimize your long-term goals while considering their mutual impact? This fifth and final part of this book will help you do precisely that.

那么，如何在考虑各项长期目标相互影响的前提下，优化这些目标呢？本书的第五部分，也是最后一部分，将帮助你做到这一点。

RACES TO THE BOTTOM

竞相压低价格

L ife is full of races to the bottom: careers, businesses, communities, and activities that eventually become a competition for who is willing to sacrifice the most.

生活中充满了恶性竞争：事业、企业、社区和各种活动最终都会演变成一场比拼谁愿意牺牲更多的竞赛。

During the initial years, skill and a decent work ethic are usually enough to get ahead. This often lures many into believing they have an easy shot at winning.

在最初几年，技术和良好的职业道德通常足以让人脱颖而出。这常常使许多人误以为自己很容易就能成功。

However, as the race progresses, competition becomes fiercer. Skill and a decent work ethic are not enough anymore. Keeping up requires an unreasonable work ethic, and getting ahead demands reckless risk-taking.

然而，随着比赛的进行，竞争愈发激烈。技巧和良好的职业道德已不再足够。想要跟上节奏需要超乎寻常的职业操守，而想要脱颖而出则需要不顾一切的冒险精神。

Participants with a narrow vision for success allow their eagerness to win to dictate their boundaries. As a result, they often find themselves with miserable lives – having either sacrificed too much or taken too much risk and lost.

那些对成功定义狭隘的人，往往因为急于求成而止步不前。结果，他们常常发现自己过着悲惨的生活——要么牺牲太多，要么承担太多风险而最终失败。

Conversely, participants with a broad vision for success are more eager to have a full life than to win any race to the bottom. As a result, they set ambitious objectives for all important aspects of their life. Then , they use these objectives to define their boundaries – what they are not willing to risk and sacrifice. And finally, they use these boundaries to decide how to compete in races to the bottom and to what point.

相反，那些对成功抱有远大愿景的人更渴望拥有充实的人生，而不是在任何恶性竞争中取胜。因此，他们会为生活中所有重要方面设定雄心勃勃的目标。然后，他们会利用这些目标来界定自己的底线——哪些东西他们不愿意冒险和牺牲。最后，他们会利用这些底线来决定如何在恶性竞争中竞争，以及竞争到什么程度。

These are the real winners: even if they do not reach #1, they gain more from the race than they risked and sacrificed because they choose the conditions under which to compete, ultimately securing a favorable outcome.

真正的赢家是他们：即使他们没有获得第一名，他们从比赛中获得的也比他们承担的风险和牺牲要多，因为他们选择了竞争的条件，最终获得了有利的结果。

Be careful of any career, community, or hobby you participate in. Are they races to the bottom? Do they have the potential to become one?

要谨慎选择你参与的任何职业、社群或爱好。它们是否会导致恶性循环？它们是否有可能演变成恶性循环？

Races to the bottom are tricky because, initially, when the competition is not very strong, a bit of effort is sufficient to win, making them seem worth participating in. However , they get increasingly difficult and soon require excessive sacrifices. Therefore , it is important to ask ourselves to what extent it makes sense to participate in them. Not if, but to what extent.

竞相降低标准的做法很棘手，因为一开始竞争并不激烈，只需付出一点努力就能获胜，让人觉得参与其中很有意义。然而，竞争会变得越来越激烈，很快就需要付出过多的代价。因此，我们必须扪心自问：参与这种竞争到底有意义到什么程度？不是要不要参与，而是参与到什么程度。

Which races are to the bottom?

哪些种族垫底？

A race to the bottom is a race where the winner is the person who’s willing to take more risks and/or make more sacrifices.

竞相压价的竞赛是指获胜者是那些愿意承担更多风险和/或做出更多牺牲的人。

In theory, races where all participants either cannot or do not want to make excessive sacrifices are not races to the bottom. An example would be a career progression in a company where no one works beyond 5 PM .

理论上，如果所有参与者都无法或不愿做出过度牺牲，那么这种竞争就不是恶性竞争。例如，在一家公司里，如果所有人都下午5点以后才加班，那么这种职业晋升就属于恶性竞争。

However, there is no way to guarantee that participants will not make excessive sacrifices. In the previous example, no one can prevent an employee from taking work home or spending the evenings practicing some skill that will be helpful to get promoted.

然而，我们无法保证参与者不会做出过度牺牲。在前面的例子中，没有人能阻止员工把工作带回家，或者利用晚上时间练习一些有助于晋升的技能。

Therefore, it is the size of a race that determines whether it is a race to the bottom. The smaller the race, the less likely it is that among its participants, there will be someone willing to make excessive sacrifices.

因此，竞争的规模决定了它是否会演变成一场恶性竞争。竞争规模越小，参与者中就越不可能有人愿意做出过度的牺牲。

In contrast, a large race, or one with a large enough prize, is more likely to attract at least one participant aggressive enough to turn it into a race to the bottom.

相比之下，规模较大的比赛，或者奖金足够高的比赛，更有可能吸引至少一名足够激进的参与者，从而将比赛变成一场恶性竞争。

The problem with races to the bottom is that the larger the race, the larger the prize and thus the temptation to participate, but the difficulty and sacrifices required to win increase much faster than the prize. Hence , they are less worthwhile to participate in than they appear.

竞相压低价格的问题在于，竞争规模越大，奖金就越高，参与的诱惑也就越大，但获胜所需的难度和牺牲增长速度远超奖金的增长速度。因此，这类竞争的实际价值远低于表面看起来的。

Avoiding races to the bottom

避免竞相降低标准。

Avoiding races altogether is very hard, if not impossible. After all, in our lives, we are often unwilling participants in many races: school, work, and finding a partner are all competitions, even if we do not want them to be.

完全避免竞争几乎是不可能的。毕竟，在生活中，我们常常被迫参与各种竞争：学习、工作、寻找伴侣，这些都是竞争，即使我们并不希望如此。

The solution is to be extremely clear with our boundaries and only participate in races to the bottom to the extent our boundaries allow . For example, a career is a race to the bottom, but a career where you never work beyond 5 PM isn’t. Similarly , a career in sales can be a race to the moral bottom, but a career in sales done with integrity isn’t.

解决之道在于明确自身底线，并且只在底线允许的范围内参与竞相降低道德底线的竞争。例如，职业生涯本身可能是一种竞相降低道德底线的竞争，但一份从不加班到下午五点以后的职业则不然。同样，销售职业也可能是一种道德底线的竞争，但一份秉持诚信的销售职业则不然。

Again, note that this is not an invitation to minimize your ambitions. Rather , it is an invitation to maximize them. Make a list of everything you want out of life, covering all its spheres: professional, social, spiritual, fun, etc. Then , ask yourself which boundaries you will need to have to achieve all your ambitions. Only afterward, figure out which races you should compete in and to what point.

再次强调，这并非鼓励你降低自己的抱负，而是鼓励你最大限度地发挥自己的抱负。列出你人生中所有想要的东西，涵盖各个方面：职业、社交、精神、娱乐等等。然后，问问自己，为了实现所有抱负，你需要设定哪些界限。只有在此之后，才能决定你应该参加哪些比赛，以及应该做到什么程度。

If you do this exercise properly, you might achieve more in life than you might ever achieve if you focus on winning a single race to the bottom.

如果你正确地进行这项练习，你可能会在生活中取得比你专注于赢得一场输赢比赛更大的成就。

Winning races to the bottom

赢得这场向下竞赛

You can reliably win a race to the bottom only if you do not need to get #1 for it to have a net positive effect on your life, because no strategy can reproducibly get you to #1 in a race to the bottom.

只有当你不需要获得第一名就能对你的生活产生积极影响时，你才能可靠地赢得这场恶性竞争，因为没有任何策略能够保证你在恶性竞争中始终排名第一。

The previous paragraph might raise objections such as, " But Luca , obviously a mix of hard work and a great strategy can make you #1!"

上一段可能会引起这样的反对意见：“但是卢卡，很明显，努力工作加上一个好策略就能让你成为第一名！”

Yes, but let’s not confuse “winning” with “winning reproducibly.” Of course, barring cheating, everyone who wins a competition is a worthy winner, and they wouldn’t have won without hard work. However , that doesn’t mean that talent, hard work, and a great strategy can guarantee winning; at most, they guarantee a chance of winning.

没错，但我们不能把“获胜”和“持续获胜”混为一谈。当然，撇开作弊不谈，每个比赛的获胜者都是当之无愧的赢家，没有辛勤的努力，他们不可能获胜。然而，这并不意味着天赋、努力和出色的策略就能保证获胜；它们至多只能保证获胜的几率。

Let me give a concrete example. Leo Messi’s Argentina won the 2022 soccer World Cup . Did they deserve it? Totally . Were they the best team? Possibly . Were they guaranteed to win? Not at all. Betting companies gave them less than 50% odds. Why ? Because , in a large competition such as the World Cup , there are enough competitors that even the best one has only a small chance of winning.

让我举个具体的例子。梅西领衔的阿根廷队赢得了2022年世界杯。他们配得上这个冠军吗？当然配。他们是最好的球队吗？或许是。他们一定能赢吗？完全不是。博彩公司给他们的赔率甚至不到50%。为什么？因为在世界杯这样的大型赛事中，竞争者众多，即使是最好的球队，夺冠的概率也微乎其微。

In large competitions, the sheer number of competitors means there will be more than one competitor talented and hard-working enough to have a decent shot at winning. Therefore , there is no reproducible strategy for winning large competitions. So , you shouldn’t enter any non-trivial competition that wouldn’t be good for you even if you didn’t win it.

在大型比赛中，参赛人数众多，意味着会有不止一位选手既有天赋又足够努力，都有相当大的机会赢得比赛。因此，并不存在可以复制的赢得大型比赛的策略。所以，即使你最终没有赢得比赛，也不应该参加任何对你毫无益处的、非小规模的比赛。

# ↩

Smaller competitions

规模较小的比赛

Conversely, small competitions do allow for reproducible success strategies.

相反，小型比赛确实允许采用可复制的成功策略。

Because they involve a smaller group of participants, the chances of competing against very talented and hard-working individuals are lower. It is easier to become the best chess player in your town than in your country.

由于参与人数较少，与才华横溢、勤奋刻苦的棋手竞争的机会也相应降低。成为你所在城镇最优秀的棋手比成为你所在国家最优秀的棋手要容易得多。

In small competitions, you can outwork or outsmart your competitors without taking excessive risks or making undue sacrifices.

在小型比赛中，你可以通过努力或智慧战胜你的竞争对手，而无需承担过大的风险或做出不必要的牺牲。

If you happen to have bad luck and encounter a fierce competitor, it will likely be only one or two of them. You will still be able to achieve a #2 or #3 ranking.

如果你运气不好，遇到实力强劲的竞争对手，可能也只有一两个。你仍然有机会获得第二名或第三名的成绩。

And if you truly want to be #1, you can always move or pivot to another small competition. If being the best chess player in your town is impossible because a grandmaster happened to be born down the street, you can always pivot to another game.

如果你真的想成为第一，你可以随时转战其他小型比赛。如果因为街对面恰好出生了一位国际象棋特级大师，导致你无法成为镇上最好的棋手，你也可以转战其他游戏。

But what if your only dream is to become the greatest chess player in your country? In this case, you must acknowledge that it is going to be a race to the bottom, that you will have to sacrifice more than you might be comfortable with, and that you will end up with, at most, a chance at winning.

但如果你的唯一梦想是成为本国最伟大的棋手呢？在这种情况下，你必须承认这将是一场恶性竞争，你将不得不做出比你想象中更多的牺牲，最终最多也只能获得获胜的机会。

Then, of course, the choice of whether or not to participate is yours.

当然，是否参加完全取决于您自己。
