36

SPILLOVERS

溢出效应

T here are plenty of successful yet unhappy people.

有很多成功人士却并不快乐。

Sometimes, the success they sought doesn’t taste as nice as they expected. But more often, it’s because they discover that their pursuit of success had more “negative spillovers” on the rest of their life than they expected.

有时，他们追求的成功并不像他们预期的那样美好。但更多时候，是因为他们发现，对成功的追求对他们生活的其他方面产生了比预期更多的“负面影响”。

Not only should your strategy to achieve success be sustainable (so that you can pursue it long enough to guarantee success), but it should also be devoid of major negative spillovers on other areas of your life.

你的成功策略不仅应该是可持续的（这样你才能坚持足够长的时间以确保成功），而且还应该避免对你生活的其他方面产生重大的负面影响。

For example, avoid any strategy that requires you to endanger your health or marriage. It’s not worth it. More generally, avoid any strategy to achieve a given goal that’s incompatible with your other goals.

例如，避免任何会危及你的健康或婚姻的策略。这样做得不偿失。更普遍地说，避免任何为了实现某个目标而采取的、与你的其他目标相冲突的策略。

If you discover that no strategy fits this criterion, you might have incompatible goals. If so, you will have to compromise on your goals or set more conservative ones. This is not a choice: either you compromise, or life will, letting you achieve some of your goals but not others.

如果你发现没有任何策略符合这个标准，那么你的目标可能存在冲突。如果是这样，你就必须对目标做出妥协，或者设定更保守的目标。这不是一个选择：要么你妥协，要么生活会替你妥协，让你实现部分目标，而无法实现其他目标。

# ↩
37

COMPARISONS AND THE PARETO FRONTIER

比较与帕累托前沿

E very time I participate in a high school reunion, I have a choice in how I compare myself to others.

每次参加高中同学聚会，我都可以选择如何与他人比较。

One option is to notice that, among my former classmates, there is at least one who earns more than I do, at least one who has more free time than I do, and so on.

一种方法是注意到，在我的前同学中，至少有一个人的收入比我高，至少有一个人比我有更多的空闲时间，等等。

Another option is to notice that, among my former classmates who earn at least as much as I do, I'm the one with the most free time. And among those who have at least as much free time as I do, I'm the one who earns the most.

另一种解释是，在我以前的同学中，收入至少和我一样的那些人里，我的空闲时间最多。而那些空闲时间至少和我一样多的人里，我的收入最高。

Learning to view success through this lens is highly beneficial. For example, do you want to be as successful as possible, or do you want to be as successful as possible while always having dinner with your family? Then , you shouldn’t compare yourself with anyone who does not also spend all their dinners with their family.

学会用这种视角看待成功非常有益。例如，你是想尽可能地成功，还是想在尽可能成功的同时还能和家人一起吃晚饭？如果是这样，你就不应该拿自己和那些不能和家人一起吃晚饭的人比较。

Never compare yourself with someone who has different priorities or is optimizing for different objectives or for a shorter time horizon. Doing so leads to unhappiness and/or making counterproductive decisions.

永远不要与那些优先事项不同、目标不同或时间跨度更短的人比较。这样做会导致不快乐，甚至做出适得其反的决定。

The Pareto Frontier

帕累托前沿

On the previous page, I presented two ways to compare yourself to others.

在上一页中，我介绍了两种与他人比较的方法。

  1. “There is someone who earns more than I do and someone with more free time than I do."
    “有人比我挣得多，也有人比我空闲时间多。”
  2. "Among those who earn as much as I do, I have the most free time, and among those with as much free time as I do, I earn the most.”
    “在我收入水平相当的人当中，我的空闲时间最多；在我空闲时间最多的人当中，我的收入也最高。”

The second type of evaluation is called the Pareto Frontier , named after the Italian mathematician Vilfredo Pareto (the same one who invented the Pareto Rule , also called the "80/20 rule:" 20% of your customers are responsible for 80% of your problems, and so on).

第二种评估方法称为帕累托前沿，以意大利数学家维尔弗雷多·帕累托的名字命名（他发明了帕累托法则，也称为“80/20 法则”：20% 的客户造成了 80% 的问题，等等）。

In particular, I am on the Pareto Frontier if, given two metrics, A and B , among everyone who has at least as much A as I do, I have the most B , and among everyone who has at least as much B as I do, I have the most A .

具体来说，如果给定两个指标 A 和 B，在所有拥有至少与我一样多的 A 的人中，我的 B 最多；在所有拥有至少与我一样多的 B 的人中，我的 A 最多，那么我就处于帕累托前沿。

All the black dots are on the Pareto Frontier for metrics A and B

所有黑点都位于指标 A 和 B 的帕累托前沿上。

Comparing options

比较选项

The previous chapter began with a comparison between people, but the Pareto Frontier is also useful for comparing options.

上一章以人与人之间的比较开始，但帕累托前沿也适用于比较选项。

For example, without knowing about the Pareto Frontier , you might compare jobs by asking yourself which one is the highest paying. Instead , by using the Pareto Frontier , you might ask yourself better questions, such as, what\'s the highest-paying job among those that enable you to spend enough time with your family?

例如，如果不了解帕累托前沿，你可能会通过问自己哪个工作薪水最高来比较不同的工作。但是，如果运用帕累托前沿，你可能会问自己更好的问题，例如，在所有能够让你有足够的时间陪伴家人的工作中，薪水最高的是哪个？

The Pareto Frontier isn’t a revolutionary concept – many of us already make decisions using a similar mental process. However , giving it a name and making it explicit is useful because it shows that choosing a job that’s not the highest paying is not necessarily a lazy or suboptimal choice.

帕累托前沿并非什么革命性的概念——我们很多人在做决策时已经运用了类似的思维过程。然而，给它命名并明确阐述它的意义在于，它表明选择一份并非薪酬最高的工作并不一定意味着懒惰或次优。

If it’s on the Pareto Frontier of what matters to you, it is an ambitious and optimal choice.

如果它处于你所重视事物的帕累托前沿，那么这是一个雄心勃勃且最优的选择。

# ↩

The Pareto Frontier and winning long-term games

帕累托前沿与赢得长期游戏

Single-metric comparisons such as “who earns more” are toxic because they lead to feelings of inferiority and/or races to the bottom.

以“谁挣得更多”等单一指标进行比较是有害的，因为这会导致自卑感和/或竞相降低标准。

Conversely, comparing yourself to others using multi-metric comparisons such as the Pareto Frontier is a relatively healthy way to assess whether you’re being ambitious enough. If you are at the Pareto Frontier in the areas that matter to you, you’re probably doing fine (as long as being there isn’t the result of short-term optimization). Conversely , if you are far from your Pareto Frontier , you might have been too lazy or conservative.

反之，使用帕累托前沿等多指标比较方法将自己与他人进行比较，是一种相对健康的评估自身目标是否足够远大的方法。如果你在自己关注的领域达到了帕累托前沿，那么你可能做得不错（前提是达到帕累托前沿并非短期优化的结果）。反之，如果你距离帕累托前沿还很远，那么你可能过于懒惰或保守。

But perhaps more importantly, defining success in terms of Pareto frontiers helps you avoid the temptation to follow those who take excessive risks or make sacrifices you’re not willing to take.

但或许更重要的是，用帕累托前沿来定义成功，可以帮助你避免追随那些承担过大风险或做出你不愿意做出的牺牲的人的诱惑。

Instead of aiming to be the most successful, aim to be the most successful among those who play long-term games and are not willing to take excessive risks or make excessive sacrifices.

与其追求成为最成功的人，不如追求在那些进行长期博弈且不愿承担过大风险或做出过大牺牲的人中最成功的人。

Your distribution of outcomes will improve.

你的结果分布将会改善。

# ↩

Chapter summary

章节概要

You are at the Pareto Frontier if, given two metrics A and B that matter to you, among those who have at least as much A as you do, you are the one with the most B , and among those who have at least as much B as you do, you are the one with the most A .

如果对于两个对你来说重要的指标 A 和 B，在那些 A 值至少与你一样多的人中，你是 B 值最多的人；而在那些 B 值至少与你一样多的人中，你是 A 值最多的人，那么你就处于帕累托前沿。

The Pareto Frontier is a great way to compare options, but also a healthy way to compare yourself to others.

帕累托前沿是比较不同选项的好方法，也是将自己与他人进行比较的健康方法。

Most importantly, it prevents you from comparing yourself with those with a shorter time horizon than yours. That would be a toxic comparison because it sets you up for failure (you cannot compete with short-term optimizers over the short term⁠ i ) and tempts you into abandoning good long-term strategies in favor of bad short-term ones.

最重要的是，它可以防止你与那些投资期限比你短的人进行比较。这种比较是有害的，因为它会让你注定失败（你无法在短期利益上与那些只关注短期利益的人竞争），并诱使你放弃良好的长期策略而选择糟糕的短期策略。

i I mean, obviously, you can compete, but you most probably won’t win.

我的意思是，很显然，你可以参与竞争，但你很可能赢不了。

You will not do badly because good long-term strategies never do poorly, but survivorship bias almost guarantees that there will be at least a few short-term players who will beat you – at least over short time horizons.

你不会表现得很差，因为好的长期策略永远不会表现不佳，但幸存者偏差几乎可以肯定，至少会有一些短期玩家击败你——至少在短期内是这样。

38

CHOOSE REPRODUCIBLE OBJECTIVES

选择可重复的目标

L ong-term strategies have amazing potential and can help you reliably achieve your life goals, but they aren’t magical. They cannot help you reliably achieve objectives that cannot be reproducibly achieved.

长期策略具有巨大的潜力，能够帮助你可靠地实现人生目标，但它们并非万能。它们无法帮助你可靠地实现那些无法重复实现的目标。

For example, becoming #1 in the world at something is not reproducible. All it takes is someone else applying the same strategy as yours, at which point it almost becomes a coin toss.

例如，在某个领域成为世界第一是无法复制的。只要有人采用和你一样的策略，结果就几乎完全取决于运气了。

This concept is counterintuitive because of our assumption that if a competition involves skill, then becoming the most skilled guarantees victory. This is seldom true. Obviously , skill still matters and is table stakes. However , luck and other considerations still play a large role.

这个概念看似有悖常理，因为我们通常认为，如果一项竞争需要技巧，那么技巧最高者就能确保胜利。但事实并非如此。当然，技巧仍然重要，是基本条件。然而，运气和其他因素也起着至关重要的作用。

Think about chess. In appearance, chess is the quintessential skill game, as it includes no dice or other random elements. Yet , if two players of similar skill levels face each other and play a series of games, the more skilled player will only win some of them.

想想国际象棋。从表面上看，国际象棋是典型的技巧游戏，因为它不涉及骰子或其他随机因素。然而，如果两个水平相近的棋手对弈，进行一系列比赛，技巧更高的棋手也只能赢其中的一部分。

In fact, in the last Chess World Championship Finals (2023, Ding vs Nepomniachtchi ) , the winning player only won 57% of the games, excluding draws. This means there is a meaningful chance that the losing player was more skilled than the winner!

事实上，在上一届国际象棋世界锦标赛决赛（2023年，丁俊晖对阵涅波姆尼亚奇）中，获胜棋手仅赢得了57%的比赛（不包括和棋）。这意味着，败者棋艺可能比获胜棋手更高！

We often mistakenly believe that strategies depend on luck to the extent that they relate to events we have little control over. But this is wrong. For example, there are good investing strategies to bet on stocks over which we have no control, whereas chess games, where we have full control over our moves, can still be a coin toss if we face an adversary of similar skill.

我们常常误以为，策略在很大程度上取决于运气，尤其是在涉及我们几乎无法控制的事件时。但这种想法是错误的。例如，即使我们无法控制股票市场，也存在一些有效的投资策略；而下棋，即使我们完全掌控每一步棋，如果对手实力相当，结果仍然可能像抛硬币一样难以预料。

Instead, what determines whether a strategy depends on luck is its structure and how many winners there can be. Investing is luck-dependent only if we bet so aggressively that we can only afford a few wrong bets before accumulating excessive losses. And winning an award is more luck-dependent, the more limited the number of winners.

相反，决定一项策略是否依赖运气的，是其结构以及获胜者的数量。投资只有在我们采取过于激进的策略，以至于只能承受几次错误的投注就会累积巨额损失时，才真正依赖运气。同样，获奖者人数越少，获奖就越依赖运气。

Only goals that allow enough winners and can be played many times are reproducible.

只有那些能够产生足够多获胜者并且可以多次进行的目标才是可复制的。

Choose reproducible goals. Or , at least, acknowledge that you chose non-reproducible ones and that, therefore, no matter your talent and determination, you have at most a chance at achieving them, but no guarantee.

选择可复制的目标。或者，至少要承认你选择了不可复制的目标，因此，无论你的才能和决心如何，你最多只有实现这些目标的机会，而没有保证。

Chapter summary

章节概要

No strategy can guarantee success for goals that only allow a limited number of winners or a limited number of trials.

对于只能产生有限数量的获胜者或只能进行有限次数尝试的目标，任何策略都无法保证成功。

The first step to reproducible success is to choose reproducible goals.

实现可复制成功的第一步是选择可复制的目标。

THE 1% LIFE

1%的生活

W hen I was a kid, I thought I had no chance of getting a great wife. After all, there were plenty of people fitter than me, plenty more charismatic than me, plenty wealthier than me, etc.

小时候，我觉得自己没机会娶到好妻子。毕竟，比我身材好、比我更有魅力、比我富有等等的人比比皆是。

Then, one day, a friend told me, “ Luca , if you don’t become overweight, you will be in the top 30% of the population by physique. If you get a decent job, you will be in the top 30% by wealth. If you aren’t crazy and can sustain a normal conversation while cracking a joke or two, you will be in the top 30% by interpersonal skills. And if you manage to do all three at the same time, you will be in the top 10% of bachelors, perhaps even in the top 5%.”

有一天，一个朋友对我说：“卢卡，如果你不发胖，你的体格就能排进人群前30%。如果你找到一份体面的工作，你的财富就能排进人群前30%。如果你不疯，还能一边正常交谈一边讲一两个笑话，你的人际交往能力就能排进人群前30%。如果你能同时做到这三点，你就能跻身单身汉的前10%，甚至可能排进前5%。”

It turns out that the bar isn't that high if you look at the aggregate instead of individual attributes.

如果从整体而不是单个属性来看，就会发现标准并没有那么高。

If one of your goals is, say, to live a top 1% life – a life better than 99% of your fellow compatriots – you do not need to be in the top 1% by wealth or health to get there. Similarly , if you want to be, say, a top 1% professional, you can probably realize that you can achieve that by being in the top 20% in skills, the top 20% in work ethic, and very good at not making major mistakes.

如果你的目标是过上顶尖1%的生活——比99%的同胞都过得更好——你并不需要拥有顶尖的财富或健康才能实现这个目标。同样地，如果你想成为顶尖1%的专业人士，你或许会意识到，只要你的技能、职业道德都达到前20%，并且很少犯重大错误，你就能实现这个目标。

But is top 1% really achievable?

但跻身前 1% 真的可行吗？

I do believe that, barring rare debilitating conditions, a top 1% life is truly achievable, especially if you consider the top 1% in the context of the Pareto Frontier . Again , not a top-1% income, but a top-1% life.

我相信，除非患有罕见的严重疾病，否则跻身顶尖1%人群的生活是完全可以实现的，尤其是在帕累托前沿的框架下考虑这顶尖1%人群时。再次强调，我指的不是顶尖1%的收入，而是顶尖1%的生活。

I might be wrong, and maybe what’s truly achievable for most readers of this book is the top 2% (or some other percentage). That’s not the point.

我可能错了，也许对这本书的大多数读者来说，真正能够达到的水平只有前2%（或其他某个百分比）。但这并不是重点。

The point is that the path toward excellence and a great life involves going broad and narrow.

关键在于，通往卓越和美好人生的道路既包括走广路，也包括走窄路。

We often get the opposite impression because those who are excellent often have a skill at which they’re extremely good. But this often obscures the fact that they are also much better than average at plenty of other skills, and that without such broad proficiency, their narrow excellence would be nearly useless.

我们常常会产生相反的印象，因为那些优秀的人往往在某一方面技艺超群。但这常常掩盖了这样一个事实：他们在许多其他技能方面也远超平均水平。如果没有这种广泛的技能，他们在某一方面的卓越成就几乎毫无用处。

Take any NBA star known for their excellent offensive skills, like Ray Allen or Steph Curry . Yes , their offensive skills are extraordinary. But their defensive skills are also above average! If you think about it, there are plenty of basketball players who are excellent at some particular skill but never make it to the pros because of their lack of some other indispensable skill.

以雷·阿伦或斯蒂芬·库里这样以进攻技巧著称的NBA球星为例。没错，他们的进攻技巧确实非凡。但他们的防守技巧也高于平均水平！仔细想想，有很多篮球运动员在某些方面非常出色，但却因为缺乏其他一些不可或缺的技能而最终无法进入职业联赛。

Narrow excellence requires broad excellence to yield good outcomes.

狭义上的卓越需要广义上的卓越才能取得良好的成果。

Hence, my encouragement is to go broader before going narrower.

因此，我的建议是先拓宽视野，再缩小范围。

This doesn’t mean spreading yourself too thin. It means realizing that if you go narrow and don’t also go broad, going narrow won’t matter.

这并不意味着要分散精力。而是要意识到，如果你只专注于狭窄的领域而不去拓展广度，那么专注于狭窄的领域是毫无意义的。

Think about your life as a whole and try to succeed in all the aspects that matter to you significantly – family, career, health, wealth, etc. Otherwise , succeeding in one area will feel like it didn’t matter.

把人生看作一个整体，努力在所有对你来说至关重要的方面取得成功——家庭、事业、健康、财富等等。否则，在一个领域取得成功会让你觉得一切都毫无意义。

Prioritize going broad over going narrow. If you go narrow but don’t also go broad, having gone narrow won’t have mattered.

优先考虑广泛涉猎而非狭窄领域。如果你只关注狭窄领域而没有同时关注广泛领域，那么之前关注狭窄领域的做法就毫无意义。

HAPPINESS RULES

幸福法则

“What has to happen in order for you to feel good? Do you have to have someone hug you, kiss you, make love to you? Must you make a million dollars? […] If you make [that], the million dollars doesn’t give you any pleasure. It’s your rule that says, “ When I hit this mark, I’ll give myself permission to feel good.

TONY ROBBINS

“你得发生什么才能感到快乐？你需要有人拥抱你、亲吻你、与你做爱吗？你必须赚到一百万美元吗？[…] 即使你赚到了一百万美元，它也不会给你带来任何快乐。重要的是你自己给自己定下的规矩：‘当我达到这个目标时，我才允许自己感到快乐。’”——托尼·罗宾斯

W hat needs to happen for you to feel happy?

什么事情发生才能让你感到快乐？

Not the fleeting kind of happiness that’s followed by hollowness, but the real kind of happiness, the kind that warms your heart and makes you feel proud of your choices.

不是那种转瞬即逝、随后便空虚的幸福，而是真正的幸福，那种温暖人心、让你为自己的选择感到自豪的幸福。

What rules of yours determine when you permit yourself to be happy?

你遵循哪些规则来决定何时允许自己感到快乐？

Unless you know your happiness rules, your strategy will be misguided.

除非你了解自己的幸福法则，否则你的策略将会误入歧途。

Examples of happiness rules

幸福法则示例

Here are some examples of happiness rules, some great, and some less so. Can you figure out which is which? ( The answer is below the list.)

以下是一些幸福法则的例子，有些很好，有些则不然。你能分辨出哪些是好哪些是坏吗？（答案在列表下方。）

  1. “I give myself permission to be happy once I get my income above $ X per month.”
    “只有当我的月收入超过 X 美元时，我才会允许自己感到快乐。”
  2. “I give myself permission to be happy every time I complete a good piece of work.”
    “每当我完成一项出色的工作时，我都会允许自己感到高兴。”
  3. “I give myself permission to be happy when my spouse says (s)he loves me.”
    “当我的伴侣说他/她爱我时，我才允许自己感到快乐。”
  4. “I give myself permission to be happy every time I spend quality time with my loved ones.”
    “每当我和爱的人共度美好时光时，我都会允许自己感到快乐。”

My preference would be for rules #2 and #4. That’s because rules #1 and #3 imply you will spend most of your time being unhappy (even if you're doing great!), whereas rules #2 and #4 allow you to be happy most days.

我更倾向于选择规则 2 和 4。因为规则 1 和 3 意味着你大部分时间都会感到不快乐（即使你做得很好！），而规则 2 和 4 则能让你在大多数日子里都感到快乐。

The key is to find rules that allow you to be happy most days without, of course, falling into complacency.

关键在于找到一些规则，让你在大多数日子里都能感到快乐，当然，前提是不能陷入自满情绪。

# ↩
41

IT’S CLOSER THAN WE THINK

比我们想象的更近

I n 2023, the judges of the prestigious Gilbert et Gaillard international wine competition awarded the gold medal to a $2.70 supermarket wine they deemed “exceptional” (they were tricked by a fake label).

2023 年，著名的吉尔伯特·盖拉德国际葡萄酒大赛的评委们将金奖授予了一款售价 2.70 美元的超市葡萄酒，他们认为这款酒“非常出色”（他们被假标签蒙蔽了）。

A bottle of good wine is cheap; it's a bottle of good wine with an expensive label that is expensive. Similarly , going out is cheap; it’s going out to an expensive place that’s expensive.

一瓶好酒本身并不贵；一瓶贴着昂贵标签的好酒自然就贵了。同样，外出就餐本身并不贵；去高档场所就贵了。

These might very well be platitudes, but they’re ignored platitudes.

这些话或许只是老生常谈，但却是被忽视的老生常谈。

“90% of a millionaire lifestyle is already available to you,” wrote Mark Baker in his “ No Money Millionaire .” I think he’s right. I genuinely feel I live like a millionaire without being one – perhaps precisely because not having “becoming a millionaire” as one of my life goals is so freeing. It enables me to have more time, to work on the projects I like, to live close to my parents even though it’s not the most conducive city for business, and, in general, it makes all other life goals so much easier to attain.

马克·贝克在他的《白手起家：百万富翁》一书中写道：“百万富翁生活方式的90%其实已经触手可及。” 我觉得他说得对。我真心觉得，即使我并非百万富翁，我的生活也像个百万富翁——或许正是因为“成为百万富翁”并非我的人生目标之一，才让我感到如此自由。这让我拥有更多的时间，去做自己喜欢的事情，即使我所在的城市并非最适合经商，也能住在父母附近。总而言之，这让我更容易实现其他的人生目标。

(“The average of your top five friends influences your income and expenses,” I say.)

（我说：“你最常联系在一起的五个朋友的平均收入和支出会影响你的收入和支出。”）

I’m not advocating for frugality here. Instead , I’m suggesting that there’s a high opportunity cost in wanting more than you need in one area of your life because it will make it harder to attain what you need in other areas of your life.

我并不是提倡节俭。相反，我的意思是，在生活的某个领域追求超出自身需求的东西会带来很高的机会成本，因为它会使你在其他领域更难获得所需。

Nor am I saying to lower your ambitions. Instead , I’m saying to raise them! Aim for what you need, not just in a single area of your life but in all of them!

我并不是说要降低你的目标。相反，我的意思是要提高你的目标！要追求你真正需要的东西，不仅在生活的某个领域，而是在所有领域！

This might require some introspection about what you really need and the ability to resist moving the goalposts once you achieve that.

这可能需要你反思自己真正需要什么，以及在实现目标后能够抵制改变目标的诱惑。

“Remember when you wanted what you have now?”

KATELYN GLEASON (ELIGIBLE CEO)

“还记得你曾经多么渴望拥有现在的一切吗？”凯特琳·格里森（合格的首席执行官）

# ↩

Chapter summary

章节概要

There is a high opportunity cost in wanting more than you need.

想要得到超出自己需要的东西，会带来很高的机会成本。

Be ambitious and try to achieve more than you need, but only when it doesn't come at the cost of something else you need in another area of your life.

要有雄心壮志，努力取得超出你所需成就的成就，但前提是这不会以牺牲你生活中其他领域所需为代价。

“It’s insane to risk what you have and need for something you don’t really need.”

WARREN BUFFETT

“为了你并不真正需要的东西而冒险失去你拥有和需要的东西，这简直太疯狂了。”——沃伦·巴菲特

CONCLUSIONS

结论

# ↩

In Part I of this book,

本书第一部分，

We have seen that the key to winning long-term games is to stop playing them as a succession of separate short-term games. Instead , play short-term games not to win them but to increase your chances of winning the long-term game.

我们已经看到，赢得长期博弈的关键在于停止将它们视为一系列独立的短期博弈。相反，参与短期博弈的目的不是为了赢得它们，而是为了增加赢得长期博弈的几率。

We have also seen that you can win long-term games without addressing common causes of failure, but the chances are that you won’t. To have a good chance of winning long-term games, you must be aware of common sources of failure and proactively address them.

我们也看到，即使不解决常见的失败原因，你也能赢得长期比赛，但这可能性不大。要想提高长期比赛的胜率，你必须了解常见的失败根源，并积极主动地加以解决。

Then, we went through the three components of good long-term strategies: they are sustainable, constructive, and inevitable.

然后，我们探讨了良好长期战略的三个组成部分：可持续性、建设性和必然性。

Finally, we have seen that if you optimize each component of a strategy individually, you won’t have an optimal strategy. Instead , you should follow an iterative approach and optimize for the distribution of outcomes.

最后，我们看到，如果单独优化策略的每个组成部分，就无法得到最优策略。相反，应该采用迭代方法，并针对结果分布进行优化。

# ↩

In Part II of this book,

本书第二部分，

We have seen how long-term strategies are truly superior to short-term ones.

我们已经看到，长期战略确实优于短期战略。

If it seems otherwise, it is either because of survivorship bias or because we are focusing on short-term performance. Of course , short-term strategies deliver better short-term performance, but if long-term performance is what matters to you, make long-term evaluations.

如果结果看起来并非如此，那要么是因为幸存者偏差，要么是因为我们过于关注短期业绩。当然，短期策略往往能带来更好的短期业绩，但如果你更看重长期业绩，那就应该进行长期评估。

Remember the image below (from the chapter on survivorship bias)? Always ask yourself, does my strategy look more like Alice’s or Bob’s ?

还记得下图（出自关于幸存者偏差的章节）吗？经常问问自己，我的策略更像是爱丽丝的策略还是鲍勃的策略？

Of course, you also want to ensure you don’t have a bad long-term strategy that begins like Bob’s but ends up like Alice’s . You still need to take effective action, and you still need to do it with urgency, trying to succeed as fast as possible – but only as fast as long-term evaluations allow. In other words, only as fast as possible without compromising your long-term assets or your chances of success.

当然，你也要确保你的长期战略不会像鲍勃那样开局顺利，最终却像爱丽丝那样以失败告终。你仍然需要采取有效的行动，而且仍然需要争分夺秒，力求尽快取得成功——但速度必须以长期评估允许的为准。换句话说，速度只能在不损害你的长期资产或成功几率的前提下尽可能快。

# ↩

In Part III of this book,

本书第三部分，

We have seen the importance of not merely considering the long term but also leveraging it.

我们已经认识到，不仅要考虑长远，还要充分利用长远优势。

We discussed the importance of playing iterated games, which you play not to maximize what you get out of the current interaction but to make the next one better.

我们讨论了进行迭代游戏的重要性，这种游戏的目的不是为了最大化当前互动带来的收益，而是为了使下一次互动变得更好。

We also saw that short-term games are about getting a larger share of the pie, whereas long-term games are also about growing the pie.

我们还发现，短期游戏的目标是获得更大的市场份额，而长期游戏的目标则是把蛋糕做大。

We discussed the importance of building long-term assets (such as skills, habits, and trust) and of doing so even when it doesn’t look like a good time, because it never will be a good time. If you never build them, you will never grow beyond an early plateau.

我们讨论了积累长期资产（例如技能、习惯和信任）的重要性，而且即使现在看起来时机不佳，也应该这样做，因为永远不会有所谓的“好时机”。如果你从不积累这些资产，你的发展就永远无法突破早期的瓶颈期。

We saw how many talented and determined people fail to achieve success because they kill their Goose . They have some asset (a skill, a product, a reputation, a relationship), and in a bid to get more yield, they squeeze it to the point of damaging its capacity to produce yield.

我们看到，许多才华横溢、意志坚定的人最终失败，是因为他们杀鸡取卵。他们拥有一些资产（技能、产品、声誉、人脉），为了追求更高的收益，他们过度榨取这些资产，最终损害了它们创造收益的能力。

Finally, we have seen the importance of only seeking success solid enough to act as an effective foundation for your long-term goals.

最后，我们已经认识到，应该只追求足够坚实的成功，以此作为实现长期目标的有效基础。

# ↩

In Part IV of this book,

本书第四部分，

We have seen the importance of derisking.

我们已经认识到降低风险的重要性。

Just as brakes are not for driving slowly but to enable driving fast, risk management is not a burden but an enabler of rapid growth.

就像刹车不是为了减速而是为了快速行驶一样，风险管理不是一种负担，而是快速增长的推动力。

Much of derisking involves learning what you need to learn before you get hurt. This means learning from the failures of others and preempting the possible ways in which you might fail – for example, by using pre-mortems and fishbone diagrams.

降低风险的关键在于防患于未然，在受伤之前就了解你需要学习的知识。这意味着从他人的失败中吸取教训，并预先防范你可能犯的错误——例如，通过事前分析和鱼骨图等方法。

We have also seen that you should not be satisfied with a strategy for your long-term goals that might work; instead, you should seek a strategy that cannot fail. Failure is acceptable for projects but not for your life goals.

我们也看到，你不应该满足于一个可能奏效的长期目标策略；相反，你应该寻求一个万无一失的策略。失败对于项目来说是可以接受的，但对于你的人生目标来说则不可接受。

# ↩

Finally, in Part V of this book,

最后，在本书第五部分中，

We discussed holistic success.

我们探讨了整体成功。

We have seen the importance of avoiding races to the bottom – competitions where even winners lose. Or , at the very least, to only enter them on your conditions and never compromise your boundaries (as long as they are reasonable, of course) .

我们已经看到了避免陷入恶性竞争的重要性——在这种竞争中，即使是赢家也是输家。或者，至少应该只在自己设定的条件下参与，并且永远不要妥协自己的底线（当然，前提是这些底线是合理的）。

We have also learned about the Pareto Frontier and the opportunity to evaluate your life in a way that considers all trade-offs.

我们还了解了帕累托前沿，以及通过权衡所有利弊来评估人生的机会。

And the importance of never comparing yourself to people with a shorter time horizon than yours or with narrower goals.

还有一点很重要，那就是永远不要把自己和那些时间跨度比你短或者目标比你窄的人比较。

I concluded the book with an invitation to think about what your happiness rules are and to avoid seeking more than you need when doing so would endanger your other life goals.

我在书的结尾邀请读者思考自己的幸福法则，并避免追求超出自身需求的东西，以免危及其他人生目标。

FISHBONE DIAGRAMS

鱼骨图

W hile pre-mortems are an extremely powerful tool, they are by no means sufficient for developing a comprehensive list of what could go wrong. You might have blind spots or simply forget something important.

虽然事前验尸分析是一个非常强大的工具，但它远不足以列出所有可能出错的地方。你可能会有盲点，或者只是忘记了一些重要的事情。

Here is a tool to help you: fishbone diagrams. They are traditionally used in manufacturing for root cause analysis, but I also use them with my clients to de-risk their projects and ventures.

这里有一个工具可以帮到你：鱼骨图。它传统上用于制造业的根本原因分析，但我也会用它来帮助我的客户降低项目和投资的风险。

The following picture is an example. It is a diagram that looks like a fishbone (hence the name) and is read from right to left. It begins with a failure (the “fish head,” in this case, “my book didn’t become a bestseller”) and continues with four possible categories of causes (the four “main bones”), which in turn branch out into many possible root causes.

下图就是一个例子。这是一个形似鱼骨的图表（因此得名），阅读方向是从右到左。它以一个失败事件（在本例中是“鱼头”，即“我的书没能成为畅销书”）开始，接着列出了四种可能的原因类别（四根“主骨”），而这些类别又各自分支出许多可能的根本原因。

An example of a fishbone diagram. A larger image is available at Luca - Dellanna.com /fishbone

鱼骨图示例。更大尺寸的图片可在 Luca-Dellanna.com/fishbone 查看。

Traditionally, fishbone diagrams are used for post-mortems. If your latest marketing campaign didn’t work, you might draw a fishbone diagram to figure out what caused the problem.

传统上，鱼骨图用于事后分析。如果你的最新营销活动效果不佳，你可能会绘制鱼骨图来找出问题所在。

Of course, it is possible to figure out root causes without using fishbone diagrams. However , drawing one decreases the chance of leaving out something important.

当然，不用鱼骨图也能找出根本原因。但是，绘制鱼骨图可以降低遗漏重要信息的概率。

I find fishbone diagrams very useful for pre -mortems. Of course, you could conduct effective pre-mortems without drawing a fishbone diagram, but drawing one will make them even more comprehensive and might even reveal some of your blind spots.

我发现鱼骨图对事前分析非常有用。当然，即使不画鱼骨图，你也可以进行有效的事前分析，但画鱼骨图会让分析更加全面，甚至可能揭示你的一些盲点。

In the following pages, you will find a few examples of fishbone diagrams applied to some common life goals. Before that, let’s look at four tips for effective fishbone diagrams:

接下来的几页中，你会看到一些鱼骨图应用于常见人生目标的示例。在此之前，让我们先来看看有效绘制鱼骨图的四个技巧：

  1. Ask yourself both what could fail and how others failed in related situations.
    问问自己哪些方面可能会失败，以及其他人在类似情况下是如何失败的。
  2. Write down any possibility, no matter how unlikely. You don’t have to address every risk, but you must consider every risk.
    把所有可能性都写下来，无论可能性多么小。你不必考虑所有风险，但必须考虑到每一种风险。
  3. The largest bones should be as mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive as possible.
    最大的骨骼应该尽可能相互排斥且具有完备性。
  4. Always ask yourself multiple times, “ What else?”
    要反复问自己：“还有什么？”

Two examples of fishbone diagrams

鱼骨图的两个例子

Larger images are available at Luca - Dellanna.com /fishbone

更大的图片可在 Luca-Dellanna.com/fishbone 查看。

Notes on the example diagrams

示例图表说明

Due to the constraints of creating a small yet clear picture, the previous diagrams are not a comprehensive list of all possible root causes but show only the top ten or fifteen. Most probably, while reading them, you noticed at least a few important omissions.

由于篇幅所限，需要绘制一幅简洁明了的图表，因此之前的图表并未列出所有可能的根本原因，而仅展示了最重要的十到十五个。很可能，您在阅读这些图表时，已经注意到至少有一些重要的遗漏。

That’s okay. The important thing is that you got the gist of the exercise and are ready to reproduce it for your own goals.

没关系。重要的是你掌握了练习的要点，并准备好根据自己的目标进行练习。

Fishbone diagrams are useful. They take more time than simple pre-mortems but are more complete. The practice of dividing the fish spine into four or six “main bones” representing categories of root causes and then dividing the main bones into many smaller ones forces you to be more exhaustive in your analysis, which in turn reduces your blind spots.

鱼骨图很有用。虽然比简单的事前分析更耗时，但更全面。将鱼骨分成四到六根“主骨”，分别代表根本原因的类别，然后再将主骨细分为许多更小的骨，这种做法迫使你进行更彻底的分析，从而减少盲点。

It is crucial that you perform this exercise in written form. The act of drawing the bones and splitting them into smaller ones helps you consider all possibilities. Moreover , it yields a drawing to show your partner, friend, or colleague to get their comments and further reduce your blind spots.

务必以书面形式完成这项练习。绘制骨骼并将其分解成更小的部分，有助于你考虑所有可能性。此外，你还可以将绘制好的图展示给你的伙伴、朋友或同事，征求他们的意见，从而进一步减少你的认知盲点。

Try the fishbone diagram exercise on your most important long-term goal. I promise it will lead to at least one major insight that will dramatically increase your chances of achieving it.

不妨试试用鱼骨图分析你最重要的长期目标。我保证它至少会让你获得一个重要的洞见，从而大大提高你实现目标的几率。

Remember: the fishbone head contains not a desired success but a hypothetical failure, for the same reason why studying failures is just as important as studying successes, if not more.

记住：鱼骨图的头部所包含的不是期望的成功，而是假设的失败，原因与研究成功一样重要，甚至更重要。

MANAGING BETS

管理赌注

F or most successful people, a defining project propelled them to stardom: Mark Zuckerberg’s Facebook , J.K . Rowling’s Harry Potter , Travis Kalanick’s Uber , etc. Most often, however, it wasn’t clear at the beginning that it would become the defining project of their life. It started as “just another project.”

对于大多数成功人士而言，一个具有里程碑意义的项目将他们推向了巅峰：马克·扎克伯格的Facebook、J·K·罗琳的《哈利·波特》系列、特拉维斯·卡兰尼克的Uber等等。然而，大多数情况下，一开始并不清楚这个项目会成为他们人生的标志性事件。它最初只是“另一个项目”。

Uber was just one of many projects Kalanick juggled in 2010. Zuckerberg started quite a few software projects before Facebook . Sure , most of those were tiny, but was it so obvious before the fact that Facebook would become so big? Probably , for at least some time, it looked like “just another project.” And J.K . Rowling wrote another novel and some minor projects before her world-famous Harry Potter book series.

Uber只是卡兰尼克在2010年同时推进的众多项目之一。扎克伯格在Facebook之前也启动了不少软件项目。当然，其中大多数规模很小，但在Facebook日后发展壮大之前，这些项目真的那么显而易见吗？或许至少在一段时间内，它们看起来都只是“另一个项目”。而J·K·罗琳在创作举世闻名的《哈利·波特》系列之前，也写过另一部小说，并参与过一些小型项目。

Most successful people start with a portfolio of bets that later converge to a single, major, winning bet. The keyword is “later.”

大多数成功人士都是从一系列投注开始，最终汇聚成一次重大的、制胜的投注。关键在于“最终”。

You do not necessarily need to work on many bets at once, but you must entertain the possibility that you might have to work on many bets before one succeeds. And so, have a strategy that considers that.

你不一定需要同时进行很多投注，但你必须考虑到可能需要多次投注才能最终赢一笔的可能性。因此，制定策略时要考虑到这一点。

Bets and Strategies

投注和策略

In this book, I use the term “bet” very liberally to refer to any activity that might or might not work: a project, a job, a romantic date, or even spending time in a new city.

在这本书中，我非常随意地使用“赌注”一词来指代任何可能成功也可能失败的活动：一个项目、一份工作、一次浪漫的约会，甚至是在一个新的城市度过一段时间。

Strategies are made of a series of bets.

策略是由一系列赌注组成的。

Even in strategies that succeed on the first try, that first try was a bet, even though it might not seem like it in hindsight.

即使是那些第一次尝试就成功的策略，第一次尝试也是一种赌博，尽管事后看来可能并非如此。

Failure to acknowledge that all strategies comprise a series of bets causes us to go all-in on a single project that might fail.

如果不能认识到所有策略都包含一系列的赌注，就会导致我们孤注一掷地投入到一个可能失败的项目中。

Instead, good strategies always (always!) consider the possibility that our first few attempts might fail- otherwise, they’re bets, not strategies.

相反，好的策略总是（总是！）考虑到我们最初几次尝试可能会失败——否则，它们就只是赌博，而不是策略。

Therefore, good strategies avoid going all-in on any single project and assume that more than one project will be required to succeed (though, obviously, the fewer tries, the better).

因此，好的策略是避免把所有资源都投入到任何一个项目中，并假设需要多个项目才能成功（当然，尝试次数越少越好）。

A tweet by David Vassallo , founder of the Small Bets community.

Small Bets 社区创始人 David Vassallo 的一条推文。

Managing your bets

管理你的投注

In Part IV , we have already seen how, when considering a single project, it is difficult to know whether to stick with it longer or abandon it for the next opportunity. However , you can identify patterns in your behavior across multiple projects by observing whether you always drop projects early or never drop them voluntarily. You can then use this information to adjust your approach in the opposite direction of your typical pattern.

在第四部分中，我们已经看到，在考虑单个项目时，很难判断是应该继续坚持还是放弃以等待下一个机会。然而，通过观察你是否总是提前放弃项目，或者是否从不主动放弃项目，你可以识别出你在多个项目中的行为模式。然后，你可以利用这些信息，调整你的方法，使其与你通常的行为模式相反。

My strategy: alternating

我的策略：交替

As an author, I constantly face the following dilemma: should I work on a new book idea, or should I promote my latest one?

作为一名作家，我经常面临这样的两难选择：我应该继续构思新的书稿，还是应该继续宣传我的最新作品？

My solution is simple: I spend half my time developing new ideas and half my time expanding on the idea that has brought me the most success so far.

我的解决方案很简单：我花一半时间开发新想法，另一半时间扩展目前为止给我带来最大成功的想法。

This framework might enable you to both consider new ideas and develop a project long enough for its fruits to blossom.

这个框架或许能让你既思考新的想法，又能让你开展一个足够长时间的项目，使其结出硕果。

Of course, do not take the “half/half” literally. It could be 70/30, 30/70, or any other split. I do not even take the split too seriously myself, as I often work for weeks on a single side of it. What matters is the general principle: alternating is better than either extreme.

当然，不要拘泥于“一半一半”的字面意思。它可以是70/30、30/70，或者任何其他比例。我自己也不太在意这个比例，因为我经常连续几周只专注于其中一方面。重要的是基本原则：交替进行比走极端要好。

Between bets

下注之间

What matters in the short term is a bet’s outcome. But in the long term, all that matters is whether the current bet makes your future bets more likely to succeed , perhaps because of the know-how you gained or the trust and relationships you built.

短期内最重要的当然是赌注的结果。但从长远来看，真正重要的是当前的赌注是否能提高你未来赌注的成功率，这或许是因为你从中获得了经验，或许是因为你建立了信任和人脉关系。

Develop the habit of designing, executing, and evaluating your bets to maximize the learnings and long-term assets you get out of them (knowledge, skills, habits, trust, relationships, etc.)

养成设计、执行和评估你的投资决策的习惯，以最大限度地从中获得经验和长期收益（知识、技能、习惯、信任、人际关系等）。

Hence, here is an important question to ponder:

因此，这里有一个值得深思的重要问题：

How many bets must you make to learn enough to make your success inevitable?

你必须下多少注才能学到足够的经验，从而确保成功？

How many speeches must you make to become a good public speaker? How many products do you need to launch to become a competent entrepreneur?

要成为一名优秀的公众演说家，你需要发表多少次演讲？要成为一名合格的企业家，你需要推出多少款产品？

How many failures do you need to experience to succeed? Ensure you have a strategy that can afford that number of attempts.

你需要经历多少次失败才能成功？确保你的策略能够承受这些尝试次数。

Hopefully, you will succeed faster, maybe even on your first try. But if you want your success to be inevitable, you must be able to afford to make many attempts and start making them as soon as possible.

希望你能更快成功，甚至可能第一次尝试就成功。但如果你想确保成功，就必须有能力进行多次尝试，并且越早开始尝试越好。

Learn from your failures

从失败中吸取教训

On the one hand, you want a strategy enabling you to make many attempts, but on the other hand, you want to succeed as quickly as possible, which requires turning your failures into the biggest steps forward possible.

一方面，你需要一个能够让你进行多次尝试的策略；但另一方面，你又想尽快取得成功，这就要求你把失败转化为前进的最大一步。

Here are a few ideas to achieve that:

以下是一些实现这一目标的建议：

  1. Bet not to win but to experiment: do test your assumptions, try a new approach, and gather information about what works and what doesn’t.
    下注不是为了赢，而是为了实验：检验你的假设，尝试新的方法，并收集有关哪些方法有效、哪些无效的信息。
  2. Use your bets to build skills, relationships, trust, and other assets that last in time. They will make your future bets more likely to succeed.
    利用你的投注来培养技能、人脉、信任和其他持久的资产。这些都会增加你未来投注成功的几率。
  3. Never risk your long-term assets. No bet of yours should, in case of failure, destroy your health, capital, relationships, and trustworthiness.
    永远不要拿你的长期资产冒险。任何赌注都不应该因为失败而损害你的健康、财富、人际关系和信誉。

Do take short-term bets, but always take them as part of your long-term strategy, so that they support it rather than impair it.

可以进行短期投资，但一定要将其作为长期战略的一部分，这样才能起到支持长期战略的作用，而不是损害长期战略。

Perfectionism and its opposite

完美主义及其反义词

Perfectionism is problematic because it limits the number of attempts you will make in your lifetime. That said, the opposite of perfectionism is also problematic. Doing things poorly will not help you progress.

完美主义的问题在于它会限制你一生中尝试的次数。话虽如此，完美主义的反面也存在问题。把事情做得糟糕并不能帮助你进步。

Find the sweet spot where you put in enough effort to allow good things to happen, but not so much effort that you reduce the number of good things you can make happen.

找到合适的平衡点，既要投入足够的努力让好事发生，又不能投入过多的努力以至于减少了好事发生的数量。

The trick to finding this sweet spot is to stop considering activities and projects one by one and instead consider them as an iterated game.

找到这个最佳平衡点的诀窍在于，不要逐个考虑活动和项目，而是将它们视为一个迭代的游戏。

To understand what I mean, take a look at the following two charts (which are obviously qualitative and not quantitative).

为了理解我的意思，请看以下两张图表（显然是定性的，而不是定量的）。

The chart above refers to a single project. By itself, it’s not very actionable. However , consider the second chart, which takes into account that the less time you spend on a single project, the more you can undertake.

上面的图表指的是单个项目。单凭它本身，指导意义不大。但是，请参考第二个图表，该图表考虑到，你在单个项目上花费的时间越少，你就能开展更多的工作。

These two charts illustrate a counterintuitive principle. To maximize a project’s chances of success, dedicate as much effort as possible to it. However , to maximize your chances of success, work on as many projects as possible, dedicating enough effort to each to achieve a sufficient level of quality to give them a proper chance to succeed.

这两张图表阐明了一个反直觉的原则。为了最大限度地提高项目的成功率，应该尽可能多地投入精力。然而，为了最大限度地提高你个人的成功率，应该尽可能多地参与项目，并在每个项目上投入足够的精力，以达到足够的质量水平，从而使它们有充分的机会获得成功。

Of course, there is no precise formula for determining how much time and effort to invest in a project. However , you should structure your projects to gain insight as quickly as possible into whether that will be the project that will yield the results you desire.

当然，并没有一个精确的公式来决定在一个项目上应该投入多少时间和精力。但是，你应该合理规划项目，以便尽快了解该项目是否能够带来你想要的结果。

This often involves narrowing the scope of the project to assess as early as possible the compatibility between your skills and the demand for your project (e.g., whether your skills and the project align with market needs, or whether your contributions to a relationship meet your partner’s needs and vice versa).

这通常涉及缩小项目范围，以便尽早评估您的技能与项目需求之间的兼容性（例如，您的技能和项目是否符合市场需求，或者您对合作关系的贡献是否满足合作伙伴的需求，反之亦然）。

How many bets do you need?

你需要下注多少次？

While some entrepreneurs succeed with their first product, many others need to iterate on their product a few times, or even dozens of times. And while some entrepreneurs succeed with their first startup, others find success with their second, third, fifth, or tenth.

有些创业者凭借第一款产品就获得了成功，但许多其他创业者需要对产品进行几次甚至几十次的迭代。同样，有些创业者在第一次创业就取得了成功，而另一些创业者则在第二次、第三次、第五次甚至第十次创业后才获得成功。

The same applies to authors, people dating, and so on.

这同样适用于作家、恋爱中的人等等。

Of course, you will hopefully succeed with your first or second bet. But more likely, you will succeed with your third or thirtieth.

当然，你第一次或第二次下注或许会成功。但更有可能的是，你会在第三次甚至第三十次下注时才成功。

Your strategy must allow you to take many bets if needed.

你的策略必须允许你在必要时进行多次投注。

This requires you to pay attention to two considerations:

这需要你注意以下两点：

  1. Play each bet with enough urgency to still have time to play many others, but without rushing to the point that you cannot work on it well enough to give it a chance to succeed.
    对待每一笔投注都要足够紧迫，这样你还有时间去玩其他很多注，但不要操之过急，以至于无法好好对待每一笔投注，从而错失成功的良机。
  2. Be reasonably frugal with your time, money, trust, and other assets, so you retain enough to afford many other bets.
    在时间、金钱、信任和其他资产方面要合理节俭，这样你才能留有足够的资金去进行许多其他的尝试。

Too many people fail because they excessively deplete their financial capital, social capital, health, or available time, preventing them from taking further bets.

太多人失败是因为他们过度消耗了自己的财力、社会资本、健康或可用时间，从而无法再进行进一步的尝试。

Be more frugal and risk-conservative. Reliably winning long-term games requires being able to play many times.

要更加节俭，更加保守。要想在长期游戏中持续获胜，就需要多次参与。

Chapter summary

章节概要

Most long-term strategies require you to take enough bets that might not work out, to increase the chance that at least one will bring you the success you want.

大多数长期策略都需要你进行足够多的可能不会成功的尝试，以增加至少一次成功的机会。

For those strategies to work reproducibly for you , you must ensure you can take many calculated risks.

要想让这些策略能够持续有效地为你带来益处，你必须确保自己能够承担许多经过深思熟虑的风险。

This requires you not to spend too much time and too many resources on each bet, and to take those bets in such a way that their failure does not preclude your ability to take further bets.

这就要求你不要在每笔投注上花费太多时间和资源，并且要以这样的方式进行投注：即使投注失败，也不会妨碍你进行进一步的投注。

MIXED FEELINGS

五味杂陈

“Your brain knows what to do only when it has a clear association about what it needs to avoid and what it needs to move toward.

For money, we often send mixed signals […], and when you give your brain mixed messages, you’re going to get mixed results. ”

TONY ROBBINS

“只有当大脑清楚地知道应该避免什么、应该追求什么时，它才能知道该怎么做。在金钱方面，我们常常发出矛盾的信号[……]，而当你给大脑传递矛盾的信息时，你就会得到矛盾的结果。”——托尼·罗宾斯

T here are many reasons why you might procrastinate on a task once. But if you procrastinate on the same task two or more times, it’s usually a sign that you are uncomfortable with it.

你拖延一次任务的原因可能有很多。但如果你拖延同一项任务两次或两次以上，这通常表明你对这项任务感到不自在。

Unless you address this discomfort, you will procrastinate on the task indefinitely – or at least until it’s too late.

除非你解决这种不适感，否则你会无限期地拖延这项任务——或者至少会拖延到为时已晚。

There are two main reasons why a task might feel uncomfortable, and the rest of this chapter addresses them:

导致人们感到不适的任务主要有两个原因，本章余下部分将逐一探讨：

  1. You associate mixed values or emotions with an action or outcome.
    你将复杂的价值观或情感与某个行为或结果联系起来。
  2. You aren’t convinced that completing the task is worth the effort.
    你并不确信完成这项任务值得付出努力。

Mixed values

混合值

Here are a few examples of how mixed values associated with an action or outcome can prevent action:

以下是一些例子，说明与某一行为或结果相关的混合价值观如何阻碍该行为的发生：

  • You want to get rich, but also think wealthy people are generally evil or unhappy.
    你想变得富有，但又认为有钱人通常都很邪恶或不快乐。
  • You want to sell your product or service, but also believe that selling means pestering people.
    你想推销你的产品或服务，但你也认为推销意味着纠缠别人。
  • You want to dress attractively, but also associate that with morally loose people.
    你想穿得漂亮，但又会将这种打扮与道德败坏的人联系起来。
  • You want to have sex, but also associate it with sin or STDs .
    你想发生性行为，但又会把它与罪恶或性传播疾病联系起来。
  • You want to ask a question, but whenever you did in the past, your former boss would get angry or make a fool out of you.
    你想问个问题，但过去每当你这样做时，你的前老板都会生气或者让你出丑。

In all the cases above, mixed values or mixed emotions prevent you from taking action or doing it with the conviction required to succeed.

在上述所有情况下，价值观或情绪的冲突都会妨碍你采取行动，或者妨碍你以成功所需的信念去行动。

Ask yourself if you have mixed feelings or emotions associated with the actions you must take to succeed.

问问自己，对于为了成功必须采取的行动，你是否感到五味杂陈或情绪复杂。

If so, do not ignore this limitation. It might be an emotional limitation, but it’s a limitation nevertheless, and it will keep limiting you until you address it.

如果是这样，请不要忽视这种局限。它或许是一种情感上的局限，但它终究是一种局限，而且如果你不解决它，它就会一直限制着你。

Correcting mixed values or emotions

纠正混淆的价值观或情绪

I do not know of a single solution that always works, but here are two options that often work relatively well:

我不知道有什么万能的解决方案，但以下两种方法通常效果比较好：

  1. Spend time with virtuous people who already do what you need to do. For example, if you have mixed feelings about selling, spend time with salespeople who genuinely help people. Or , if you have mixed feelings about acquiring wealth, spend time with wealthy people who are also good. Even a one-hour conversation might be enough to convince you that it is possible to achieve success without compromising your values.
    多花时间与品德高尚、并且已经做到你所需要做的事情的人相处。例如，如果你对销售感到矛盾，那就多和那些真心实意帮助他人的销售人员交流。或者，如果你对获取财富感到矛盾，那就多和那些既富有又品德高尚的人交流。哪怕只是短短一小时的谈话，也可能足以让你相信，在不违背自身价值观的前提下，获得成功是完全可能的。
  2. Find a way to do what you must do in the easiest and most pleasurable way possible. If you do not like building professional relationships, do not try to attend large conferences yet; that might be too much. Instead , look for a smaller, easier step, such as inviting your favorite senior colleague for coffee. If that goes well, you will start building positive emotional associations, which will chip away at the negative ones you might have had.
    想办法以最轻松、最愉悦的方式完成你必须做的事情。如果你不喜欢建立职业关系，那就暂时不要尝试参加大型会议；那可能压力太大。不妨从更小、更容易的步骤入手，比如邀请你最喜欢的资深同事喝咖啡。如果一切顺利，你就能开始建立积极的情感联系，从而逐渐消除你可能存在的负面情绪。

Whenever you feel paralyzed, take a step back and look for a smaller step forward, prioritizing momentum over effectiveness. ( Of course, after you achieve momentum, you will want to focus on effectiveness, but until then, prioritize getting started and building positive emotional associations with what you are uncomfortable with.)

每当你感到束手无策时，不妨退后一步，寻找更小的前进方向，优先考虑势头而非效率。（当然，当你获得势头后，你自然会想要关注效率，但在此之前，优先考虑的是迈出第一步，并建立与你感到不适的事物之间的积极情感联系。）

What if it’s not worth it?

如果根本不值得呢？

Another common reason for procrastination is that you are not convinced that a given action is worth the time and effort.

拖延的另一个常见原因是，你并不确信某项行动值得花费时间和精力。

Or, more subtly, you might believe it is worth the time and effort in general, but not for you.

或者，更委婉地说，你可能认为它总体上值得投入时间和精力，但并不适合你。

For example, someone who can't bring themselves to exercise regularly might believe that if they did, they would get fitter. And they might believe that, for most people, it would be worth it. But they might not be convinced that for them, a life where they exercise and get fit would be better than a life where they don’t exercise and don’t get fit. Maybe they really like the free time they get from not exercising, or they really dislike going to the gym!

例如，有些人无法坚持规律运动，他们可能认为如果坚持锻炼，身体就会更健康。他们也可能认为，对大多数人来说，锻炼是值得的。但他们可能并不确信，对他们而言，锻炼并拥有健康体魄的生活会比不锻炼、不拥有健康体魄的生活更好。也许他们真的很享受不锻炼带来的自由时间，或者他们真的很讨厌去健身房！

It is not a logical evaluation but an emotional one. Therefore , logical arguments do not influence it.

这并非逻辑判断，而是情感判断。因此，逻辑论证对其无效。

Using logic to convince yourself will only convince the non-emotional part of your brain (which is probably already convinced). Instead , use experiences to convince the emotional part of your brain.

用逻辑说服自己只能说服你大脑中不带情感的部分（而这部分可能早已被说服）。相反，应该用经验来说服你大脑中感性的部分。

Do what the previous page suggested: spend time with people who regularly benefit from what you're not convinced of doing and/or figure out a smaller step forward, prioritizing actionability over effectiveness.

按照上一页的建议去做：花时间与那些经常从你不确定要做的事情中受益的人在一起，和/或想出一个更小的前进步骤，优先考虑可操作性而不是有效性。

COMMITTING TO THE LONG TERM

着眼长远

T he previous chapter, “ Mixed Feelings ,” introduced the importance of commitment.

上一章“复杂的情感”介绍了承诺的重要性。

However, just as a previous chapter introduced the difference between High - Quality Success and Low - Quality Success , there is also such a thing as High - Quality Commitment and Low - Quality Commitment .

然而，正如前一章介绍了高质量成功和低质量成功之间的区别一样，也存在高质量承诺和低质量承诺。

Low- Quality Commitment occurs when someone declares a long-term time horizon but focuses their actions mostly on the short term. For example, managers who say they have a long-term time horizon but spend most of their time putting out fires and none training their subordinates, or investors who say they have a long-term time horizon but spend most of their time finding short-term bets.

低质量承诺指的是某人声称自己着眼于长期目标，但实际行动却主要集中在短期利益上。例如，有些管理者声称自己着眼于长期目标，但却把大部分时间花在救火上，而忽略了对下属的培训；又如，有些投资者声称自己着眼于长期目标，但却把大部分时间花在寻找短期投资机会上。

Conversely, High - Quality Commitment occurs when someone declares a long-term time horizon and their actions match this preference. For example, managers who spend most of their time training their subordinates and building long-term capabilities, or investors who spend most of their time finding opportunities with the potential for long-term growth and building long-term relationships.

相反，高质量承诺是指某人明确了长期目标，并且其行动也与此相符。例如，管理者将大部分时间用于培训下属和构建长期能力，或者投资者将大部分时间用于寻找具有长期增长潜力的投资机会和建立长期合作关系。

In short, you cannot judge your commitment by your words, goals, or even your strategy. You can only judge it by the choices you make and the actions you take.

简而言之，你不能仅凭言辞、目标甚至策略来判断你的决心，只能通过你的选择和行动来判断。

What do your actions say about your commitment? Is it low or high quality?

你的行为体现了你的投入程度吗？是低质量的还是高质量的？

It’s a bad sign whenever you start worrying about ‘the next quarter’ because it proves you don’t have enough conviction to not even care about ‘the next quarter.’”

IAN CASSELL

当你开始担心“下一个季度”时，这是一个不好的迹象，因为它证明你没有足够的信念去完全不在乎“下一个季度”。——伊恩·卡塞尔

The quote not only provides an example of evaluating your commitment by your actions but also shows that unless you took long-term actions during the previous months, focusing on the long term this month will be hard, if not impossible.

这段引言不仅举例说明了如何通过行动来评估你的承诺，而且还表明，除非你在前几个月采取了长期行动，否则本月专注于长期目标将非常困难，甚至是不可能的。

It’s a vicious circle. And like all vicious circles, the key to stopping it is to take the action that breaks it, even when there’s no time or energy to take it. For example, train your people even if you feel like you don’t have the time. That will lead to fewer fires to put out in the future and, therefore, more time for you to take longer-term actions.

这是一个恶性循环。而所有恶性循环的终结之道，在于打破它，即便你没有时间或精力去行动。例如，即使你觉得没时间，也要培训你的员工。这样一来，未来需要处理的突发事件就会减少，从而让你有更多时间去制定更长远的计划。

COMMITTING TO THE LONG TERM WHILE RETAINING FLEXIBILITY

着眼长远，同时保持灵活性

I f you dislike long-term commitments, I have some good news: playing the long game does not necessarily mean making long-term commitments. For example, being nice to customers, getting to know them, creating goodwill, and building trust are all actions that only make sense if you are committed to the long term but are not long-term commitments that reduce your flexibility.

如果你不喜欢长期承诺，我有个好消息：着眼长远并不一定意味着要做出长期承诺。例如，善待客户、了解客户、建立良好关系和赢得信任，这些行为只有在你致力于长期发展的情况下才有意义，但它们本身并不是会降低你灵活性的长期承诺。

Of course, do not take actions that are disproportionately costly in absolute terms. For example, do not buy the highest-tier professional gear for your first month of practicing a new sport. Doing so would not only be very inefficient but also constitute a major loss if you were to change your mind and decide to switch to another sport.

当然，不要采取绝对成本过高的行动。例如，不要在练习一项新运动的第一个月就购买最顶级的专业装备。这样做不仅效率低下，而且如果你改变主意想改练其他运动，还会造成重大损失。

Instead, do engage in habits that only make sense with a longer time horizon: ask questions, learn skills, build trust and relationships, etc.

相反，要培养一些只有在更长远的时间跨度内才有意义的习惯：提出问题、学习技能、建立信任和人际关系等等。

Committing to the long term means rejecting the shortcuts that would make sense if you were there for the short term and adopting the habits that would make sense only if you were there for the long term.

着眼长远意味着拒绝那些只顾短期利益的捷径，并养成那些只有着眼长远才能养成的习惯。

LEARNING & ADAPTATION

学习与适应

P laying the long game requires a lot of learning and adapting. You do not yet know everything you need to know to succeed, but if you gather the missing knowledge along the way, you will become the kind of person who achieves the success you seek.

着眼长远需要大量的学习和适应。你现在可能还没有掌握成功所需的一切知识，但如果你在前进的道路上不断积累缺失的知识，你终将成为能够实现你所追求的成功的那种人。

Moreover, your current plan is probably not complete or correct enough to get you where you want to be, but if you adapt it along the way, keeping yourself on a trajectory toward success, you will almost inevitably arrive there.

此外，你目前的计划可能不够完善或正确，无法带你到达你想去的地方，但如果你在前进的过程中不断调整，保持朝着成功的方向发展，你几乎必然会到达那里。

This chapter contains practical tips to help you learn and adapt. But remember these two general principles:

本章包含一些实用的学习和适应技巧。但请记住以下两个基本原则：

  1. Learning and adaptation should be built into your strategy. Any strategy that does not include enough time and margin of error to learn and adapt along the way is not a serious strategy.
    学习和适应应该融入你的战略之中。任何没有预留足够时间和容错空间来学习和调整的战略都算不上真正的战略。
  2. Play iterated games so they produce learning and adaptation. Structure your tasks and interactions so that you learn from them and make future ones more effective.
    反复进行游戏，以促进学习和适应。合理安排任务和互动，以便从中吸取经验教训，使未来的游戏更加高效。

Metapractice

元实践

Why do some people develop a skill very quickly at first but then stop making meaningful progress?

为什么有些人一开始能很快掌握一项技能，但之后却停滞不前，无法取得实质性的进步？

Sometimes, the reason is that they have stopped practicing the skill. They only use it to get things done, but they no longer focus on improving.⁠ i

有时，原因是他们停止了练习这项技能。他们只是用它来完成任务，但不再专注于提升技能。

Another reason is that when they do practice, they just focus on improving the skill.

另一个原因是，当他们练习时，他们只专注于提高技能。

Conversely, when long-term players practice, they focus on improving both their skill and their practice.

相反，长期从事足球运动的球员在训练时，会专注于提高自己的技能和训练水平。

They ask themselves, “ Am I learning enough from practice? If not, how can I tweak my practice to learn more from it? Should I take notes? Should I record my practice? Should I get a mentor or a trainer? Should I set objectives at the beginning of the practice?”

他们会问自己：“我从练习中学到的东西足够吗？如果没有，我该如何调整练习方式才能学到更多？我应该记笔记吗？我应该录下练习过程吗？我应该找个导师或教练吗？我应该在练习开始时设定目标吗？”

Do not just practice your skills; also practice your practice.

不要只练习你的技能；还要练习你的练习方法。

I call this Metapractice .

我称之为元实践。

Surrender

投降

“We do not choose our gifts. They choose us. A mark of maturity is surrendering to the person you actually are instead of the one you wish you were. Most people never get such clarity, and they’re stunted for life. […] Surrender to your gifts.”

DAVID PERELL

“我们无法选择自己的天赋，而是天赋选择了我们。成熟的标志是接受真实的自己，而不是你希望成为的自己。大多数人从未获得这种觉悟，他们的人生也因此受阻。[…] 接受你的天赋吧。”——大卫·佩雷尔

First of all, let me clarify that “surrendering to who you are” does not mean you won’t have to learn and grow. To achieve your goals, you will have to improve yourself, and believing otherwise is delusional.

首先，我要澄清一点，“接受真实的自己”并不意味着你不需要学习和成长。为了实现你的目标，你必须不断提升自己，否则就是自欺欺人。

Instead, “surrendering to who you are” means accepting the ways in which who you are can help you achieve your goals, even if those ways aren’t exactly how you imagined you’d attain happiness and fulfillment.

相反，“臣服于真实的自己”意味着接受真实的自己能够帮助你实现目标的方式，即使这些方式与你想象中获得幸福和满足的方式并不完全相同。

Here are two underrated ways in which people fail:

以下是人们失败的两种常被低估的方式：

  1. Refusing to surrender to their gifts. Some people do not merely want to succeed; they want to succeed in a very specific way . So , they unnecessarily restrict their options or stack the odds against themselves. I often say that you cannot choose the cards you are dealt, but you can choose which game to play with them.
    有些人不愿接受自己的天赋。他们不仅想要成功，还想以某种特定的方式成功。因此，他们会不必要地限制自己的选择，或者让自己陷入不利的境地。我常说，你无法选择手中的牌，但你可以选择用它们玩什么游戏。
  2. Refusing to learn the lessons the world tries to teach them. Chronic frustration is a common symptom of stubbornness.
    拒绝吸取世界试图教会他们的教训。长期的挫败感是固执的常见表现。

The effort trap

努力陷阱

A common bottleneck to learning is what I call the effort trap: the belief that through sheer effort, we can overcome that thing we know we need to learn but don’t want to.

学习中常见的一个瓶颈是我称之为“努力陷阱”的东西：人们认为，通过单纯的努力，我们可以克服我们明知需要学习但却不想学习的东西。

This belief is problematic for three reasons:

这种观点存在三个问题：

  1. Often, effort is not enough on its own. You either learn the lesson you do not want to learn, or you will keep failing. ( Paraphrasing Paulo Coelho : failure is life's way of teaching you a lesson you do not want to learn.)
    很多时候，光靠努力是不够的。你要么会吸取你不想吸取的教训，要么就会一直失败。（套用保罗·科埃略的话：失败是生活教你不想吸取的教训的方式。）
  2. At the beginning of your career, you can overcome problems caused by the lessons you do not want to learn with a bit of effort. However , as you proceed through life, overcoming problems through effort alone requires more and more effort, and you will have less and less time to do so.
    在职业生涯初期，你或许可以通过一些努力克服因不愿吸取教训而带来的问题。然而，随着人生阅历的增长，仅靠努力解决问题所需的精力会越来越大，而你可用于解决问题的时间也会越来越少。
  3. Even if effort alone could suffice as an alternative to learning a lesson we do not want to learn, the required effort is so large that it comes with massive opportunity costs. You will proceed so slowly that you will not be able to undertake enough bets or projects to make your success inevitable.
    即使单凭努力就能避免吸取我们不愿吸取的教训，但所需的努力如此巨大，以至于会带来巨大的机会成本。你的进展会如此缓慢，以至于你无法进行足够多的尝试或项目来确保成功。

Notice when you use effort to overcompensate for a lesson you don’t want to learn. Then , surrender to that lesson. Or to the consequences of not learning it.

注意你何时会用过度的努力来弥补你不想吸取的教训。然后，要么接受这个教训，要么接受不吸取教训的后果。

i This is often the symptom of a shortened time horizon and/or lost faith in the idea that improving one’s skill will meaningfully improve their quality of life. For example, some people do not exercise because they do not believe they can get fitter. But many more do not exercise because they do not believe that getting fitter would improve their life enough to offset the time and effort required to workout. The bottleneck isn’t whether practicing will improve their skills but whether the improvement from practice will improve their quality of life.

这通常是由于人们的目光短浅，或者对提升技能能够切实改善生活质量这一理念失去信心的表现。例如，有些人不锻炼是因为他们不相信自己能变得更健康。但更多的人不锻炼是因为他们不相信健康带来的改善足以抵消锻炼所需的时间和精力。问题的关键不在于练习能否提升技能，而在于练习带来的技能提升能否改善生活质量。

48

DON’T BE TOO SMART

别太聪明

“90% of success can be boiled down to consistently doing the obvious thing for an uncommonly long period of time without convincing yourself that you’re smarter than you are.”

SHANE PARRISH

“90%的成功可以归结为：在一段异常长的时间里，始终如一地做显而易见的事情，并且不要自欺欺人地认为自己比实际更聪明。”——肖恩·帕里什
# ↩

M any people succeed thanks to some kind of innovation that gives them an edge.

许多人之所以能够成功，是因为某种创新让他们拥有了竞争优势。

But plenty more talented people have failed to achieve success because they have spent too much time trying to reinvent the wheel.

但还有很多更有才华的人因为花了太多时间试图重新发明轮子而未能取得成功。

I’m not saying you shouldn’t innovate – if you can, great!

我不是说你不应该创新——如果你能创新，那就太好了！

However, innovation has opportunity costs and introduces risks.

然而，创新也存在机会成本和风险。

Therefore, innovate only as little as necessary and leverage what already exists as much as possible.

因此，创新应尽量少做，并尽可能利用现有资源。

Do not reinvent the wheel

不要重复发明轮子

I’m confident in your ability to reinvent the wheel. Still , the question is not whether you are capable, but whether it’s worth it.

我相信你有能力重新发明轮子。但是，问题不在于你是否有能力，而在于这样做是否值得。

And in particular, the question is not whether the new wheel is better than the old one, but whether it is so much better that it was worth the time and effort to develop it.

尤其值得关注的是，新轮子是否比旧轮子好，而新轮子是否好到值得花费时间和精力去开发。

Many innovations pass the first test but not the second one.

许多创新都能通过第一道考验，但过不了第二道考验。

Risk

风险

Reinventing the wheel comes with another undesirable property: whatever you invent will be less reliable than the tried-and-tested solution.

重新发明轮子还有另一个不好的方面：你发明的任何东西都不如经过实践检验的解决方案可靠。

Obviously. It’s called “tried and tested” for a reason.

当然。它之所以被称为“久经考验”，是有原因的。

Again, this doesn’t mean that you should not innovate. Instead , it means you probably lack the time to deal with the effort, testing, and maintenance required by more than one or two innovations.

再次强调，这并不意味着你不应该创新。而是意味着你可能缺乏时间来处理一项或两项以上创新所需的精力、测试和维护工作。

So, be extremely deliberate and conservative with how much you innovate, and do not reinvent more than one or two wheels.

因此，在创新方面要格外谨慎保守，不要重复发明超过一两个轮子的东西。

The pleasure of innovation

创新的乐趣

Many of us, myself included, love innovation and think of ourselves as artisans or craftspeople directly involved in all steps of our product's creation.

包括我在内的许多人都热爱创新，并将自己视为工匠或手艺人，直接参与产品创造的各个环节。

If our definition of success involves being a craftsperson, that is perfectly fine. However , if it involves major financial success or impact at scale, we might have to evolve from artisans to entrepreneurs and/or scale our products or services. This almost necessarily means using as many standard components as possible, except for the one or two innovations that are the biggest differentiators.

如果我们对成功的定义是成为一名匠人，那当然没问题。但如果成功意味着巨大的经济成功或大规模的影响，我们或许需要从匠人转型为企业家，或者扩大产品或服务的规模。这几乎必然意味着尽可能多地使用标准化组件，只保留一两项最具差异化的创新。

A hobby

爱好

For some of us, innovation is what we are most passionate about and proud of in our work.

对我们中的一些人来说，创新是我们工作中最为热衷和引以为豪的部分。

However, we should treat unnecessary innovations as a hobby. If we want to do it outside our “work hours,” great. But we should never work on over-innovation instead of working on the core project. Nor should we let over-innovation delay our journey toward success.

然而，我们应该把不必要的创新当作一种爱好。如果想在“工作时间”之外进行创新，那当然很好。但我们绝不应该为了过度创新而耽误核心项目。我们也不应该让过度创新阻碍我们走向成功。

COMMON GOALS AND HOW TO MAKE THEM MORE REPRODUCIBLE

共同目标及其可复制性

I n this chapter, I examine a few common goals and share some thoughts on how I approach them (or would approach them) to make them more reproducible.

在本章中，我将探讨一些常见的目标，并分享一些关于我如何（或将如何）实现这些目标的想法，以使它们更具可复制性。

The discussion of each goal is not meant to be exhaustive – otherwise, each goal would require a standalone book! Instead , the objective of this exercise is simply to provide you, the reader, with some examples of how the concepts illustrated in this book could be applied to real-life goals.

对每个目标的讨论并非旨在面面俱到——否则，每个目标都需要单独成书！相反，本练习的目的仅仅是为读者提供一些例子，说明本书阐述的概念如何应用于现实生活中的目标。

If there’s any specific goal you would like me to write about, let me know by emailing me at Luca @ Luca - Dellanna.com

如果您有任何希望我撰写的具体目标，请发送电子邮件至 Luca@Luca-Dellanna.com 告诉我。

Goal #1: A brilliant career

目标一：辉煌的职业生涯

First of all, I would be more specific about what this goal entails: is it the earnings potential, professional fulfillment, or prestige?

首先，我想更具体地说明一下这个目标包含什么：是收入潜力、职业成就感还是声望？

Then, I would ask myself what careers are Pareto Frontier optimal for what I seek. For example, if I didn’t care about prestige but cared a lot about earnings, I would ask myself, what careers are not prestigious but pay well?

然后，我会问自己，哪些职业最符合我的帕累托前沿目标。例如，如果我不在乎声望，但非常在意收入，我会问自己，哪些职业虽然不显赫但收入丰厚？

I would also consider any values or constraints of mine. For example, if I cared about spending quality time with my family, I would ask myself, “ What careers pay well but allow me to be home early every evening?” This might seem banal, but many people miss this step and regret it later.

我还会考虑自身的价值观和限制。例如，如果我重视与家人共度美好时光，我会问自己：“哪些工作既收入丰厚，又能让我每天晚上早点回家？”这看似微不足道，但很多人却忽略了这一步，事后后悔不已。

Once I have defined my preferred career, I would apply some of the learnings from the “ Derisk , derisk, derisk” chapters. I would ask myself, what are the common reasons why people in this career fail or drop out, and what can I do to prevent them?

一旦我确定了自己理想的职业，我就会运用“降低风险，降低风险，降低风险”章节中的一些经验。我会问自己，从事这个职业的人失败或退出的常见原因是什么？我能做些什么来避免这些情况发生？

I would also do a pre-mortem: let’s imagine I follow my preferred career but fail to progress. What could have happened, and what can I do about it now? Drawing a fishbone diagram might also help.

我还会进行事前分析：假设我从事自己喜欢的职业，但却未能取得进步。可能是什么原因导致的？我现在又能做些什么？绘制鱼骨图或许会有帮助。

Finally, I would consider goals and risks outside of my career. For example, in what ways might I end up unhappy even if I achieve my professional goals?

最后，我会考虑职业之外的目标和风险。例如，即使我实现了职业目标，我最终可能会在哪些方面感到不快乐？

# ↩

Goal #2: Getting a promotion

目标二：获得晋升

I know: this is a sub-goal of the previous page’s objective. But this is the beauty of the derisk, derisk, derisk approach: just like a fractal, you can apply it at multiple levels to improve your chances of success at each level.

我知道，这只是上一页目标的子目标。但这正是“降低风险、降低风险、再降低风险”方法的妙处所在：就像分形一样，你可以将其应用于多个层面，从而提高每个层面的成功率。

First, it’s important to prevent your career from becoming a race to the bottom. Therefore , begin by determining your boundaries and only afterward draft a plan to get a promotion while remaining within those boundaries.

首先，要避免职业生涯陷入恶性竞争。因此，首先要明确自己的底线，然后再制定晋升计划，并确保晋升始终在这些底线之内。

Another critical consideration is that while there are many ways to get a promotion, only some also increase your chances of getting the following promotion. These are the approaches that avoid taking shortcuts and instead rely on building skills, trust, and a solid reputation.

另一个关键因素是，虽然晋升途径有很多，但只有少数途径能提高你下次晋升的几率。这些途径不走捷径，而是依靠技能积累、信任建立和良好声誉。

Then, as usual, I would derisk, derisk, derisk by asking myself, what are the possible reasons that talented and determined people fail to achieve a promotion? Common answers include focusing on demonstrating one’s competence in their current job while forgetting to also demonstrate competence in their next one, failing to build the right relationships and a reputation of reliability and proactiveness, or working for a boss or company that isn’t growing or supportive of their employees’ growth.

然后，像往常一样，我会不断降低风险，反复问自己：那些才华横溢、意志坚定的人为何无法获得晋升？常见的答案包括：只专注于展现自己在当前工作中的能力，却忽略了在下一份工作中展现同样的能力；未能建立良好的人际关系，也未能树立可靠和积极主动的声誉；或者为一家自身发展停滞不前、不支持员工成长的上司或公司工作。

Finally, I would regularly ask myself, “ What does my trajectory look like? And is it leading me where I want to be, fast enough and with enough certainty? If not, what changes should I make?”

最后，我会经常问自己：“我的发展轨迹是什么样的？它是否能以足够快的速度和足够的确定性将我带到我想去的地方？如果不是，我应该做出哪些改变？”

# ↩

Goal #3: Launching a successful product

目标三：成功推出产品

No matter how talented and hard-working you are, you cannot guarantee that your first product will be successful. It might take a few attempts, or even several – both for you to find something others want, for you to develop the skills to build it, and for you to grow your audience and reputation so that you can distribute it to those who would buy it.

无论你多么才华横溢、勤奋努力，都无法保证你的第一个产品一定会成功。你可能需要尝试几次，甚至好几次——既要找到人们想要的东西，也要培养开发产品的技能，还要积累受众群体和口碑，才能将产品推广给潜在买家。

Hence, your primary focus should be on launching as many products as required to achieve success. This requires, among other things, keeping your expenses low (so that you can afford to stay in this career longer and thus launch more products) and iterating on them quickly enough.

因此，你的首要任务应该是推出足够多的产品以取得成功。这需要你做到很多方面，包括控制成本（这样你才能在这个行业待得更久，从而推出更多产品）以及快速迭代产品。

That said, there are entrepreneurs who launch product after product yet fail to succeed. To prevent this, your secondary focus should be on ensuring that each product you launch builds long-term assets-for example, your skills, reputation, audience, or relationships.

话虽如此，也有些创业者不断推出产品却依然失败。为了避免这种情况，你的另一个重点应该是确保你推出的每个产品都能为你积累长期资产——例如，你的技能、声誉、受众或人脉关系。

No plan is perfect, so you should also constantly review your execution. Are you progressing quickly enough? Are you growing your skills, audience, and reputation?

没有完美的计划，所以你也应该不断审视自己的执行情况。你的进展速度够快吗？你的技能、受众和声誉是否在增长？

Finally, as usual, derisk, derisk, derisk. Study how others with a similar objective to yours have failed. Learn from their mistakes before they become your own.

最后，一如既往，降低风险，降低风险，降低风险。研究那些与你目标相似的人是如何失败的。在重蹈覆辙之前，从他们的错误中吸取教训。

# ↩

Goal #4: A happy retirement

目标四：幸福退休

Given that this is a very broad objective, I would begin by defining it more precisely. What does a happy retirement mean to you?

鉴于这是一个非常宽泛的目标，我建议先对其进行更精确的定义。对您而言，幸福的退休生活意味着什么？

For example, let’s say it means being healthy, having a loving family, and being financially comfortable. We should plan for each of these three sub-objectives separately, yet continuously check that our plan to achieve one won’t negatively impact the others.

例如，假设它指的是拥有健康的身体、一个充满爱的家庭和经济上的富足。我们应该分别制定这三个子目标的计划，但同时也要不断检查，确保实现其中一个目标的计划不会对其他目标产生负面影响。

Let’s work on the sub-objective of being healthy, and let’s reverse-engineer it. What does being healthy at 80 mean to you? And what does that translate to in the present? For example, let’s say that, for you, being healthy at 80 means being able to climb a flight of stairs in one go. Given the well-known phenomenon of sarcopenia – the loss of muscle mass and strength that occurs as we age – how many flights of stairs should you be able to climb in one go now, at your current age? According to Dr . Peter Attia’s book Outlive , which inspired this example, to be able to comfortably climb stairs when you are 75, you need to be in the top 5% of people by cardiovascular fitness. Are you there yet? And if not, what should you start doing to get there as soon as possible?

让我们来探讨“健康”这个子目标，并反向推演一下。对你而言，80岁时的健康意味着什么？这在当下又意味着什么？例如，假设对你来说，80岁时的健康意味着能够一口气爬上一层楼梯。考虑到众所周知的肌肉减少症——随着年龄增长而出现的肌肉量和力量的下降——以你目前的年龄，你现在应该能够一口气爬多少层楼梯？根据彼得·阿提亚博士的著作《长寿》（Outlive，本书启发了我们举这个例子），要想在75岁时能够轻松爬楼梯，你的心肺功能需要达到前5%。你现在达到这个标准了吗？如果没有，你应该从现在开始做些什么才能尽快达到这个标准呢？

Remember: the power of derisking and, in general, the contents of this book are all about detecting problems before they are painful and while you still have time to address them. I always say that problems grow to the size they need to be acknowledged. If you want an easy life with only small problems, strive to acknowledge them as early as possible.

记住：降低风险的力量，以及本书的整体内容，都在于如何在问题变得棘手之前发现它们，并在你还有时间解决它们的时候及时应对。我常说，问题会发展到需要被重视的程度。如果你想要轻松的生活，只有一些小问题，那就努力尽早发现并解决它们。

Goal #5: Investing

目标五：投资

If investing were my core occupation, here are a few considerations I would make.

如果投资是我的核心职业，我会考虑以下几点。

First of all, I would clarify my time horizon – is it 1 year, 10 years, or 30 years? Not only should this be a fundamental factor in deciding my investing strategy, but I should also avoid comparing myself to anyone with a shorter time horizon; doing so might mislead me into taking a level of risk that’s optimal for them but suboptimal for me.

首先，我要明确我的投资期限——是1年、10年还是30年？这不仅应该是我制定投资策略的一个基本因素，而且我还应该避免与投资期限较短的人进行比较；这样做可能会误导我，让我承担对他们来说是最佳但对我来说并非最佳的风险水平。

Secondly, I would figure out what long-term assets I must build to succeed. Financial capital, obviously, but what else? Skills ? Access to investing opportunities? Relationships ?

其次，我会思考为了成功，我必须积累哪些长期资产。当然，资金是必不可少的，但还有什么呢？技能？投资机会？人脉关系？

Thirdly, I would derisk, derisk, derisk by asking myself how other investors failed. I would be careful to consider both bad investing decisions and bad non-investing decisions – the latter including both work-related non-investing decisions, such as hiring a bad advisor, and non-work-related decisions, such as neglecting their health.

第三，我会通过反复思考其他投资者失败的原因来降低风险。我会仔细考虑糟糕的投资决策和非投资决策——后者包括与工作相关的非投资决策，例如聘请了不称职的顾问，以及与工作无关的决策，例如忽视自身健康。

Finally, I would set myself periodic reminders to evaluate my trajectory, not just based on my recent outcomes but also on a broader evaluation of the long-term assets I built, the risks I took, and the sacrifices I made. Based on this broader evaluation, what does my trajectory look like, and is it leading me where I want to be, with a good enough distribution of outcomes? If not, what changes should I make?

最后，我会定期提醒自己评估发展轨迹，不仅要基于近期的成果，还要更全面地评估我积累的长期资产、承担的风险以及做出的牺牲。基于这种更全面的评估，我的发展轨迹是怎样的？它是否正引领我走向理想的未来，并取得足够均衡的成果？如果不是，我应该做出哪些改变？
